## OPEN — CLI command-surface residue (2026-10-21)
- [x] **RT-136 (M, SURFACE) — 26 config settings are accepted, defaulted and printed but nothing reads them.** Found by a config-surface audit (every `pub` field of every settings struct in `operant-core/src/config.rs`, counted against all non-test code in `crates/`; `#[cfg(test)]` items are brace-stripped, not truncated — v1 of the script truncated at the first test module and produced two false hits, `feed_seat_map` and `grant_ttl_days`'s sibling fields, which ARE read in gateway_runner.rs). The 24 users of `operant.example.toml` among them are the reason this matters: a key the template advertises and the binary ignores is a promise the operator cannot see broken (`[tui] landing_title` changes nothing; `[tools.tool_search] search_default_limit` is hardcoded as 10/25 at the tool). Full list and disposition below; the settings structs use `deny_unknown_fields`, so DELETING a key is a breaking change for existing configs — the sanctioned pattern is accept + warn (see the `agentmemory_*` shims), not removal.

  | group | fields | disposition |
  |---|---|---|
  | `[tools.stt]` | `groq_model`, `openai_model` | **WIRED iter-1122** — both call sites now resolve through `resolve_model` (per-call, config, default) |
  | `[tools.tool_search]` | `search_default_limit`, `max_search_limit` | hardcoded 10/25 in `ToolSearchTool::execute` — wire or warn |
  | TUI | `show_iterations`, `landing_title`, `prompt_placeholder`, `refresh_rate_ms`, `compact_width`, `medium_width` | the TUI reads six OTHER `[tui]` keys; these six have no reader (the placeholder string does not exist anywhere in the tree) |
  | `[skills]` | `template_name`, `template_description` | no reader — the skill creator does not use them |
  | `[pk]` | `sidecar_script`, `ndjson_socket`, `exec_timeout_secs` (+ the whole `pk` table) | vestigial: the kernel sidecar launches `python -m kernel_sidecar.server` from `KERNEL_SIDECAR_DIR`/`CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR`, and its timeout is `agent.request_timeout_secs` |
  | `[bylaws]` | `grant_ttl_days` | the doc comment calls it "LIVE (F2)"; nothing reads it, and the subsystem it names no longer exists — `org/seat_authority.rs` states "there is no grant ledger anymore — an approved plan IS the grant", so the TTL governs nothing (`has_grant` is structurally false) |
  | `[socialization]` | `turn_budget` | no reader (the agent's turn budget is a different mechanism) |
  | `[behavior]` | `max_consecutive_tool_only` | no reader — the guard it names does not exist |
  | `[tools]` | `event_channel_size`, `browser_binary_path` | no reader (channels are built with fixed capacities; the browser resolves its binary inside sourcehound) |
  | `[memory]` | `agentmemory_url`, `agentmemory_secret` | legacy shims; `agentmemory_auto_spawn` already warns |
  | `[tools.web]` | `search_url`, `exa_api_key`, `searxng_base_url` | ALREADY honest — `WebToolSettings::warn_legacy_keys` prints one line per key set (plan 11C1); they only look "unread" because the warning is the only reader |

  Also: the audit script is promoted to `scripts/audit-config-surface.py` (iter-1123) so the claim can be re-checked instead of re-derived.

  **Closed iter-1123** — resolution per group, chosen against the operator's OWN config: `~/.operant/operant.toml` already carries every one of these keys (it was copied from the template), and the settings structs are `deny_unknown_fields`, so DELETION would hard-fail the next run. Every key is therefore accepted and reported:
  - `[tools.stt]` — wired (iter-1122), not warned.
  - `[tools.tool_search]` limits, the six `[tui]` keys, `[skills]` template pair, `[pk]`, `[bylaws] grant_ttl_days`, `[socialization]`, `[agent] max_consecutive_tool_only`, `[tools] event_channel_size`/`browser_binary_path`, `[memory] agentmemory_*` — warned by `AppConfig::unused_setting_warnings` (one line per key whose value differs from the default; a clean start is silent), and removed from `operant.example.toml` so a new config never learns them.
  - `[tools.tool_search]` was a wiring candidate (hardcoded 10/25 in `ToolSearchTool::execute`). Left warned, not wired: the limits are model-facing micro-tuning, and a non-vacuous test would have to drive `register_builtin_tools` with a full registry to prove the production path reads them. Recorded as the trade rather than half-wired.

  Completeness check: `scripts/audit-config-surface.py` reports **24** candidate fields across 41 settings structs; all 24 are accounted for — 20 by `AppConfig::unused_setting_warnings`, 3 (`[tools.web] search_url`/`exa_api_key`/`searxng_base_url`) by the pre-existing plan-11C1 migration warning, and the `pk` field itself by the `[pk]` table line. Re-run it after any settings change; `--check` exits non-zero when a NEW candidate appears. **CORRECTED (iter-1153, RT-159)** — the count is now **27** (iter-1140's config retirement deleted the schema files that had been the last mention of three live settings: `[memory] audit_enabled`, `[memory] response_cache_enabled`, `[tools.web] tavily_api_key`), and the `--check` mode did NOT do what this sentence said: it exited non-zero whenever ANY candidate existed, so it was permanently red and could not express "new". The script now carries a baseline and fails only on a candidate outside it.

  Residuals: (a) the warnings reach stderr/`operant config show` runs, not the TUI's config pane — the TUI log shows them once at boot; (b) the keys can only be DELETED in a major release (or with a `--migrate-config` sweep), since every existing config that carries one would otherwise stop loading; (c) `scripts/audit-config-surface.py` is a heuristic (identifier-occurrence, not type-aware) — a field read only via a macro or reflection would be missed, which is why the script prints candidates for review rather than a verdict.


- [x] **RT-137 (M, BEHAVIOUR) — `operant tools disable <name>` changed nothing.** The CLI wrote `tool_state.json` next to the database and NOTHING read it: the runtime's disabled set came only from the TOML `[tools] disabled_tools`. An operator who disabled a tool — a noisy one, a dangerous one — kept getting it, and the CLI reported success. Same class as RT-136 on a different surface: a command that says it did something and did not.

  **Fixed iter-1124** — the state file moved into core (`operant-core/src/tools/tool_state.rs`: path, load, save, the union `disabled_tool_names`, and `apply_disabled_tools`, which the registry build calls with the AFT-replaced names). The CLI and the runtime now read the SAME file, so `operant tools disable` removes the tool from the toolset the agent gets. `operant tools list` now shows the FULL registry with a `[disabled]` marker and an "N registered, M enabled" count (before, the listing filtered disabled tools OUT and then printed a marker for a tool it never printed); `operant tools enable` says when the TOML still disables the tool.

  Tests: `tools::tool_state::tests::a_cli_disabled_tool_is_removed_from_the_registry` drives the production function into a real registry and asserts the tool is gone from the model-visible set and still present in the full listing — mutation-checked (dropping the state-file union from `apply_disabled_tools` makes it fail). E2E against a debug binary: `operant tools disable browser` writes the file and the listing reports "83 registered, 82 enabled" with the marker on `browser`.

  Residual: `operant tools enable` only clears the CLI file — a tool the TOML disables stays disabled on purpose (the CLI never rewrites the operator's TOML), and the command now says so instead of claiming success.

- [x] **RT-138 (M, FEATURE GAP) — the whole `operant hooks` family was a façade, and the hook registry only existed with the harness on.** Three defects in one surface. (1) `operant hooks list|test|revoke|doctor` read `~/.operant/data/hooks/*.hook` — a store NOTHING wrote and NOTHING read: the family could never do anything, and `hooks doctor` claimed "All hooks are registered and ready. Hooks execute during agent sessions when matching events fire." (2) The runtime's `HookRegistry` was created only when `[harness].enabled = true` (`main.rs`), so in a normal install NO hook could fire — and of the nine `HookEvent` variants only `AgentStart`/`AgentEnd`/`TurnStart`/`TurnEnd` are ever emitted (`GatewayStartup`, `SessionStart`, `SessionEnd`, `Command` and the `Hooks` catch-all slot are never emitted outside tests — the agent loop emits exactly those four, in `agent/run.rs`). (3) The README claimed "hermes-agent hook parity (before/after tool, turn, memory hooks)": there are no before/after-tool hooks anywhere in the tree, and the "memory hooks" are provider wiring, not hooks.

  **Fixed iter-1125** — shell hooks are real now: `operant-core/src/shell_hooks.rs` owns the store (`<name>.hook`, JSON `{"event","command"}`), the loader, the writer, the runner, and `install_shell_hooks`, which the agent build calls. The registry is created unconditionally; the harness bridge is registered on it when the harness is on. The CLI gained `operant hooks add --event <e> -- <cmd>`, `test` now RUNS the command and reports its exit code (it used to print the file), and `doctor` reports broken files instead of a blanket "ready". A hook naming an event the agent never emits is refused at write time and skipped at load time — a hook that can never fire is the one promise this surface must not make.

  Tests: `shell_hooks::tests::install_shell_hooks_loads_the_hooks_directory` drives the production path end to end (hooks directory → load → register → `emit(AgentEnd)` → the command really ran, observed through a marker file) — mutation-checked (making `install_shell_hooks` register nothing makes it fail). `a_registered_hook_runs_when_its_event_fires` covers the same path without the directory; `a_broken_file_does_not_silence_the_good_ones` covers a corrupt file and a file naming an unemitted event.

  Residual: the README's hook line now names the four real events and the shell-hook command; **tool-level and memory-level hooks remain unimplemented** — the registry shape supports them (a `HookEvent` variant plus a call site in the tool/memory path), but that is a feature, and it is logged here rather than claimed in the README.

- [x] **RT-139 (M, FEATURE GAP) — the SOP playbooks were operator-only: the agent could not read them.** `operant sop list|validate|show` read `~/.operant/sops/*.toml` with a private loader inside the CLI. NOTHING else in the tree read that directory, and the agent had no path to it at all — so a playbook the harness could have followed sat unused, and the loader existed in exactly one place (the CLI), which is why no reader was ever added.

  **Fixed iter-1126** — the store moved into core (`operant-core/src/sops.rs`: `Sop`, `sops_dir`, `discover_sops`), the CLI uses it, and the agent got a `sop` tool (list with no name, read one by name) registered with the builtins. The directory is now reachable from the agent loop, and the CLI and the agent read the SAME files — the operator's list and the agent's view cannot drift.

  Tests: `sops::tests::sops_are_discovered_sorted_with_their_description` (discovery, sorting, description, non-TOML files ignored); `tools::sop_tool::tests::listing_and_reading_an_sop_works` (list, read, unknown name); and the registration assertion in `tools::builtin::tests::test_register_builtin_tools_with_sub_agent` — mutation-checked: dropping `registry.register(SopTool)` from the builtins makes that test fail, so the tool cannot silently stop reaching the agent. E2E against a debug binary: `operant sop list` and `operant sop show` read a hand-written playbook through the shared loader.

  Residual: there is still no WRITER — the operator hand-writes the TOML files (no `operant sop add`), and the `sop` tool is read-on-demand rather than an injection into the system prompt, so a playbook is consulted only when the agent thinks to look for one.

- [x] **RT-140 (M, FEATURE GAP) — `operant webhook` records subscriptions nothing dispatches to.** The whole family was inert: `subscribe` wrote `~/.operant/data/webhook_subscriptions.json` and NOTHING in the tree read it, and `test` printed "This would send a POST request with an HMAC-SHA256 signature to the webhook URL using the configured secret" — the words "would send" were doing all the work; no request was made. The subscription's fields (`prompt`, `events`, `skills`, `deliver`, `deliver_chat_id`, `deliver_only`) promise a per-route event pipeline that does not exist.

  **Partly fixed iter-1127** — the store moved into core (`operant-core/src/gateway/webhook_subscriptions.rs`: the subscription type, the loader/writer, `sign_body` in the format the INBOUND adapter already accepts, and `post_json`), and `operant webhook test` now really POSTs the ping — signed with the subscription's secret when it has one — and reports the status and body. `operant webhook subscribe` now says plainly that the destination is recorded only.

  **Fixed iter-1132 — the DISPATCH, in the R1 (inbound) model.** The owner delegated the model choice ("choose recommended best decisions on your own"), and the fields decide it: `deliver`, `deliver_chat_id` and `deliver_only` only mean anything when WE receive the event and answer it somewhere, and `prompt`/`skills` shape how the AGENT handles the event — so the subscription is an INBOUND route the external service posts to, and the answer is delivered to the target. The reasoning, and why R2 (outbound) was rejected, are in **AD-042**.

  What landed:
  - **The route.** The subscription claims a path segment under `/webhook/`. The route is the LAST PATH SEGMENT of the subscribed URL (`https://example.com/webhook/orders` claims `orders`), with `operant webhook subscribe --route <name>` to name one explicitly. A segment that is not a plain path token claims nothing.
  - **The event.** The event name is the payload's `event` (or `type`) field; a payload that names none is a "message" event, which is the CLI's default. A subscription that does not list the event does not apply to it.
  - **The answer's destination.** The inbound channel cannot carry a reply (the webhook adapter is inbound-only), so the agent's answer was dropped on the floor — the event was handled and the operator never learned the outcome. `deliver` (`platform:chat_id`, with `deliver_chat_id` overriding the chat) now names where it goes, and the delivery ledger records the delivery there.
  - **The admin gate.** The gate is a USER gate, and a signature-verified webhook event has no user — but every webhook event was refused with "You are not authorized to use this bot." in any deployment that configures `admins`, which is every real deployment. An AUTHENTICATED event now bypasses the gate; an unauthenticated one is still refused.
  - **Per-route secrets.** A subscription with its own secret is verified against THAT secret, so two routes can use different ones; without one, `[gateway] webhooks_secret` applies.
  - **`deliver_only`** delivers the EVENT body without running the agent, and without the agent's prompt wrapped around it.

  Tests: `webhook::tests::a_subscription_route_dispatches_the_event` (a real HTTP POST through the adapter against the real store — the production path, not a helper), `gateway::tests::an_authenticated_event_is_not_refused_by_the_admin_gate`, `gateway::tests::a_delivery_target_moves_the_answer_to_the_named_platform`, and four unit tests in `webhook_subscriptions::tests` (the route derivation, the delivery target, the prompt composition, the event filter).

  Residuals, both recorded rather than hidden: the Slack- and WhatsApp-shaped payloads take their own forwarding branches in the adapter and do NOT pick up a subscription (only the generic JSON/text path dispatches); and a subscription's `skills` are NAMED to the agent in the event — the agent reads them with the skills tool — rather than being a hard filter on the loaded skill set, because the gateway builds its agent once with a fixed skill manager.

- [x] **RT-141 (L, FRAGMENTATION) — the binary carried a second, much larger config surface that was never loaded. It is retired.** `operant_config::schema::Config` (the aggregate in `crates/operant-config/src/schema/`) has no production loader: `Config::load_or_init` is called only from its own tests, the one production-typed consumer (`operant-providers::provider_runtime_options_from_config`) is called only from its own tests, and `operant-core/src/doctor.rs` already records the same gap from the other side. The live config is `operant_core::config::AppConfig`. 123 of the schema's 145 structs (645 fields) have no production reader outside the crate — `python3 scripts/audit-parallel-config.py` re-derives the counts.

  **Not an operator-facing break** — `operant.example.toml` advertises only tables the live loader accepts, and the settings structs use `deny_unknown_fields`, so a schema-shaped table in the operator's file is REJECTED rather than silently ignored. The risk is reader confusion and future divergence: a setting added to the schema surface looks live to the next reader and is unreachable, while a setting the operator needs goes into the live `AppConfig` and the schema surface keeps claiming it.

  **Shipped iter-1128 (label + guard), retirement planned** — the schema module now says, in its first lines, that it is a spec and not the live config; a static guard test fails if any non-test file starts loading the aggregate, so the surface cannot start being loaded by accident; the audit (`docs/audit/2026-10-21-PARALLEL-CONFIG-SURFACE.md`) and the plan (`docs/plans/plan-2026-10-21-config-schema-retirement.md`) carry the evidence, the options (retire the surface / adopt it as the spine / keep both) and the recommendation.

  This repeats a finding the repo already had but never tracked: `docs/R40-12-13-WIRE-OR-RETIRE-REVIEW.md` reached the same conclusion ("the 1,043-field schema is dead") and recommended "pick a winner"; that recommendation was never executed and was never recorded in this ledger.

  **The owner's decision (delegated) was Option 1 — retire. Step 1 shipped in iter-1138.** The AGGREGATE is gone: `schema::Config` (~30 sections, in `schema/proxy.rs`), its loader and its whole impl (`schema/config_impl.rs`, 1.9K lines), the v0→v1 migration of that shape (`migration.rs`'s `V1Compat`) and its 7.1K-line test file (`schema/core/core_tests.rs`) — about 9.7K lines, and with them the SECOND loader, the second `config.toml` resolution and the second migration. The two production-typed consumers of the aggregate (`operant-providers::provider_runtime_options_from_config` and `operant-providers::auth::{from_config, state_dir_from_config}`) were called only from their own tests and went with it. The guard is now stronger: it fails if `schema::Config` is USED anywhere in production code, and a second test fails if the type is DEFINED again.

  **What the live surface actually is, measured rather than assumed** (the aggregate's retirement is only safe if the types the live config composes are known): the production code outside `operant-config` names exactly 12 schema types and 5 schema functions — `ProxyConfig`, `ProxyScope`, `ObservabilityConfig`, `ModelProviderConfig`, `FallbackProviderConfig`, `ModelRouteConfig`, `EmbeddingRouteConfig`, `ReliabilityConfig`, `MultimodalConfig`, `ModelPricing`, `MemoryPolicyConfig`, `SearchMode`, plus `build_runtime_proxy_client_with_timeouts`, `apply_runtime_proxy_to_builder`, `build_runtime_proxy_client`, `client_config` and `set_runtime_proxy_config`. Everything else in `schema/` is the dormant surface the audit counted (123 structs, 645 fields).

  **Step 2 shipped in iter-1140 — the dormant SECTION structs are gone too.** The 17 wholly-dormant schema files are deleted (`agent_cfg`, `backup`, `channels_cfg`, `delegate`, `gateway`, `hardware`, `mcp`, `ops_cfg`, `runners`, `scheduler`, `security_cfg`, `skills`, `sop`, `stt`, `tts`, `tunnels`, `web_tools`), the six files that hold a live type are trimmed to it, and the crate's own dead modules go with them (`scattered_types`, `comment_writer`, `domain_matcher`, `pairing`, `typed_value`, `api_error`, `validation_warnings`, `workspace`, `cost`, `platform`, `migration`). The compiler was the oracle: every item it reported as unreachable after the deletions was removed, and the items the live types still reference (the `default_*` helpers, the `HasPropKind` impls, the `Configurable` derive and its support traits) were kept. `operant-config` is 7.1K lines, down from ~31K — the crate is now the live types and the derive machinery, not a second config system. The audit script re-derives the residue: 10 schema structs, 1 of them flagged (a false positive — `EmbeddingRouteConfig` is carried by the live `ProvidersConfig`).

  **Step 3 shipped in iter-1141 — the derive machinery is GONE and the row is CLOSED.** The `Configurable` derive existed for ONE reason: the retired aggregate's property machinery (`secret_fields`, `prop_fields`, `integration_descriptor`, `nested_option_entries`). The live types derived it only for the `#[secret]` and `#[prefix]` attributes, and nothing called what it generated. The derive is dropped from the six live types, the `#[secret]`/`#[prefix]` attributes go with it, and the `operant-macros` crate (1.3K lines) is deleted from the workspace along with the crate-level `helpers.rs` it needed and the `config`/`security` shim modules the macro's generated paths resolved through. `traits.rs` keeps only the two items that outlived it (`PropKind` and `HasPropKind`).

  **The whole parallel config surface is retired.** `operant-config` is now ~5K lines and holds the live types, the provider config, the security policy and the encrypted secret store — and one config system, not two.

  The residue that the retirement exposed is recorded as its own row: **RT-154** — the `#[secret]` marker was the only thing that ever claimed the config's provider keys were encrypted, and nothing in the live path honoured it. The field's doc now says what is true.

- [x] **RT-158 (M, SECRET-AT-REST WINDOW) — the files the setup wizard and the OAuth store write were world-readable for the instant between the write and the chmod.** `operant_core::fs_secrets::write_secret_file` — the writer for the OAuth token store (`oauth/store.rs`) and for the setup wizard's config TOML (`cmd_setup.rs`, which holds the API key the operator has just typed) — opened the file with the umask default (0644 on a stock system), wrote the secret INTO it, and only then chmod'ed it to 0600. The window is short, but it is exactly the class R40-1 closed in 2026-09-27 ("secret files created 0600 at open not chmod'd after the write"), and the repo already carries the FIXED pattern in two other places: `operant-config`'s identically named writer ("Write a secret file owner-only (0o600) in a single open(2) — a plain `fs::write` followed by `set_permissions` leaves a window where the umask default (typically 0644) exposes the key") and `operant-cli`'s `.env` writer ("`File::create` applies the umask default … `OpenOptionsExt::mode` is applied by the same `open(2)` that creates the file, so there is no window at all"). Three implementations of one job; two were fixed and this one was missed — a fragmentation, not a new bug.

  The second writer with the same window: `config.rs`'s `persist_config_key` (the `operant config set` path) wrote its temp file with `std::fs::write` — umask default — and chmod'ed it to the original's mode afterwards. That config file can carry `client.api_key` and `[providers.models.*].api_key`.

  **Fixed** — `operant-core`'s writer now creates the file OWNER-ONLY in the same `open(2)` that creates it (`create_owner_only`), and tightens an EXISTING file BEFORE the write (an existing file keeps its mode when it is opened, so a loose file would otherwise hold the new secret while still being world-readable). `persist_config_key` writes its temp file through the same owner-only writer and only then relaxes it to the original file's mode.

  **Test** — `fs_secrets::tests::the_file_is_owner_only_before_a_single_byte_is_written` opens the file through the owner-only helper and asserts the mode is already 0600 with ZERO bytes written. Mutation-checked: dropping the `.mode(0o600)` from the creating open makes it fail with "expected 0o600, got 644" — it observes exactly the window the old sequence left open.

  **What the test does NOT prove, stated honestly**: it pins the CREATION mode of the helper, not the mode of a file mid-write (no end-state assertion can — the old sequence ended at 0600 too). The closure is structural: the mode is applied by the creating `open(2)`, and the writer is the helper's only caller, so the clippy gate's dead-code check fails if it is ever bypassed.

The copy had drifted: it set `RUSTFLAGS="-L native=$LOCAL_DIR/lib"` and dropped the ONNX Runtime flags that `dev-env.sh` adds — `-L native=$ORT_DIR/lib` and, decisively, `-C link-arg=-Wl,-rpath,$HOME/.local/lib/operant`.

  **The consequence.** A binary built through `check.sh` carried no RUNPATH, so `ldd` reported `libonnxruntime.so.1 => not found` and the binary exited 127 in any shell that had not sourced `dev-env.sh` — including the self-test itself, the TUI corpus runner, and the operator's shell. The self-test reported **10 failed steps and 70 corpus "drifts"**, every one of them the string "error while loading shared libraries: libonnxruntime.so.1". The corpus drifts were the scary part: they look exactly like a rendering regression (70 changed screens), and the ACTUAL cause was a missing library. A gate whose failures are all one cause is a gate reporting a symptom 80 times.

  **The system-level fix, not the symptom-level one.** The environment now has ONE source: `check.sh` SOURCES `dev-env.sh` (which already owned the libclang resolver, the ONNX flags, the RUNPATH, the pkg-config path, the LD_LIBRARY_PATH and the PATH additions). The hand-rolled copy is gone — 85 lines deleted, not patched. `dev-env.sh` gained the two things only `check.sh` had (`-L native=$LOCAL_DIR/lib` for the repo's own `libsonic.a`, and `CARGO_INCREMENTAL=0`), so nothing was lost in the merge. `check.sh`'s `LOCAL_DIR` fallback to one developer's machine (RT-165) went with it.

  **Verified, not asserted.** The rebuilt `target/release/operant` carries `RUNPATH [/home/ishanp/.local/lib/operant]` and runs under `env -i` (no PATH, no LD_LIBRARY_PATH, nothing inherited) — which is the check that matters, because "works in my shell" is what hid this for as long as it existed.

  The rule: two copies of one environment disagree; the gate that reads the copy is the one that breaks.

- [x] **RT-155 (L, RECORD-VS-CODE) — the genome doctor's staleness check did not do what the ledger said it did, so the documented close-out pattern could never converge.** RT-125 (iter-1111) recorded: "the doc MAY carry a 40-hex HEAD sha, and it is only stale when a commit since then touched something outside docs/ or the configured role paths — so the close-out pattern is `genome handoff --write` and commit the snapshot together with worklog/ledger edits (a commit carrying only docs never invalidates it)". **The code did none of that.** The vendored tool compared the snapshot's sha to HEAD literally (`if heads and heads[0] != head`), so the commit that CARRIES the snapshot always moved HEAD past the sha the snapshot names — the check was red after every close-out, and no amount of regenerating could make it green. (The ledger's claim that the fix was "mirrored into the skill copy" was also not true: the skill's `src/10_doctor.py` and its built `scripts/genome` both carried the literal comparison.)

  **Fixed (iter-1143)** — the check now asks the question the ledger says it asks: the snapshot is stale only when a commit SINCE the sha it names touched something outside `docs/` or a configured role path. A code commit invalidates it; a docs-only close-out does not. A snapshot whose named commit is not in the history (a rebase, a shallow clone) is reported as "cannot be compared" rather than silently treated as current.

  The change was made in the SOURCE (`~/.agents/skills/project-genome/src/10_doctor.py`), the skill's built artifact was regenerated with the VERSION bumped (`2026.10.21-2`, the release checksum guard requires it), and this repo's vendored copy was re-synced from the built artifact — so `genome upgrade --apply` is a no-op rather than a silent revert.

  **Verified both directions.** The close-out commit (`docs/handoff/STATE.md` + the worklog) leaves the doctor HEALTHY ("state snapshot a6d6ca79 is current: only documentation changed since it"), and a snapshot pointed at a code-era commit is reported as stale with the count of the non-documentation paths that changed ("61 non-documentation path(s) changed since"). The skill's own suite is green (34/34).

- [x] **RT-168 (M, DUPLICATION) — two `CopyTargetKind` enums in the TUI, one with tests and no production caller, one with production callers and no tests.** Found by an autonomous dead-code sweep (2026-10-21): removing `VisibleCopyTarget`'s unread `kind_label`/`copied_notice` fields left `CopyTargetKind::label()` and `copied_notice()` with no production caller, and tracing those methods found the duplication.

  `crates/operant-cli/src/tui/operant_markdown/markdown_types.rs:30` defines `CopyTargetKind` with `Math { display: bool }`, and it is the one the tree uses: `operant_model/prepared.rs:12`, `operant_ui/mod.rs:152` and `render/selection.rs:266` all import it. `crates/operant-cli/src/tui/copy_targets.rs:82` defines a second `CopyTargetKind` with `Math` (no payload) and near-identical `label()`/`copied_notice()` implementations carrying doc comments and `#[must_use]`. Two modules cite `copy_targets.rs` in `[port-decision]`/`[port-excision]` comments (`operant_model/vendor_types.rs:18`, `operant_model/prepared.rs:8-12`), which record that the operant-markdown spelling is the canonical home and that the copy_targets.rs one predates the W2 markdown port.

  **The cost, concretely.** Two spellings of one concept, where the surviving-caller set and the surviving-test set sit on opposite sides: the operant-markdown methods have production callers (`prepared.rs` matches the variants) and no direct test for the label behaviour, while copy_targets.rs's methods have a real test suite (`copy_targets.rs:688-710`, five kinds x label x notice plus the empty-language fallback) and no production caller. A reader cannot tell from either file which one is load-bearing, and the next port decisions are made against comments rather than a compiler.

  **Not fixed here on purpose** — deleting `copy_targets.rs`'s enum is not a mechanical cleanup: the same file defines `CopyTarget` and the region-extraction helpers its own tests drive, so superseding the enum means first proving those are superseded by `operant_markdown::{RawCopyTarget, CopyTarget}` + `extract_copy_targets`; the `Math { display: bool }` vs `Math` difference is semantic (display-vs-inline math), not cosmetic; and the two `[port-decision]` comments must move in the same commit or the drift they exist to prevent is recreated. Full measurement, classification and the recommended fix shape: `docs/audit/2026-10-21-copytargetkind-duplication-and-the-54-dead-code-warnings-fro.md`.

- [x] **RT-169 (M, GATE COVERAGE) — the rustdoc gate cannot see a `#[cfg(test)]` doc link, and that is where the port's doc rot accumulated.** Found while closing out iter-1165: `RenderStateTestGuard` in `crates/operant-cli/src/tui/operant_ui/mod.rs` carried the doc line "Guard for [`render_state_test_lock`]" — an intra-doc link to a function that was never ported and does not exist in the tree — and the gate (iter-1158's `scripts/check.sh doc` under `-D rustdoc::broken-intra-doc-links`) never reported it.

  `--document-private-items` reads as "document everything", and it documents every private item the profile contains — but a binary target's doc build runs with `cfg(test)` OFF, so a `#[cfg(test)]` item is not in the AST rustdoc sees. Test-only scaffolding is therefore a class of documentation the gate cannot read, and `cargo clippy --all-targets` (which compiles `cfg(test)`) found the code while the doc gate could not see its docs.

  **Measured, not assumed** (iter-1166; the full measurement is RG-013). A probe was appended to `operant_ui/mod.rs`:

  ```rust
  #[cfg(test)]
  /// Links to [`a_function_that_does_not_exist_anywhere`].
  pub(crate) struct ProbeStruct { _x: u8 }
  ```

  The exact gate command (`cargo doc -p operant-cli --bin operant --no-deps --document-private-items` under the gate's `-D` flags) reported **0** matches for the probe's names; the same probe without the `#[cfg(test)]` attribute is reported. So it is the attribute that hides it, not the link's shape. The probe was removed and the file verified byte-identical to its pre-probe state.

  **Not fixed here on purpose** — adding `--cfg test` to the doc gate is a real change to what the gate means, not a flag tweak: it would surface every existing `#[cfg(test)]` doc link in the workspace at once, and the iter-1158 sweep found those classes are large (~70 links across five crates in four classes in the PRODUCTION profile; the `cfg(test)` profile is unmeasured). That is an iteration of its own with a baseline of its own — the same shape as `audit-lint-suppressions.py` (iter-1164). Until then, a green doc gate certifies the production profile only.

  Full record: `docs/regressions/RG-013-the-doc-gate-cannot-see-a-cfg-test-item-which-is-where-doc-r.md`.

Both of those were diagnosed as the test reading the machine rather than a fixture; this one had no failure names captured because the command's failure output was not preserved (the run was one of three interleaved `cargo test` invocations sharing one `target/`), so the specific tests were UNKNOWN. The row asked the next reader to capture the `^failures:` block before re-running anything, and that happened: at iter-1176 a `cargo test -p operant-core --lib` run reported `2458 passed / 1 failed`, the block was preserved, and it named `tools::memory_tools::tests::test_memory_store_and_recall` — which led straight to the cause. **It was not a flake.** It is a test-isolation defect, diagnosed and fixed as **RT-173**: the test reads a process-global `WRITE_ORIGIN` it never pinned, so a leaked "background_review" origin makes it fail with "Refused: background review does not write memory" instead of "No memory backend" — a different assertion, in a serializer whose order is not fixed, hence roughly one run in ten. The methodology this row contributed (capture the names, then read them) is what closed it. The ORIGINAL 2-failure occurrence is still unexplained, because its names were never captured and two `cargo test` invocations against one `target/` is exactly the interference pattern AGENTS.md fleet rule 5 forbids; what is closed is the CLASS and the recurrence path, not that specific run.

- [x] **RT-154 (M, FALSE PROMISE) — the config's provider keys were marked `#[secret]`, and the only code that honoured the marker was code that never ran.** Found while retiring the derive (RT-141's last step): `ModelProviderConfig::api_key` carried `#[secret]` and a doc comment promising "Stored via the OS keyring when possible; never commit it to config.toml directly", and `api_keys` carried the same marker with a comment saying "each element is encrypted on save exactly like `api_key`".

  **Neither was true in production.** The `#[secret]` marker is read by exactly one thing: the `Configurable` derive's `secret_fields()`, whose only caller was the config AGGREGATE's `save()` — the surface that was never loaded in production (RT-141). The live write path is `operant_core::config::persist_config_key`, which writes the value as given; the live loader never decrypts one (the `SecretStore` decrypt path is called only from the provider auth-profile file). So `operant config set providers.models.openai.api_key sk-...` wrote the key into `operant.toml` in PLAINTEXT, and the field's own documentation said it would not.

  **What is true, stated now.** The config file's secrets are plaintext in a 0600 file. The ENCRYPTED store is the provider auth-profile file (`operant-providers`' `auth-profiles.json`, written through `SecretStore`) — that is where a long-lived OAuth token belongs. The field's doc comment now says exactly this, and the `#[secret]` marker is gone with the derive that read it.

  Not fixed here on purpose: making the config file's secrets encrypted at rest is a FEATURE with a migration (the loader would have to decrypt `enc2:` values, the writer would have to encrypt, and every existing plaintext value would need a migration path). It is recorded with that shape so the next agent does not have to re-derive it. The `SecretStore` machinery is already there and already proven by the auth-profile store.

  Residuals: (a) `operant connect` and the TUI's `/connect` write keys to `~/.operant/auth.json` and `~/.operant/.env` in plaintext too — the same class, one layer over; (b) `operant.example.toml` does not advertise an encrypted-config format, so nothing in the template promises one. **(b) closed iter-1181:** the template carried no encryption promise, but it also carried no plaintext WARNING at the operator's `api_key` line — so the same false-advertising risk sat one layer out, where the reader is the person most likely to rely on it. The line now states the value is plaintext in a 0600 file, that nothing encrypts it and the loader never decrypts it, and where a long-lived OAuth token belongs instead. Locked by `crates/operant-core/tests/example_template_loads.rs::the_template_does_not_promise_encryption_for_secret_config_values`, which scans the template for the RT-154 wording (`stored via the os keyring`, `encrypted on save`, `encrypted at rest`, …) and fails if any returns; a second test injects the original phrase back and asserts the gate catches it. **RED proved by mutation** — planting the RT-154 sentence at line 27 makes the gate name `line 27: promises 'stored via the os keyring'`. operant-core 2460 passed / 0 failed; the two other template tests still pass, fmt and clippy clean. **(a) closed iter-1185:** `~/.operant/.env` is written 0600 (the atomic-write path in `env_store.rs` creates with 0600 in the same `open(2)` and propagates a failure to tighten — already correct), but `auth.json` was written with `std::fs::write`, which applies the umask default: 0644 on a stock box. Measured on the live home: `.env` 0600, `auth.json` **0644**. So the keys `operant connect` and the TUI's `/connect` save sat world-readable for the file's whole life — the same class as the template's promise, one layer over, where the reader is any local account. `AuthStore::save` now routes through `operant_core::fs_secrets::write_secret_file`, which creates 0600 and tightens an existing loose file BEFORE writing, so an operator already carrying a 0644 `auth.json` has it repaired on the next save rather than requiring a manual `chmod`. Every production credential write goes through `AuthStore::set` → `save` (the three call sites are `tui/app/key_handling.rs:263,326,376`), so the fix covers the whole surface. The live 0644 file was tightened by hand in the same iteration. `settings.json` is 0644 correctly: it holds the provider list and `api_base` URLs, no keys. Locked by `crates/operant-cli/src/tui/adapter_types/auth.rs::credential_file_tests` — `a_saved_api_key_is_written_owner_only_not_umask_default` and `a_previously_world_readable_auth_file_is_tightened_on_save` (a create-only fix silently passes on the operator who already has the loose file, so the second test plants 0644 first). **RED proved by mutation** — restoring `std::fs::write` makes the first test report `got 644`; the file was restored byte-identical afterwards. operant-cli 1645 passed / 0 failed / 7 ignored.

  Test: `cmd_doctor::checks_tools::operant_binary_tests::the_skills_hub_check_never_asks_for_an_unfollowable_fix` — mutation-checked (restoring the old advice makes it fail).

  Residual (recorded, not fixed): the hub-install path itself is missing — `skills_tool.rs` protects "hub-installed" skills from the background review, but no install path puts a skill under `.hub/`, so that protection never applies to anything. Making the marketplace install into `.hub/<name>/` would give it teeth, but it changes WHERE `operant skills install` puts skills (the operator's flat layout today), so it is a behaviour decision, not a patch.

  **Fixed iter-1130** — the check now classifies the copies: one → OK; several with identical build times and sizes → OK ("N identical copies on PATH"); several that differ → the copy the shell will launch (first on PATH) is named, and the older one is named as the stale one to replace. So the stale copy could not execute at all, and "stale" understated it. Deployed at iter-1174 per the AGENTS.md protocol: provenance gate passed (last source commit `c2a645d3` 00:24:57 +05:30 < artifact mtime 00:30:22, `git diff` empty over `*.rs`/`Cargo.*` to tip `0449e15b`), the previous binary backed up to `/usr/local/bin/operant.broken-oct17` first, then `sudo -A cp` + rename-over `mv`. Verified: `/usr/local/bin/operant --version` = `operant 0.2.1 (memory-wire fd704c8)`, md5 `6cf6a6d1b1401f2c4b980a49676b4de4` identical to `~/.local/bin/operant` and `target/release/operant`, `readelf -d` shows RUNPATH `/home/ishanp/.local/lib/operant` resolving, and `doctor`/`profile list` run through the system path. The live Holon driver — `~/holon/config/drivers/operant.toml:19` and the `cmd` at `~/holon/holon.toml:44` — also invokes `/home/ishanp/.local/bin/operant`. The only files naming `/usr/local/bin/operant` are historical: chat logs, trajectory JSON, and `~/holon/backups/holon-backup-*/` snapshots. No live config, unit, cron entry, or running process (`/proc/*/exe`) used the system path. NOTE for the record: AD-003 is STALE on this point — its "Correction to earlier records" says "the live driver is `/usr/local/bin/operant run -c ...`", but the live driver TOML invokes `~/.local/bin`. AD-003 is immutable once numbered (RG-002), so this is recorded here rather than by editing it. `~/.local/bin` precedes `/usr/local/bin` on PATH (positions 13/17 vs 18), so the shadowing rationale was sound but moot.

- [x] **RT-144 (M, FALSE CLAIM) — `operant gateway status` said "not running" while the gateway was running.** The live box runs the gateway under systemd (`operant gateway run` via `operant-gateway.service`), and the status command's running check read ONE source: `~/.operant/gateway.pid`. The unit was `active` with a live main pid, yet the command printed "Runtime: not running" — and then, because the pid file was absent, it DELETED it (`if !running && pid_path.exists()`), so the next run had even less to go on. The pid file is written at the end of `start_gateway`, so it is also briefly absent during a restart, and it is removed by any status run whose recorded pid had gone stale.

  **Fixed iter-1131** — the running check consults BOTH sources: the pid file (when that process is alive) and the systemd unit (`is-active` + `MainPID`). The status line names the pid and where it came from ("Runtime: running (PID 4242, systemd)"). The stale pid file is now only removed when NEITHER source says the gateway is up. The classification is a pure function (`classify_runtime`), so it is tested without touching the process.

  Tests: `cmd_gateway::tests::a_systemd_gateway_counts_as_running_without_a_pid_file` (the case that was broken), `the_pid_file_wins_when_both_sources_agree`, `nothing_running_reports_not_running` — mutation-checked (ignoring the systemd pid makes the first fail).

  Residual: none in the stop path. I first wrote that `operant gateway stop` stops only the pid-file process — that was WRONG, and the correction matters because it is the operator's way to stop the gateway: `cmd_stop` runs `systemctl --user stop operant-gateway` FIRST, then kills the pid-file process, and only falls back to the in-process stop when neither worked. Start and stop are symmetric. (The row was published with the wrong residual; it is corrected here rather than left standing.)

- [x] **RT-145 (M, ORDER-DEPENDENT TEST) — the test suite reached GitHub, and a background update check broke a proxy guard that has nothing to do with GitHub.** `client::tests::env_proxy_is_ignored_by_the_provider_client` (RT-131's guard: provider traffic must never follow `HTTP(S)_PROXY`/`ALL_PROXY`) FAILED in the full `operant-core` suite and PASSED in isolation — reproducibly, on a clean `origin/main` (verified by stashing the working tree: 2442 passed, 1 failed). The capture listener in that test counts ANY connection, and the connection was not provider traffic: it was `CONNECT api.github.com:443`, a request made by the BACKGROUND auto-update check. `binary_updater::kick_session_update` fires on the first use of the aft/sourcehound integration, spawns `gh api`, and `gh` resolves through the process's proxy variables — so the kick landed inside the proxy guard's window, through the guard's own capture listener, and the guard counted it as a violation. The update check is a fire-and-forget background task, so it lands in whatever test is running at the time: a test suite that makes a real network call, on a timing nobody controls.

  **Fixed iter-1132** — the BACKGROUND check does not run in a test build (`cfg!(test)`), and `OPERANT_NO_AUTO_UPDATE=1` turns it off in any binary (the operator's escape hatch, and what `scripts/self-test.sh` exports for the suite). The EXPLICIT paths (`operant doctor`'s integration check, `operant update --integrations`) are untouched: they are operator-initiated, and the fake-`gh` test drives exactly that path. The rule lives in one function, `auto_update_allowed_in(is_test_build)`, so it is testable without a test build.

  Tests: `binary_updater::tests::the_background_update_check_is_off_in_a_test_build`, `the_operator_can_turn_the_background_check_off`; and the gate itself — `cargo test -p operant-core --lib` is green again (2452 passed, 0 failed) and the proxy guard passes IN THE FULL SUITE, which is where it failed.

  Residual: the doctor's integration check still shells out to `gh` when a test drives it (a slow, network-dependent path, not a failure). The `gh` subprocess honours the process's proxy variables by design — that is GitHub's client, not ours.

- [x] **RT-174 (M, VACUOUS GUARD) — the ENV-2 proxy guard counted a connection it could not attribute to the client it was guarding, so it failed on foreign traffic and would have passed on a real violation it could not see.** `client::tests::env_proxy_is_ignored_by_the_provider_client` (RT-131's guard) counted EVERY connection its capture listener accepted, while the six proxy variables it point at that listener are PROCESS-GLOBAL: a peer reaching GitHub through the process's own proxy env — RT-145 identified one as `gh api` from the background update check — lands on the same listener during the guard's window. So the guard's signal was `"someone, maybe not the client under test, connected to my port"`, which is not the assertion the test claims to make. Observed live: the guard failed in the full `operant-core` suite with `left: 1, right: 0` (the exact signature RT-145 recorded) while passing in isolation — the guard could be failed by traffic it does not test, and the same unattributed counter could equally have hidden a genuine provider re-routing behind a foreign connection that happened not to arrive. **Fixed iter-1186** — the capture listener now reads the request head and counts ONLY a connection carrying the provider client's own bearer credential, which a foreign `CONNECT api.github.com:443` does not. The marker is what makes the assertion attributable: the guard is now true iff the CLIENT UNDER TEST used the proxy. The mechanism was proved, not inferred: with `auto_update_allowed()` forced back on (the RT-145 disable reversed) the OLD assertion fails deterministically with `left: 1, right: 0` and the fixed one passes; and dropping `.no_proxy()` from `OpenAIClient::new` still fails the fixed guard with `left: 1, right: 0`, so the strengthening did not buy its immunity by blinding the test. operant-core 2460 passed / 0 failed / 1 ignored in the full lib suite, which is where the defect lived; fmt and clippy clean.

- [x] **RT-175 (M, TIMING-SENSITIVE TEST) — a background-scheduler test slept a fixed wall-clock window and failed on a loaded box while passing in isolation.** `context::rollup::tests::spawned_maintenance_builds_rollups_on_interval` asserted that `spawn_rollup_maintenance` builds day rollups, but it waited with one `tokio::time::sleep(250ms)` for a scheduler ticking every 30ms and then read the result ONCE. Wall-clock waiting assumes the scheduler task gets real time to run, and under the full 2460-test lib suite on a 24-core box it does not — the test failed there and passed in isolation, the classic load-sensitive shape. **Fixed iter-1187** — it polls for its own condition on a bounded deadline (300 x 10ms), the shape its sibling `spawned_maintenance_stops_on_abort` already uses. The test's subject is the condition, so the wait is for the condition, not for a clock. **The first mutation attempt was WRONG and is worth the record:** removing the scheduler's immediate first pass did NOT fail the fixed test, because the 30ms interval loop builds the rollup anyway within the 3s poll window — so that mutation named a behaviour the test never claimed. The valid mutation is making the scheduler inert entirely, which fails it with `scheduler must build day rollups automatically, got: []` (and fails the sibling with `first pass must build sess_a rollup`). **A test whose fix cannot be proved false by a mutation that actually breaks the behaviour it tests is not fixed, it is silenced** — the same lesson as iter-1176's probe design and iter-1182's soft-line-break trap, at the mutation level. Restored byte-identical afterwards; three consecutive full lib suites 2460 passed / 0 failed / 1 ignored; fmt and clippy clean.

  **The cause, found by tracing the writes (iter-1136).** `App::new` calls `set_active_theme_enum`, which writes the PROCESS-GLOBAL role palette. The failure message named the wrong colour, which is why it read as mysterious.

  **The evidence** (a temporary `set_palette` trace, since removed): the failing runs show the writer's backtrace — `set_palette` <- `sync_role_palette` <- `set_active_theme` <- `set_active_theme_enum` <- `app/init.rs:43 (App::new)` <- `render/mod.rs:192 (make_app)` <- `render/mod.rs:152 (the_ported_layout_republishes_the_hit_test_cells)` — landing between the theme-asserting test's own write and its read.   **The fix** is the pattern the two twin helpers already use: the test takes the palette lock for its body, exactly like the theme-asserting tests do. No production code changed — the palette is written once at startup in production, and the lock is `#[cfg(test)]` only.

  What the trace also settled, for the next agent: the palette has TWO globals — `theme_colors::ACTIVE` (18 fields, QUANTIZED to the terminal depth) and the vendored role table (UNQUANTIZED) — and the frame's cells come from the operant palette while the assertion compares against the role table. They agree only when the terminal is 24-bit; in a test process `TERM` is usually unset, so the depth is 16. A future fix that compares them must compare like with like.

  **Measured (iter-1134), so the next agent does not start from zero:** 1 failure in 3 full `cargo test -p operant-cli --bin operant` runs, and 6 consecutive green runs in the same tree minutes later — the rate is load-dependent, not a fixed property. (The cause was found later, in iter-1136 — see above.)

- [x] **RT-172 (M, GATE COVERAGE) — RG-013 prescribed the second doc profile and iter-1166 recorded it as "an iteration of its own"; that iteration had never been attempted, and its stated reason was untested.** iter-1166's row says adding `--cfg test` "would surface every existing `#[cfg(test)]` doc link in the workspace at once" — a forecast about a command nobody had run. iter-1176 ran it, and the forecast is wrong in a way that matters: it is not a blocker, it is a DETOUR. Three measurements, all taken before any code was written:

  1. **`--cfg test` is not a cargo argument.** `cargo doc -p operant-cli --bin operant --cfg test` fails with `error: unexpected argument '--cfg' found`, and so does `cargo rustdoc ... -- --cfg test`. cargo 1.98.0 parses it itself rather than forwarding it, so the honest spelling is `RUSTDOCFLAGS="--cfg test"`.
  2. **The flag must be scoped to ONE crate.** `RUSTDOCFLAGS="--cfg test" cargo doc -p operant-cli --document-private-items` (no `--no-deps`) bleeds the cfg into every third-party dependency: the run dies with 13 **E0433 `cannot find module or crate quickcheck`** from `memchr`, a crate nobody is documenting. `--workspace` has the same problem. So the gate is one `cargo doc` per workspace crate, not one for all of them.
  3. **`--no-deps` makes the profile UNBUILDABLE, not merely blind** — which is the part that changes the recommendation. `cargo doc --no-deps` does not resolve `[dev-dependencies]` at all, so any crate whose test code imports one fails on an unresolved import before rustdoc runs: `operant-core` reports `unresolved import mockito` plus five `serial_test` errors, `operant-cli` reports `serial_test` (one use, `main.rs:3659`). The cfg(test) profile therefore MUST build dev-deps, and measuring 1+3 is why the earlier row could not tell "this surfaces many broken links" from "this cannot compile at all".

  Fixed iter-1176: `scripts/check-doc-test-profile.sh` (wired as `./scripts/check.sh doc-test`) documents each workspace crate separately with `--cfg test` on `RUSTDOCFLAGS`, one crate per invocation, dev-deps named via `--extern`, `--no-deps` ON, and `--document-private-items` under the production gate's `-Dwarnings`. **The gate then found a REAL cfg(test) defect it existed to find: `context_management.rs:2032` and `:2050` carried `[6]` — an array INDEX in prose that rustdoc reads as an intra-doc link, so `error: unresolved link to \`6\`` under `-D rustdoc::broken-intra-doc-links`.** That is the same class as iter-1166's `<RS>` (a literal sequence rustdoc reads as HTML): real text, invisible to a human, fatal to the gate. Both are escaped now (`\\[6\\]`). The port's doc rot was not fully fixed by iters 1160-1165 after all — the clippy passes caught code, and this class of defect only shows up in the TEST profile, which no gate could read until this one existed.

  So the row's claim that all 11 crates are green is the CLAIM THE MECHANISM SUPPORTS, and it is re-stated as: every crate's test profile compiles AND no `cfg(test)` doc link in the workspace is broken, verified by a gate measured BOTH DIRECTS by iter-1179 — it fails on the planted RG-013 shape (naming the broken link and classifying it as this crate's own) and is clean across all 11 crates with the probe removed.

  A gate that cannot fail certifies nothing, so the iteration also ships `scripts/tests/doc_test_profile_gate_test.sh`: it appends a `#[cfg(test)]` struct linking a non-existent identifier to `operant-core/src/config.rs` (the exact RG-013 shape), asserts the gate REPORTS `operant-core` failing AND names the broken link, removes the probe, and asserts the gate is clean again. Both directions, so a green run cannot be an artifact of the gate seeing nothing. The probe file is restored byte-identical from a backup via a trap, the way RG-013's own probe was.

  **The new gate had FOUR of its own defects before it could be trusted, each caught by running it rather than by reading it — which is the whole argument for shipping a failing-probe test alongside any new gate.** (a) Its crate-list regex scanned the whole manifest and returned every crate TWICE (members + the `workspace.dependencies` table), so each crate was documented twice. (b) It passed a bare `--bin`, and `--bin` takes an argument: all ten lib-only crates failed with `error: "--bin" takes one argument.` / `No binaries available.` — and because the filter only looked for the crate's own name, that error was DISCARDED and every crate printed `OK`. A gate green about a command it never ran. (c) With (b) fixed, `operant-cli` — the one crate with a binary, the bin the whole repo exists to build — was handed `--bin operant-cli`, which does not exist, because the name regex lacked `re.M` and `^` anchored at the string start (`[[bin]]` itself), returning `[]`, so the fallback silently supplied the PACKAGE name. (d) **The worst one, and the reason the mechanism is now three steps rather than one:** dropping `--no-deps` so dev-deps resolve also documents the DEPENDENCIES' cfg(test) profiles, `memchr`'s needs `quickcheck` (its own dev-dependency, absent here), cargo dies with `could not document \`memchr\`` and never reaches our crate — and the gate, reading only cargo's summary lines, printed **GREEN for all 11 crates with a broken `cfg(test)` doc link planted in operant-core**. A green that means "cargo never got there". Fixed by: reading targets per manifest, using `--bins` (which needs no argument), filtering diagnostics to paths under this crate, and — decisively — compiling the crate's test profile first and passing dev-deps via `--extern name=path` so `--no-deps` can stay ON and no third-party profile runs at all. A gate that exits non-zero without naming THIS crate is now reported as `BROKEN`, never as a pass.

  **The lesson this iteration pays for twice, and it is the one RG-013's Law should carry forward:** a gate can be green about a command it never successfully ran, and every one of those four defects was invisible in the source and obvious in the output. The only discipline that finds it is a probe that MUST fail — `scripts/tests/doc_test_profile_gate_test.sh` plants the RG-013 shape and asserts the gate names it, then removes it and asserts the gate is clean again. The probe test itself had a defect of the same shape (its `BASH_SOURCE` is `scripts/tests/<name>.sh`, so the repo root is TWO levels up; the first version ran from `scripts/` and failed loudly with the cwd printed — loud is right, but it cost a second run). This is the same family as iter-1168's suppression-gate regex (`RE_ATTR` could not align the `cfg_attr` form) and iter-1171's own residues: **a gate whose parsing is wrong is green about nothing.**

  **iter-1177 hardening: running the probe test exposed TWO MORE defects in the same family, and the second is the worst shape of all — a false GREEN caused by the detector of the detector.** (e) **The probe test's contamination was undetectable, so it poisoned the run it was meant to judge.** A prior probe run was killed by the tool harness's wall-clock timeout with SIGKILL, which gives the `EXIT` trap no chance to run, so the probe stayed appended to `operant-core/src/config.rs`. The next run appended a SECOND copy, cargo failed with `error[E0428]: the name DocTestProfileGateProbeZz is defined multiple times`, the gate's STEP 1 declined the crate, and the gate printed **GREEN with the broken link sitting in the file** — the exact class it exists to catch. The trap was not the guard (any SIGKILL bypasses it); the guard is a pre-check that refuses to start on a contaminated target and restores from `git checkout --`, because the probe's own backup is the thing most likely to be missing. (f) **PROBE 1 could not distinguish a false green from a real one.** Its assertion only tested for `FAIL operant-core`, so when the gate answered `SKIP operant-core` the test reported the same unhelpful message it would give for a gate that saw nothing at all. A doc-link warning cannot break a test compile (rustdoc and rustc are different passes), so a `SKIP` on the probe means the probe is malformed or the target is dirty — never that the crate is genuinely unbuildable — and it now fails with that specific message. **The gate's own six defects are recorded in the commit body and the WORKLOG:** `set -e` inherited from `scripts/dev-env.sh` line 13 aborted the whole script on the first `cargo doc` rc=101 (the loop looked broken; bisecting mapfile/timeout/pipefail/command-substitution each cost a run before the cause was found); the dev-dep extern picker was wrong THREE times in a row — a 33-candidate `lib<name>-*.rmeta` glob, then the fingerprint's `deps` array (which is `[hash,name,public,extra]` with no path in it), then that picker's own inverted `is_dir() is False` filter that silently excluded every path — before the working mechanism (`cargo test -p <crate> --no-run -v`, whose `--extern name=path` pairs ARE the crate's own resolution, reused for rustdoc); `touch src/lib.rs` CREATED an empty `lib.rs` for binary-only operant-cli and so changed the target set cargo resolved; and `--lib --bins` together fails on a binary-only crate, so operant-cli was skipped as an unbuildable test profile when its profile compiles cleanly.

- [x] **RT-188 (H, FALSE SUCCESS) — `web_crawl` on a stock sourcehound 1.8.0 (v2 surface) returns a sitemap LINK LIST, not crawled pages. CLOSED same-day (this audit).** Live-verified through the deployed binary: `operant run` → web_crawl on https://example.com answered "the sourcehound backend reports it does not serve `web.crawl`" and offered to fall back to web_scrape — while the SAME server answered the v2 `crawl` composite directly. Root cause was THREE defects stacking: (1) `WebCrawlTool::execute` never sent `mode: "crawl"` — v2's `crawl` composite is dual-mode (`surface::CrawlInput.mode` defaults to `"map"`, a sitemap/link listing), so even after `crawl_wire_name` correctly re-routed the wire name, the call answered a DIFFERENT question with `success: true` (verified live: `crawl {url}` → `{links:[], count:0, provider:"sitemap-parser"}` vs `crawl {url, mode:"crawl"}` → `pages[1]{url,title,content,depth}`); (2) the call carried no `format: "json"` (iter-1210's contract, applied to search only), so even a correct crawl answered in TOON text `unwrap_tool_result` cannot parse into a page list — which reads to the agent as an empty crawl; (3) an ORDERING bug found by live-verifying the deployed fix itself: `crawl_wire_surface` read the advertised set BEFORE `call()` spawned the client, so the FIRST web_crawl in a process (the common case — no prior call forced the handshake) still walked the `None` arm, sent the v1 name, and got the v2 server's "tool not found" verdict — the unit tests' probe-call preambles had forced the handshake early and masked exactly this. The tool's own failure message ("does not serve web.crawl") came from the pre-iter-1204 advertised-set inference firing on the v1-name absence before dispatch. Fix: `crawl_wire_name` → `crawl_wire_surface` returning `(wire_name, needs_mode)`, which now forces the handshake (`self.client()`) before reading the advertised set; the call sends `mode: "crawl"` only on v2 (a v1 server never receives the key) plus `format: "json"` always. Evidence: `a_v2_crawl_names_crawl_mode_and_asks_for_json` (mutation-proved RED), `a_v1_crawl_sends_no_mode`, `first_crawl_call_resolves_the_v2_surface_before_dispatch` (mutation-proved RED for the ordering half: removing the handshake-force fails it), `first_crawl_call_on_a_v1_server_keeps_the_granular_name`, `a_dead_sourcehound_binary_degrades_to_the_v1_surface_not_a_panic`, plus `scrape_and_extract_ask_for_json` pinning the same format contract on the scrape/extract tools (the same latent defect, closed here rather than left for the next audit). *(Number corrected from RT-180 in the same unpushed edit: a peer's test-infra row took RT-180 first.)*

Found in the second red-team pass over the codex-architecture-deepen port (`docs/audit/2026-11-01-ponytail-audit-codex-architecture-deepen-implementation.md`), which found three defects that the FIRST pass's green mutation masks had certified as fixed; the lesson recorded there is that a mutation guard proves the guard fires, not that the behaviour is correct. What stays OPEN (as of iter-1657): the consumer, not the emission site. iter-1631 SHIPPED the emission at turn END (the plan's specified tail seat was architecturally impossible, per the measurement below), and iter-1635 carried the classification; what no subscriber does is READ or render the value, and iter-1655 added that `TurnBreakdown::is_exclusive()` and `TurnAttribution::render()` have no production caller either. The plan's own text (`docs/plans/2026-10-31-codex-architecture-deepen-execution-outline.md` §Row 3) is precise about what is missing: build the four-span exclusive breakdown (`total` from `turn_start.elapsed()`, `inference` from the per-call LLM durations, `tools` from `tool_duration_for`, `user_wait` from the estop/pause hold, `overhead` as the `saturating_sub` residual) and render it on the volatile `<turn_context>` tail beside the `<context_budget>` block at `agent/run.rs` (the block that rides every request below the latest user message, so no prompt-cache invariant is touched). The types exist and are tested; the arithmetic and the state model are not the gap. **AN ATTEMPT WAS MADE the same day and found the emission site is ARCHITECTURAL, not plumbing (measured, not guessed).** The plan says to render the block on the volatile `<turn_context>` tail beside `<context_budget>` in `agent/run.rs`. That tail is inside `build_messages`, which is reached ONLY through `run()` -> `turn_context::build_turn_context` (`run.rs:337`) -> `build_messages` (`turn_context.rs:219`), and it runs EXACTLY ONCE PER TURN BEFORE THE LOOP STARTS (the loop then only appends to the `Vec<Message>` it returned). So at the moment the tail is written, no model call has happened and no tool has run: `turn_inference` and `turn_tools` are still zero and `saw_inference` is still false. A block emitted there would render `n/a` for every span on every turn, forever, which is the RT-199 failure wearing a better label. Emitting on the LAST iteration does not work either, because the frozen prefix and history must stay byte-stable across the turn's requests or the provider cache is invalidated on every tool iteration. **The half-finished wiring was reverted rather than shipped** (accumulators, `SpanDuration` folding, a `turn_tool_duration()` accessor added at `agent/stream.rs`, and the call site in `build_messages`); `agent/stream.rs`'s `turn_tool_duration()` accessor was kept because it is correct, useful, and harmless (it reads the per-turn map that `clear_tool_durations` already resets per turn, and returns `None` rather than `Duration::ZERO` when nothing was timed). What was NOT reverted is the measured finding, which is now in the module header so the next agent does not repeat the attempt.

**Two options, both measured, and the choice is the operator's:**

1. **Emit at turn END, off the request path** (RECOMMENDED). The numbers are complete by then and the natural home already exists: `TurnEnd` (`turn_end.rs`), which carries per-turn counters and already reaches every subscriber (TUI, gateway, trajectory, logs). Cost: extend `TurnEnd` with four `Duration`s and make one more capture. It does NOT put the block in the prompt, so the model would not see it. That may be fine, because "why did this turn take 40s" is a question the OPERATOR asks and the operator reads `TurnEnd`.
2. **Thread the timings into the turn-context build.** Change `build_messages` to take the span inputs and have `run()` build the tail on the LAST iteration. Cost: one new signature, a second tail build site, and a real risk to the frozen-prefix guarantee iter-39 depends on. It only buys prompt visibility.

Guards for whichever option is chosen: the double-count guard (both `inference` and `tools` including the inter-tool gap must fail the sum==total assertion) and the `Incomplete`-state guard (the report must fail to compile or fail to fire if it collapses back to a `u64`). Also required: `user_wait` stays `Unmeasured` rather than becoming `0s`, because the approval gate is a synchronous decision (`approval::check_tool_approval`) with no wall-clock wait to time at the loop.

The §6 read also fixes the DIRECTION for that wave: the sanctioned fix shapes there are composition, caps, labels, namespaces and retention discipline — a score cut is barred as a fitted constant of the min-max-normalised score — so the operant-side port (a seeded bank plus an A-J-shaped graded battery mirroring §4) exists to gate those mechanisms, never to tune a threshold number itself.

## CLOSED — Crash on TTS init and the ONNX Runtime pin (2026-10-19)

Filed from the user's crash log: `thread 'tokio-rt-worker' panicked at .../ort-2.0.0-rc.12/src/lib.rs:211:45: Failed to initialize ORT API`, then `terminated by signal SIGABRT`, plus the repeated `[memory]` warnings in the same log. Each row lists its evidence. H = process abort; M = user-visible; L = hygiene. **All six rows are closed** (CR-1..CR-6): the release profile unwinds (CR-3), the engine starts on its own task (CR-1), ONNX Runtime 1.24.4 is installed under `~/.local/lib/operant` (CR-2), and the doctor probes the engine instead of trusting the config (CR-4).

- [x] **CR-1 (H) — the process aborts when the TTS engine starts.** `ort` 2.0.0-rc.12 calls `GetApi(ORT_API_VERSION)`, and its `default` features include `api-24` (`ort` Cargo.toml `default` list), so `ORT_API_VERSION` is 24 (`ort-sys` `src/version.rs`: `17` plus the `api-18`..`api-24` bits). `kokoro-tiny` 0.1.0 depends on `ort` without disabling defaults, so `cargo tree --offline -e features -i ort-sys` shows `api-24` enabled through `kokoro-tiny` → `operant-core`. The installed `~/.local/lib/operant/libonnxruntime.so.1` is 1.20.1. Probing it with `OrtGetApiBase` returned a non-NULL API for `GetApi(17)` and `GetApi(20)`, and NULL for `GetApi(21)`, `GetApi(23)`, and `GetApi(24)`. `ort`'s `expect("Failed to initialize ORT API")` panics, and `[profile.release] panic = "abort"` (`Cargo.toml:115`) turns that panic into SIGABRT. The only route into `ort` is `TtsEngine::new` (`crates/operant-core/src/tools/tts_tool.rs:913-915`). The default TTS provider is `kokoro` (`tts_tool.rs:63`), so a `text_to_speech` call without an explicit provider reaches it. The trigger in the user's session is not known. Fix: CR-2 (a runtime at 1.24 or newer). The `api-24` default cannot be removed from operant's own manifest, because Cargo unions features and `kokoro-tiny` requests `ort`'s defaults; that needs a `kokoro-tiny` release or a `[patch]`. Partly fixed iter-970: the engine starts on its own task, so an ORT panic is a tool error, and the release profile unwinds (AD-016; test `a_panicking_engine_start_is_a_tool_error`, mutation fails it). Open until the deploy installs ONNX Runtime 1.24.4 on this machine. Closed iter-975: the deploy installed ONNX Runtime 1.24.4 under `~/.local/lib/operant`. The row's probe now returns non-NULL for `GetApi(24)` on the installed library, so the `ort` panic cannot occur. The live TTS path was not called in this session; the probe is the verification.

- [x] **CR-2 (H) — the build and install scripts pin ONNX Runtime 1.20.1 for an `ort` that needs API 24, and nothing checks the match.** Pins: `scripts/install.sh:97` (copies the 1.20.1 lib into `~/.local/lib/operant`), `scripts/dev-env.sh:24`, `scripts/check.sh:21`, `scripts/setup-build-env.sh:81-83` (1.20.1 and 1.21.0), and `AGENTS.md:528-532` (`ORT_LIB_LOCATION`, `LD_LIBRARY_PATH`). The release build linked and installed with exit 0, so the mismatch appears only at runtime. Runtimes that already serve API 24 are on this machine: `libonnxruntime.so.1.25.1` (`~/Documents/knowledge-base/HoloOS/.mempalace-venv/lib/python3.14/site-packages/onnxruntime/capi/`) and `libonnxruntime.so.1.30.0` (`~/.venvs/hindsight/lib/python3.12/site-packages/onnxruntime/capi/`); both returned non-NULL for `GetApi(24)`. Fix: vendor a 1.24+ release under `local/`, point the four scripts and AGENTS.md at it, and have `install.sh` probe `GetApi(24)` before it copies the lib. Partly fixed iter-970: the pins are 1.24.4 in every script, AGENTS.md and the skill; `install.sh` refuses a library without API 24 (AD-017). Open until the deploy copies the 1.24.4 library into `~/.local/lib/operant`. Closed iter-975: the deploy copies the 1.24.4 library into `~/.local/lib/operant` (the closure condition). The new binary resolves `libonnxruntime.so.1` to 1.24.4 (`ldd`), the gateway started on it, and the installed binary's md5 matches the running executable.
