## CLOSED — the vim modes' catalogue rows, and Ctrl+C in a vim mode (found 2026-11-06, iter-1770)

- [x] **RT-225 (M, FALSE HELP + DESTRUCTIVE SURPRISE) — two defects in the
  vim surfaces, both found by auditing the catalogue as a (context, chord)
  matrix against the vim dispatch.**
  1. **Rows in the wrong context.** `n` and `N` repeat the last search
     forward and backward, and the dispatch accepts them in **Normal** mode
     (`vim_mode == VimMode::Normal`). The catalogue filed them under
     **VimSearch**, so `/keys` told the operator that pressing `n` in the
     search line finds the next match — in the search line `n` is an
     ordinary character and types an "n" into the pattern. The rows moved to
     VimNormal, where the dispatch actually takes them. The search line's
     Enter row also said "Next match" when it runs the search from the start
     (skip = 0), so it finds the FIRST match; it now says "Find the pattern".
  2. **Ctrl+C in a vim mode wiped the composer's text.** The catalogue's
     VimCommand and VimSearch rows have always said "Ctrl+c — Exit to Normal
     mode", but the app's Ctrl+C arm had no vim-mode guard: it cleared the
     prompt input and started the quit confirmation. An operator who pressed
     Ctrl+C to abort a half-typed vim command lost their whole prompt and was
     asked whether they wanted to quit the application. **Fixed in the
     dispatch**, because the catalogue's contract is the sane one and it is
     what vim does: Ctrl+C in any vim mode other than Insert/Normal now
     leaves the mode (to Normal) and touches nothing else. The visual
     contexts' rows were added, since the same path serves them.
  **Pinned.** `ctrl_c_leaves_a_vim_mode_without_touching_the_prompt` asserts
  the mode is left, the text is intact, and no quit confirmation starts (it
  fails "Ctrl+C must leave Command for Normal mode" without the guard).
  `the_vim_catalogue_rows_are_pinned_per_context` pins the eight rows this
  iteration touched, per (context, chord) — the context column is what tells
  the operator which mode a chord belongs to, so a row in the wrong context
  is a lie about WHERE the chord works. Moving `n` back to VimSearch fails it
  by name.

## CLOSED — a count argument was silently turned into a different count (found 2026-11-06, iter-1772)

- [x] **RT-226 (M, SILENT WRONG VALUE) — the commands that take a count
  parsed it with `unwrap_or(default)`.** `/copy [N]` and `/undo [N]` share
  `parse_last_n`, and every unparseable argument became **1**:
  - `/copy abc` copied one message and never mentioned the argument it could
    not read;
  - `/copy -3` (negative) and `/copy 99999999999999999999` (overflow) did the
    same;
  - `/undo abc` silently undid **one turn** the operator never named;
  - `/undo 0` was clamped **up** to 1 — rewinding a message the operator had
    asked not to rewind.
  **And the zero case lied.** `/copy 0` is a real answer (the corpus's own
  test pins it: zero copies nothing rather than becoming the default), but
  it fell through to the empty-selection branch and reported *"No messages to
  copy — the transcript is empty."* — about a transcript with six messages in
  it. An operator who reads that and believes it goes looking for messages
  that are right there.
  **Fixed.** A count the operator typed is either a count or an error:
  `parse_last_n` returns a `Result`, and the arms name the argument they
  could not read (`/copy: "abc" is not a count — use a whole number.`).
  `/undo 0` says it needs at least one turn and undoes **nothing**. `/copy 0`
  says the count was 0 — and the empty-transcript notice now fires only when
  the transcript really is empty.
  **Pinned.** `an_unreadable_count_is_an_error_not_silently_the_default`
  covers `"abc"`, `"-3"` and the overflowing number on both commands, and
  asserts `/undo` pends no undo the operator did not name;
  `copy_zero_is_honoured_and_does_not_blame_an_empty_transcript` asserts the
  zero case says what it is and does NOT say the transcript is empty.

## CLOSED — `/output-style verbose` cycled the style instead of setting it (found 2026-11-06, iter-1773)

- [x] **RT-227 (M, SILENT WRONG VALUE) — the operator's level became the next
  one.** The command's arm cycled `auto → stream → verbose → auto` whatever
  the argument was, so `/output-style verbose` moved the style to **stream**
  and said "Output style: stream." — the operator asked for a level and got
  the following one, with a message that looked like confirmation. An unknown
  level ("/output-style loud") was accepted the same way, with no word about
  it. This is RT-226's class (a silent argument substitution) one level down:
  the count commands turned "abc" into 1, and this turned "verbose" into
  "stream".
  **Fixed.** A named level is set (`/output-style verbose` → verbose), an
  unknown one is refused by name (`"loud" is not an output style — use auto |
  stream | verbose.`), and no argument still cycles — the behaviour the
  command had always advertised for the no-argument case. The registry's
  descriptions for `/output-style` and its `/verbose` alias now say both
  halves, because a description that says "Cycle" while the command also
  takes a level is the next version of the same lie.
  **Pinned** by `output_style_takes_a_level_argument`, which fails with "the
  named level must be set, not cycled past" when the old arm is restored; the
  existing cycle test still passes.

## CLOSED — a restored session showed none of the turn's activity, and a stream that ended with no signal was taken for a finished answer (found 2026-11-06, iter-1774)

- [x] **RT-227 (M, LOST ACTIVITY) — three invisible-surface defects: the restored transcript dropped the reasoning and the tool rows, a silently-ended stream was taken for a complete answer, and a recovered turn ran its tools without a row.**

  **The restored transcript.** Both rebuild paths — the session hub's switch (the frame loop) and the outer drain's rebuild (`/clear`, `/new`, `/undo`, the rewind) — carried the SAME lossy conversion inline: the assistant's reasoning was dropped and every tool row became a bare system line. A session restored after a restart, or switched to in the hub, therefore showed a transcript with no tool calls and no thinking: as if the agent had never run a tool. ONE converter now builds the display the way the LIVE path does — the reasoning is a `Thinking` block, the tool call is a tool row anchored after the assistant turn that asked for it, and the matching tool RESULT fills that row's output (the live `ToolStart`/`ToolComplete` pair produces the same row). An orphan result (its call is not in the transcript) keeps its content visible instead of vanishing. Pinned by four cases in `crates/operant-cli/src/tui/app/session_display_tests.rs`.

  **The silent stream end.** The SSE parser dropped the terminal `[DONE]` marker, so a provider that closed its body without it — and without a finish reason — was indistinguishable from one that answered completely. The agent took the partial as final and the operator saw a sentence cut off mid-word with no explanation. The marker is now surfaced, the OpenAI adapter marks such a stream `incomplete`, and the agent asks for a continuation ONLY when the text itself looks cut (a reply that ends on punctuation is finished — otherwise a provider that omits the marker would be charged a continuation on every turn). The answer is reassembled from both halves. Pinned by three adapter cases and by `crates/operant-core/tests/stream_incomplete_continuation.rs` (the mid-sentence stop is continued; the finished sentence is not).

  **The recovered turn ran its tools invisibly.** When a stream died mid-read the loop re-issued the request, and the replay re-emitted every `ToolStart` the dropped stream had announced, under the SAME call ids. The dedup set (which exists so one call is not announced twice WITHIN a stream) still held those ids, so the replay's announcements were suppressed as duplicates: the recovered turn's tool rows never appeared, and a row that HAD been announced kept the truncated arguments of the dropped attempt. The set is cleared before the replay. Pinned by `crates/operant-core/tests/stream_replay_tool_rows.rs` — MUTATION-PROVED: without the clear the announcement count is 2, with it 3.

  **The debug log's blind spot.** The inline picker consumes its keys BEFORE the debug publication, so the picker's keys were the one surface the event log could not see — exactly the surface a "the picker ate my key" report needs. The publication moved above the picker's gate. A live agent error is now recorded in the debug hub (the transcript card shows the operator; the log is what a bug report attaches), and a TERMINAL error exit dumps the event log: the clean exits already did, so the one run whose log the operator wanted was the one that was lost.

  Prompt context's **21 rows** — the composer's own chords, which no test
  pinned — are now pinned to their dispatch arms (Enter, Shift+Enter, Esc,
  Tab, Up, Down, Ctrl+N/E/F/W/U/Y/Z, Alt+V, F5, Alt+R, Ctrl+L/S/D, Alt+B/D),

  committed, so HEAD did not compile**. This iteration removes that arm (the

## CLOSED — the simulator could not gated an expected error, and the tests rewrote the operator's settings (found 2026-11-06, iter-1778)

- [x] **RT-229 (M, GATE GAP) — the simulator had no way to say "this run is
  EXPECTED to log errors".** `operant tui debug simulate` fails any run whose
  event log contains an error, with no opt-out. A scenario that deliberately
  drives a turn into a provider failure therefore could never be gated — and
  the moment iter-1774 made a failed turn a real event on the bus (the RIGHT
  change: "the failure must be an event on the bus, not only a stored

  errors (they are still printed) and REQUIRES at least one, so a scenario
  that stopped simulating its failure cannot quietly pass. The scenario opts
  in through the schema's existing `flags` field, so no harness change was
  needed.

## CLOSED — the footer and `/context` quoted two different windows again (found 2026-11-06, iter-1779)

- [x] **RT-231 (M, TWO DENOMINATORS, AGAIN) — the TUI's footer and the
  gateway's `/context` disagreed about the context window.** The iter-1207
  defect, back: iter-1769 changed the TUI's `refresh_context_window_size` to
  read the configured `[agent] context_window` (128k) and added
  `OperantAgent::context_window()` — public, with the doc "**Public because
  CLI and TUI surfaces must report the same denominator the agent uses**" —
  but left the gateway's `/context` on its own resolver (the models.dev cache
  with the per-provider fallbacks: anthropic → 200k). So the TUI's footer read
  `8/128k` while `/context` read `0 / 200.0k`: **the same session's two
  surfaces disagreeing about how full the context was**, and neither number was
  the one the CORE budgets against (the core budgets against the agent's
  window — the configured one, lowered by a limit a prior overflow taught us).
  **Fixed by removing the third resolver**: the gateway takes
  `agent.context_window()`, the TUI's footer takes the agent's value whenever
  the agent exists, and `gateway_context_window_for_model` is gone. The
  gateway's doc comment ("resolved EXACTLY as the TUI's
  `refresh_context_window_size` resolves it") had been false since iter-1769 —
  it now describes what the code does.
  **Pinned** by `the_tui_and_the_gateway_quote_the_agents_window`, which
  reads both sources (the repo's pattern for a cross-file contract — the
  settings applier guard does the same) and fails with "the gateway's
  /context must take the window from the agent" when the old resolution comes
  back.

## CLOSED — `/memory` was a registered command that could only print a usage dump (found 2026-11-06, iter-1781)

- [x] **RT-233 (M, A REGISTERED COMMAND THAT COULD ONLY PRINT HELP) — `/memory`
  ran `operant memory` with no subcommand, so the operator got a usage dump;
  and the `/memory on|off` form the `/help` overlay advertised was an error
  because that toggle does not exist.**
  `intercept_slash_command_with_args_impl`'s `"memory"` arm called
  `shell_out_to_subcommand("memory", args)` — it passed the operator's
  argument through verbatim. `operant memory` is a clap subcommand-group with
  NO default (`cmd_memory::MemorySubcommand` has no `#[command(subcommand)]`
  default arm), so:
  * a bare `/memory` ran `operant memory`, which printed the usage dump — the
    list of the nine subcommands — and returned. The operator asked for the
    memory-wire status and got a CLI help screen;
  * `/memory on` and `/memory off` — the form the `/help` overlay advertised
    as "Toggle memory features" — ran `operant memory on` and died with
    `error: unrecognized subcommand 'on'`. There is no on/off toggle in
    `operant memory` at all, so the advertised form never existed;
  * the registry's own description ("Memory-wire status (operant memory)")
    named the one thing the arm could not produce.

  The arm had been written for `operant memory` as it was before plan 08, when
  the command WAS an engine toggle; the plan rebuilt it as a subcommand group
  over the memory-wire store (`list | get | search | store | delete | stats |
  import | export | clear`, every one reading and writing
  `~/.operant/memory_wire.sqlite` — the SAME engine the agent recalls from)
  and nobody re-checked the TUI's call site. A command that is registered,
  advertised, and can only print usage is the "advertised-but-dead" class the
  iter-811 sweep was written to find, and it survived because
  `no_registered_tui_command_is_unwired` only checks that `handle_tui_command`
  returns TRUE — which this arm did.

  **Fixed** — the arm now sends what the operator means: a bare `/memory` is
  the status view (`operant memory stats`), and a subcommand runs for real.
  Because `shell_out_to_subcommand` splits on whitespace, a phrase argument
  (`/memory search my query`) would have reached the CLI as four argv entries
  and errored; a free-text tail therefore travels as ONE argv element
  (`shell_out_to_subcommand_args`), while flags (`--limit 5`, `--confirm`)
  stay split so `operant memory list --limit 5` still parses. The registry's
  description now names both halves ("Memory-wire status; /memory <cmd> runs a
  memory subcommand") and the overlay row that named the non-existent toggle
  is replaced.

  **Pinned** by `memory_runs_a_real_subcommand_instead_of_printing_the_usage_dump`,
  which drives the real dispatch and reads `pending_shell_command`: the bare
  case must be `["memory", "stats"]` (not `["memory"]`), a query must stay one
  argument, and flags must stay split. Mutation-proved in BOTH directions —
  restoring the pass-through arm fails the bare case, and splitting the
  free-text tail fails the query case.

## CLOSED — the /help overlay's filter was DEAD, and `/help <command>` dropped its argument (found 2026-11-06, iter-1785)

- [x] **RT-234 (M, AN ADVERTISED FEATURE THAT DID NOTHING) — the `/help`
  overlay's own contract said "only commands matching this substring are
  shown", and the Commands view never read the substring.**
  `HelpOverlay::filter` carries that doc, `handle_help_overlay_key` pushes
  every printable character the operator types into it (and Backspace pops
  one out), and `draw_keys_overlay` — the `/keys` and `/hotkeys` view —
  filters its report with it. `draw_help_overlay`, the view `/help` opens,
  never read it at all. So in the one view where the filter was reachable:
  * every keystroke was consumed by `push_filter_char` (so it never reached
    the composer), AND
  * nothing on screen changed, ever — the overlay looked frozen, with no
    filter box, no prompt and no feedback that a term was held.

  And the form that would have made it discoverable was a second lie in the
  same file: the overlay's own row reads "/help <command> — Show details for
  one command" and its footer reads "/help <cmd> for details", but the arm
  was `self.help_overlay.toggle()` — it dropped the argument on the floor,
  so `/help model` opened exactly the overlay `/help` opens.

  Both halves are the same shape: the overlay declares a behaviour in prose
  (the filter's doc, the row, the footer) that no code implements — the
  tui-feature-audit class "advertised-but-dead", and the reason
  `no_registered_tui_command_is_unwired` (which only checks that the command
  returns TRUE) could not see it.

  **Fixed.** The Commands view filters its rows the way the Keys view does:
  a row survives when ANY of its spans carries the term, so the command
  name and its description are both searchable; the title shows the term
  (" Help · model "); a term that matches nothing leaves a line that says so
  rather than an empty overlay (the Keys view reports the same way). The
  filter is applied BEFORE the scroll math, so the percentage and the clamp
  describe the filtered content. `/help <command>` opens the overlay already
  filtered on the term (`HelpOverlay::open_filtered`), and the registry's
  `/help` description now names the form so the typeahead advertises it too.

  **Pinned** two ways. (1) The dispatch half: `help_with_an_argument_opens_the_overlay_filtered_on_it`
  drives `handle_tui_command("help", "model")` and asserts the overlay is
  visible, the filter is the argument, and the content is the command
  catalogue — a bare `/help` is still a plain, unfiltered toggle. (2) The
  render half, end to end through the corpus's own harness: a new
  `help-overlay.100x30` variant types `/help model`, and the golden plus
  `assert_screen` (contains `/model`, not-contains `/changelog`) pin the
  filtered frame — seven matching rows and nothing else. Removing the filter
  from the render path makes /changelog visible and fails the variant by
  name.

## CLOSED — the /help overlay's command rows were a stale second copy of the registry (found 2026-11-06, iter-1786)

- [x] **RT-239 (M, A SECOND CATALOGUE) — the `/help` overlay kept its own
  copy of the command descriptions, and the copy had drifted; it also
  advertised argument forms that no command reads.**
  **ID NOTE (iter-1788): this row was published as RT-235 (in iter-1786) and
  the concurrent slice published a DIFFERENT RT-235 in its iter-1787 — the
  same id, two findings. This row is renumbered to RT-239 (the next free id
  after the slice's RT-237/RT-238) and its label is restored to the
  iteration that actually shipped it, iter-1786. The slice's rows keep
  RT-235/RT-236; nothing is rewritten in git history, and the renumbering is
  recorded here so a reader who finds "RT-235" in an older commit body can
  follow it to this row.**
  iter-1766 audited all 111 rows of the command TABLE and fixed four that
  no longer said what their arms do. It fixed the TABLE. The overlay's
  hand-written "Commands" section — a second copy of the same catalogue,
  written out longhand — kept the old text for those four AND drifted
  further on its own.

  **The argument forms it advertised are not implemented.** Every one of
  these rows promises a form whose arm ignores the argument:
  * `/model <name>` — "Switch to a different model": the arm ignores its
    argument and opens the model picker.
  * `/effort <level>` — "Set effort (none|minimal|low|medium|high|xhigh|max|
    swarm|swarm-deep)": the arm ignores its argument and opens a picker with
    FOUR rows (low | normal | high | max). iter-1766 fixed this row in the
    table; the overlay kept the nine-level lie.
  * `/config init` / `/config edit` — "Create default config file" / "Open
    config in $EDITOR": the arm ignores its argument and opens the settings
    screen.
  * `/plan [goal]` — "Draft a plan-only proposal as a plan card (no edits)":
    the arm TOGGLES plan mode — a read-only permission mode — and ignores
    the goal. Nothing drafts a card: a plan card is the rendering of a
    ```plan block the MODEL happened to emit.
  * `/improve resume` / `/refactor resume` — "Resume the last saved
    improve loop/plan": both handlers ignore their arguments.
  * `/save [label]` — "Bookmark session for /resume": the arm opens the
    EXPORT dialog and ignores the label. iter-1766 fixed this row in the
    table; the overlay kept the bookmark.
  * `/rename <name>|--clear` — "Set or clear current session name": the arm
    takes any non-empty argument as the new TITLE, so `/rename --clear`
    renames the session to the literal string "--clear".
  * `/login [provider]` — "Interactive or direct login": the arm ignores the
    provider and runs `operant setup provider`.
  * `/memory [on|off]` — "Toggle memory features": `operant memory` has no
    on/off subcommand at all (RT-233).

  **The descriptions of the rows that WERE implemented had drifted too:**
  `/reload` promised "Reload to newer binary if available" and re-reads
  settings from disk; `/clear` promised "Clear conversation and start
  fresh" and only clears the conversation (`/new` starts a fresh session);
  `/version` promised "Show version and build details" and prints one
  version line; `/config` promised "Show active configuration" and opens the
  settings screen; `/resume` promised a picker and opens the session hub;
  `/login` promised a direct login and runs the setup wizard.

  **And the "More commands" sweep listed commands a local session cannot
  run.** It used `registered_command_entries`, which includes the remote-only
  rows, so a LOCAL `/help` listed `/continue` and `/resumeall` — whose answer
  here is the catch-all's "registered but not wired in operant yet", while
  the typeahead (which filters exactly those rows out) did not offer them.

  **Fixed.** The overlay's command rows read their description from the
  registry — the ONE catalogue — so a hand-written copy cannot drift again.
  The argument forms no command reads are gone; the ones that exist are
  listed (`/help <text>`, `/memory <cmd>`, `/rename <name>`). Four registry
  descriptions that were themselves wrong (`/plan`, `/config`, `/resume`,
  `/login`) now say what the arms do — the overlay cannot be truthful if the
  table is not. A local `/help` lists only the commands a local session can
  run; the remote-only rows are rendered in the System section in a remote
  session, where they dispatch.

  **Pinned** by three guards over the REAL overlay (rendered into a
  TestBackend, read back as text): `every_local_command_shows_its_registry_description_in_the_overlay`
  (every local command's row carries the table's own description — the guard
  that would have caught iter-1766's half-fix), `a_local_help_overlay_does_not_list_the_remote_only_commands`,
  and `the_overlay_no_longer_advertises_argument_forms_the_commands_ignore`.
  All three are mutation-proven: restoring the sweep's old row set fails the
  remote-only guard, and restoring `/save`'s hand-written copy fails the
  other two BY NAME.

## CLOSED — the corpus's own notes claimed the typeahead paints zero rows for two-or-more-character prefixes (found 2026-11-06, iter-1788)

- [x] **RT-240 (M, A FALSE CLAIM IN THE TEST CORPUS'S OWN NOTES) — a scenario

  **ID NOTE (iter-1788): published as RT-236 — the concurrent slice's iter-1787

  uncommitted text into its own commit, so both rows were live under one id.

  `crates/operant-cli/tests/tui_scenarios/typeahead-suggestions.scenario.json`
  carried, in its notes: "OBSERVED while authoring: two-or-more-character
  prefixes ('/sk', '/he', '/ex') currently paint zero rows while
  single-character prefixes ('/', '/s', '/h', '/st') do — a real
  inconsistency worth a follow-up, but not this scenario's job."

  MEASURED 2026-11-06 with the corpus's own harness and its own pinned

  * `/sk` → paints `/skills  Show loaded skills and operant-endorsed
    recommendations`
  * `/he` → paints `/help  Show help and keyboard shortcuts`
  * `/ex` → paints `/exit  Quit (alias of /quit)`

  The popup paints its rows for every prefix, one character or more. (The
  note's own list was incoherent too — it filed `/st` under "single-character
  prefixes".)

  The claim mattered because of what a false claim costs: this is the repo's
  own regression corpus, the surface the next agent reads before touching the
  typeahead. A note naming a live defect sends that reader hunting in working
  code — or "fixing" it into a regression. The same shape as RT-216 (AGENTS.md

  RT-217 (a doc naming a help section that does not exist), one layer further
