  wrong expectation reports "Screen assertion failed: expected to contain
  '/skills Show loaded skills and operant-endorsed recommendations'".

## CLOSED — the command palette printed its category header again and again (found 2026-11-06, iter-1791)

- [x] **RT-241 (M, A GROUPING THAT WAS NOT GROUPED) — the palette's rows were
  in registration order, so the categories interleaved and every header
  printed more than once.**
  `DialogSelectState`'s renderer prints a category header whenever the
  category CHANGES (`if item.category != last_category`), which is right for
  a grouped list. The palette's rows were not grouped: they were built from
  the command table in REGISTRATION order, and the registry's order does not
  group by category — `/help`, `/?`, `/commands` (Other), `/model` (Model &
  Provider), `/models` (Other), `/refresh-model-list` (Other), `/agents`
  (Tools), `/todos` (Other) … so the header sequence ran
  Other, Other, Other, Model & Provider, Other, Other, Tools, Other, …

  The corpus's own golden showed it: "Other" appeared FOUR times in the
  first twenty rows of the palette. The mutation dump is the honest count —
  across the 114 registered commands there were **twelve** separate "Other"
  runs, so the palette printed roughly forty headers for eleven categories,
  most of them the catch-all. A palette whose headers repeat is a palette
  whose grouping is invisible.

  **Fixed.** The rows are sorted by category — a STABLE sort, so the
  registration order survives INSIDE a category — and the category enum's
  declaration order is the section order, with the catch-all **last**
  ("Other" sorted alphabetically would bury it in the middle of the list).
  `tui_category` now returns the enum rather than a display string; it had
  exactly one caller, so the sort key and the label cannot disagree.

  **Pinned** by `the_command_palette_groups_its_rows_by_category`: every
  category must be ONE contiguous run. Mutation-proven — removing the sort
  fails it by name and prints the interleaved sequence it rejected. The
  corpus golden is re-proved and now reads Model & Provider, Review &
  History, Diagnostics, … each header once.

  **RESIDUAL, named not hidden.** The category TABLE is a second catalogue
  that covers only 54 of the 114 registered commands, so 60 of them (52%)
  land in the catch-all. That is now ONE section rather than twelve runs —
  the rendering defect is closed — but the table itself is stale, and
  covering the rest is a product decision about the category set (the
  agent-flow family `/improve /refactor /fix /judge /triage` and the CLI
  shell-outs `/cron /kanban /curator /org …` are coherent families with no
  home in the current eleven), not a rendering fix.

## CLOSED — the MCP panel's tool filter could not hold an 'r' or an 'e' (found 2026-11-06, iter-1793)

- [x] **RT-242 (M, A FILTER THAT ATE ITS OWN LETTERS — AND RESTARTED THE
  RUNTIME) — typing a search term in the MCP panel could silently reconnect
  the MCP servers.**
  The MCP panel has three panes (Servers | Tools | Detail) and one text
  field: the tool list's filter, rendered as a "/ filter tools" prompt. The
  letter shortcuts — `q` (close), `a` (auth), `r` (reconnect), `e` (error
  detail) — were matched BEFORE the filter arm and carried NO pane guard, so
  they ran in every pane. The consequence, measured by driving the real
  handler: typing **"read"** left the filter holding **"ad"** — the `r`
  armed `pending_mcp_reconnect` (the runtime is reconnected on the very next
  frame, `App::run`'s drain: "the MCP panel 'r' key sets this flag … 'r'
  acts now") and the `e` toggled the error detail.

  So the panel's only way to find a tool was broken for most queries (most
  tool names contain an `r` or an `e`: create, read, execute, search, server,
  fetch), and a stray letter could drop the operator's MCP servers
  mid-session — with no undo and no confirmation.

  **Fixed.** The shortcuts act on the PANE that owns them, and the tool list
  is a plain text field again:
  * `q` (close), `a` (auth) and `r` (reconnect) — the Servers pane, which is
    the pane the panel opens on;
  * `e` (error detail) — every pane but the tool list (the error section
    lives in the detail pane);
  * every other printable character — the tool filter, in the tool panes;
  * Esc still closes from anywhere.

  The footer now says what the panel does ("Tab pane · type to filter · e
  error · a auth · r reconnect (servers)") and it FITS the narrow panel: the
  old line was already clipped at 80 columns ("r reconn").

  **Pinned** by `the_mcp_tool_filter_holds_every_letter`, which drives the
  real key handler: "read" must land in the filter, and neither the reconnect
  flag nor the error toggle may move. Mutation-proven — restoring the global
  arms leaves the filter holding "ad" and fails the assertion by name. The
  second half of the test pins the other direction: `r` on the Servers pane
  still reconnects.

  **THE SCENARIO'S OWN NOTE WAS STALE TOO.** `mcp-view.scenario.json` said
  the arm "explicitly returns false for `mcp` when args are non-empty" and
  called `/mcp r` "the documented reconnect form". Both are false: the arm
  shells out to the CLI and returns true, and `operant mcp` has NO `r`
  subcommand (its subcommands are list | add | remove | test | serve | login
  | configure), so `/mcp r` is an "unrecognized subcommand" error. The
  reconnect action is the panel's own `r` key. The note now says that.

## CLOSED — the /help overlay's lower half was unreachable, and its footer advertised three scroll keys that did not exist (found 2026-11-06, iter-1795)

- [x] **RT-243 (M, THE BOTTOM OF THE DOCUMENT WAS UNREACHABLE) — the arrow-key
  scroll stopped at line 49 of a ~200-line catalogue, and the footer
  advertised three scroll affordances that did not exist.**
  The overlay's key handler scrolled with `scroll_down(50)` — a hard-coded
  "generous upper bound", with the comment "renderer will clamp". It is
  generous for the **/keys** report (about fifty rows) and far too small for
  the **/help** catalogue: the curated sections, the "More commands" sweep
  (seventy-odd rows), the Skills section, the whole **KEYBOARD** section and
  the Input & Editing section. MEASURED by driving the real binary: after 60
  Down presses the visible window still ended inside the "More commands"
  list, and nothing below it could be reached.

  The footer made it worse. It was a vendored jcode string, and THREE of its
  five claims were false:
  * **"j/k scroll"** — there is no j/k arm. Since iter-1785 the filter is
    live, so pressing `j` (as the footer instructed) put "j" into the filter
    and hid most of the help.
  * **"Space/PageUp page"** — no arm at all.
  * **"mouse wheel"** — the overlay is not in the dialog gate, so the wheel
    fell through to the TRANSCRIPT scroll: behind the overlay, where the
    operator cannot see it.

  And the line was clipped at 80 columns ("/help <cmd> for d").

  **Fixed.** The render path knows the content's real height, so it records
  the real max scroll (a `Cell` on the overlay, reached through the read-only
  `TuiState` seam — the same shape as the skills view's
  `last_viewport_height`), and the key handler clamps to it: the whole
  catalogue is reachable and the scroll never runs past the end (a scroll
  that overshoots leaves the view stuck while the state walks back). The
  wheel scrolls the overlay instead of the transcript behind it. The footer
  now names what the panel does — "Esc to close · ↑↓/wheel scroll · type to
  filter · /help <cmd> for details" — and fits the narrow panel.

  **Pinned** by `the_help_overlay_scrolls_to_the_bottom_of_its_catalogue`: the
  render records a max of 143, and pressing Down far more times than the
  content has lines must land ON it. Mutation-proven — restoring the
  hard-coded cap stops the scroll at 50 and fails the assertion by name.
  The corpus golden carries the new footer.

  **NOT IMPLEMENTED, named:** Space/PageUp/PageDown are still unbound (the
  footer no longer claims them). A true page scroll needs the viewport
  height — which the render path has and the handler does not — so it is a
  follow-up, not a claim.

- [x] **RT-244 (M, TEST HYGIENE) — four env-store tests went red for a reason
  that had nothing to do with the code under test.**
  The env-store's file tests and its permissions test shared ONE temp-path
  generator (`operant_test_env_<pid>_<counter>`): the file tests wrote a
  FILE there, the permissions test created a **DIRECTORY** there. The
  cleanup was `remove_file`, which cannot remove a directory — so the
  directory survived, and the next process with the same pid (this sandbox
  reuses small pids within minutes) wrote its file onto it:

      called `Result::unwrap()` on an `Err` value:
      Os { code: 21, kind: IsADirectory, message: "Is a directory" }

  Four tests went red on a clean tree, with a message that named neither the
  cause nor the fix. The same class as RT-230 (a unit test reaching outside
  its own sandbox) — except that the residue was a directory and the
  collision needed a pid AND a counter to repeat.

  **Fixed**: the file tests and the directory test have separate name spaces
  (`operant_test_env_file_*` / `operant_test_env_dir_*`), and the permissions
  test removes its directory. Proved by the sequence: with the old shared
  name a run that left a directory made the next run's four file tests fail
  with EISDIR; with the split names the leftovers are gone and the suite is
  green twice in a row.

- [x] **RT-245 (M, THE COMPOSER PROMISED A KEY THAT DOES NOT EXIST) — the
  streaming hint offered "Ctrl/Cmd+Enter to send now".**
  While a turn streams, the composer paints a hint row under the draft. It
  read:

      let hint = if app.queue_mode() {
          "  Ctrl/Cmd+Enter to send now"
      } else {
          "  Ctrl/Cmd+Enter to queue"
      };

  **There is no send-now path in operant.** The key handler's alternate-Enter
  arm (`app/key_handling.rs`) has exactly two behaviours: while a turn streams
  it pushes the draft into the STEER queue (`queue_steer`, announcing "Steer
  queued"), and while idle it submits like plain Enter. Plan mode changes
  neither — it is the read-only permission mode (gated tools are denied), not
  a send mode. So the hint's promise was false for every operator who turned
  plan mode on, and the way it was false was the expensive kind: the operator
  pressed the chord the composer named and the draft went into the queue for
  the NEXT turn instead of doing what the screen said.

  The accessor the branch read was not a queue mode either. `TuiState::queue_mode`
  was documented as "Whether queue mode is enabled (true = wait, false =
  immediate)" and returned `self.plan_mode` — the read-only permission flag.
  So the name, the doc and the value all described a send mode operant does
  not have, and the ONE flag that flipped the hint to the false promise was
  the one whose meaning the accessor had misnamed. (The vestigial name comes
  from the jcode port: upstream had a real queue mode; operant wired the
  accessor to plan mode when the port landed.)

  **Fixed**:

  - the hint states ONE truth — "Ctrl/Cmd+Enter to queue" — because that is
    what the key does while the hint is visible (the hint only appears while
    a turn is streaming, so the idle submit is not even in scope);
  - the accessor is renamed `plan_mode_active()` and documents the flag it
    actually reads (the read-only plan permission mode), so the next reader
    cannot mistake it for a send mode;
  - the plan marker in the composer's right gutter is the product's own 📋
    (the gateway's plan-mode glyph) instead of the ⏳ that means "queued"
    everywhere else in the TUI (queued messages, running background tasks).

  **Pinned** by three render tests that paint the REAL composer into a
  TestBackend and read the buffer back, so the hint is pinned where it is
  painted and not only where it is computed:
  `the_streaming_hint_says_queue_and_not_send_now`,
  `plan_mode_does_not_turn_the_queue_hint_into_a_send_now_promise` and
  `an_idle_composer_offers_no_send_now_either`. **Mutation-proven**: restoring
  the old branch fails
  `plan_mode_does_not_turn_the_queue_hint_into_a_send_now_promise` by name,
  with the false promise in the failure message ("… send now").

  **RESIDUAL, named not hidden**: `InfoWidgetData::queue_mode` is a DIFFERENT
  struct's field with the same vestigial name, and it is still populated with
  the plan-mode flag (`Some(self.plan_mode)`). It feeds
  `has_data_for(WidgetKind::Overview)` as a counted "section" the Overview
  never renders, which is what keeps the Overview widget admitted when it
  would otherwise have no sections. Renaming it and giving it a rendered row
  (or counting only the sections the Overview actually paints) is the next
  iteration's subject — it is a different struct from the accessor fixed here,
  and fixing it changes what the Overview widget shows, so it does not belong
  in this change.

## Round 52 (2026-11-06) — the agentic-core gap sweep: the template, the skills paths, the aft failure surface

- [x] **RT-246 (M, THE TEMPLATE ADVERTISED A PLUGIN'S MANIFEST FIELDS AS CONFIG
  KEYS) — an operator who followed the example got a config that would not
  load.**
  `operant.example.toml`'s `[plugins]` block documented a plugin's
  `manifest.toml` with live TOML assignments:

      #   requires = ["other-plugin"]   # skipped at discovery while a named
      #   provides = ["memory.backend"] # service names other plugins' requires

  Those are the MANIFEST's fields. The config's settings structs use
  `deny_unknown_fields`, and `[plugins]` has neither key — so uncommenting
  the example produced "unknown field `requires`", and ONE unknown key
  rejects the WHOLE file: every other setting the operator had written stops
  loading with it.

  **The template's own gate caught it, and it was RED at HEAD.**
  `crates/operant-core/tests/example_template_loads.rs::every_commented_example_in_the_template_names_a_field_the_loader_accepts`
  uncomments every commented example — alone and inside its table — and hands
  it to the real loader. It named exactly the two lines above (568 and 572).
  The `capabilities` line beside them escaped the gate only by accident: its
  value (`["tool" | "memory" | …]`) is not valid TOML, so the loader answered
  with a PARSE error rather than an unknown-field verdict, and the gate reads
  only the latter.

  **Fixed**: the manifest schema has exactly ONE owner — `docs/library/plugins.md`
  already documents `capabilities`, `requires`, `provides` and the free-form
  `[config]` table, with the discovery rules (a plugin whose requires are
  unmet is skipped, transitively; `provides` are composition labels). The
  template now points there instead of repeating the schema, and the gate is
  green again (4/4).

- [x] **RT-247 (M, A FAILING AFT COMMAND SAID "unknown error" AND THREW THE
  DIAGNOSTICS AWAY) — the bridge had captured them already.**
  `AftBridge::send_request_once` builds its error from the response's
  `message` (or `error`) field and falls back to the literal "unknown error"
  when the response carries neither. The child's own stderr was never lost:
  the bridge drains stderr into a 64-line ring for exactly this purpose
  (plan 07.1, so a chatty child cannot freeze the bridge on a full pipe).
  The error path simply never read the ring.

  So a failing `aft_inspect` answered the model with a dead end that named no
  cause — and the tool's own payload (the reason the call failed) was on the
  child's stderr, one line away.

  **Fixed**: a failure with no usable message reports the child's most recent
  stderr lines (the last 5 non-empty ones, joined — a tool error has to fit
  on one line), and a response whose message IS the literal "unknown error"
  keeps that name and gains the diagnostics in parentheses. The wait for the
  ring is bounded (10 × 20 ms) because the child writes its diagnostic just
  before the failure response and the drain task fills the ring
  concurrently; a failure with no stderr at all still says "unknown error".

  **Pinned** by `aft_bridge::tests::a_failing_command_without_a_message_reports_the_childs_stderr`,
  which drives a fake aft that answers `inspect` with
  `{"success":false,"code":"E_NO_INDEX"}` and one stderr line. Restoring the
  old fallback fails it with the symptom the row names: "aft inspect:
  [E_NO_INDEX] unknown error". The same test module's `AFT_BINARY` lock was
  hoisted to module scope — it was a function-local static, so it serialised
  nothing between the two tests that point `AFT_BINARY` at a fake child.

- [x] **RT-248 (M, THE SELF-EXTENSION TOOLS COULD NEVER RUN) — the approval the
  operator had already given stopped one hop short of the tool.**
  `harness_mount` and `harness_unmount` are the agent's self-extension
  surface: the model can mount a provider onto the running kernel and tear
  it down again. Both gate on one thing:

      fn has_approval(context: &ToolContext) -> bool {
          context.metadata.get("approval").map(String::as_str) == Some("true")
      }

  and NOTHING ever set that flag. The tools are not in
  `is_permission_gated_tool`, so the permission channel never prompts for
  them; and `OperantAgent::tool_context` — the context every tool call runs
  with — carried only `session_id` and `unattended`. The operator's
  `command_allowlist` DID reach the agent (`agent_config()` copies it into
  `AgentConfig::approval_allowlist`, `approval_allowlist_from_config` seeds
  the persistent allowlist, `tool_allowed_by_allowlist` consults it), but
  the approval STOPPED there: it was never handed to the tool that asks.

  So the model could call `harness_mount` and always got:

      harness_mount requires the host's approval policy to have approved
      this tool for the current session. Ask the user to approve
      `harness_mount` (e.g. via the persistent or session allowlist), then
      retry.

  — an instruction to do the thing the operator had already done, and the
  only way to satisfy it was impossible. The module's own header was honest
  about the symptom but named the wrong culprit: it said mount/unmount were
  "stubs … until the approval layer is updated" while the tools themselves
  were complete and tested. The gap was the approval layer's HALF.

  **Fixed**: `OperantAgent::tool_context` now takes the tool name and says
  so — `approval=true` for a tool the operator's allowlist covers, nothing
  for the rest. The tool's documented route (approve the name in the
  allowlist, retry) now works, and no other tool reads the flag.

  **Pinned** by `agent::tests::an_allowlisted_tool_tells_itself_that_it_was_approved`:
  an allowlisted `harness_mount` sees `approval=true`, a tool the operator
  did not approve sees no flag. Dropping the flag fails it by name.

- [x] **RT-249 (M, A DELEGATION THAT PRODUCED NOTHING LOOKED LIKE A SUCCESS) —
  the parent received an empty tool result.**
  The parent's tool result IS the child's final message: `run_child` ran the
  child agent and returned `message.content` verbatim. A child turn can end
  with NO answer — the wall clock, the iteration budget and the grace gate
  can each stop a turn (the live incident behind iter-1783 ended one with
  `response_len=0`) — and the delegation then reported a SUCCESSFUL call
  whose content was the empty string.

  An empty result is the failure a parent cannot act on and cannot report:
  it looks like a child that had nothing to say, and the model reads it as
  "the sub-agent finished" rather than "the sub-agent died". The scratch
  gap register saw it from the outside — "`delegate_task` returned an empty
  result … No error was surfaced — just no output".

  **Fixed**: the finished turn is shaped in ONE place (`child_outcome`),
  shared by the sync, the swarm worker and the background path, and a child
  that produced no text is a NAMED failure — "The sub-agent finished its
  turn without producing any output" — rather than an empty result. A
  swarm worker that produced nothing is now a `Failed` worker, not a
  `Completed` one with nothing in it.

  **Pinned** by
  `tools::sub_agent_tool::tests::a_child_that_produced_no_output_is_a_failure_not_an_empty_result`:
  a whitespace-only child answer is an error naming the cause, a real answer
  passes through. Dropping the check fails it by name.

- [x] **RT-251 (M, THE WHEEL SCROLLED THE TRANSCRIPT BEHIND THE PANEL) — the
  mouse's overlay gate was a second, shorter catalogue.**
  **ID NOTE (iter-1802): this row was published as RT-246 — the concurrent
  slice's iter-1800 commit swept this row's UNCOMMITTED text into its own
  commit, the same accident this campaign has already repaired twice. Their own
  RT-246 (the config template) was published FIRST, in their iter-1798, so this
  row is the later publisher of the id and is renumbered forward to RT-251
  (RT-250 is left free for the slice's next row: their batch RT-246…RT-249 is
  published). Nothing is rewritten in git history; the renumbering is recorded
  here so a reader who finds "RT-246" in the iter-1800 commit body can follow it
  to this row.**
  The mouse handler decides what a click or a wheel means by asking whether a
  dialog is open. It asked by naming ten of them:

      let any_dialog = self.connect_dialog.visible
          || self.import_config_picker.visible
          || self.import_config_dialog.visible
          || self.command_palette.visible
          || self.inline_interactive.is_some()
          || self.export_dialog.visible
          || self.settings_screen.visible
          || self.stats_dialog.visible
          || self.context_viz.visible
          || self.session_hub.visible;

  The overlay catalogue — `App::overlay_flags()`, the ONE list the debug
  snapshot and `any_modal_open()` both derive from — has **29** entries. The
  nineteen the gate forgot let the wheel fall through to the TRANSCRIPT:
  the MCP view, the skills view, the journey view, the plugins hub, the
  agents menu, the diff viewer, the theme screen, the memory-file selector,
  the history-search and global-search overlays, the rewind selector, the
  permission picker, the ask-user dialog, the bypass-permissions dialog,
  the API-key / custom-provider / free-mode dialogs, the inline picker and
  the permission request.

  **What the operator saw**: they scrolled with the wheel over an open
  panel, the PANEL stood still, and the transcript moved BEHIND it — where
  it cannot be seen. The panel looked frozen (no panel in that set scrolls
  with the wheel, and none of them says it does), and the transcript had
  moved by the time the panel closed. The `/help` overlay had already been
  rescued from exactly this shape at iter-1795; the other nineteen had not.

  **Fixed**: the wheel belongs to the OPEN PANEL. The panels that scroll
  take it — the `/help` overlay (whose footer says "↑↓/wheel scroll"), the
  session hub's preview and the three list dialogs (already routed by the
  gate above) — and every other panel **absorbs** it, because a panel that
  cannot scroll must not move what is behind it. The gate now reads
  `overlay_flags()`, the catalogue that already exists, so a panel cannot
  fall through by being forgotten in a second list; a new overlay added to
  the catalogue is covered the day it is added.

  **Pinned** by a table-driven test over EVERY overlay in the catalogue:
  `the_wheel_never_scrolls_the_transcript_behind_an_open_overlay` drives the
  27 overlays that carry a `.visible` flag, and
  `the_wheel_never_scrolls_the_transcript_behind_an_option_shaped_overlay`
  drives the two the catalogue tracks as `Option`s (the inline picker and
  the permission request). Each asserts the transcript's scroll offset does
  not move. The control,
  `the_wheel_scrolls_the_transcript_when_no_overlay_is_open`, keeps the
  ordinary scroll alive — without it, "the wheel does nothing" would pass
  the other two. **Mutation-proven**: removing the catalogue guard fails
  both by name ("the wheel must not scroll the transcript behind the
  history_search_overlay panel" / "… behind the permission request").

  **RESIDUAL, named not hidden**: the CLICK path still uses the same
  hand-written gate, and the panels themselves have no mouse handling at
  all (only `DialogSelect` has a click handler), so a click inside one of
  the nineteen still reaches the transcript's selection machinery. Making
  the panels clickable is a FEATURE, and absorbing the click would take
  away the transcript text selection the repo deliberately keeps available
  behind a panel — so it is left as a separate decision, not smuggled into
  this change.
- [x] **RT-252 (M, THE WORKSPACE'S LINT GATE WAS RED) — the floating stable
  toolchain added two lints the code cannot satisfy as written.**
  `rust-toolchain.toml` pins `channel = "stable"` — a FLOATING toolchain — so
  a new stable can turn a green gate red without a line of code changing.
  `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --all-features -- -D warnings`
  reported **28 diagnostics** across four crates:

  **(1) `double_must_use` — 28 sites.** `async_trait` puts a bare
  `#[must_use]` on every async method it generates ("this async function
  ignores its future"), and this workspace has 28 traits whose async methods
  return a `Result` — which is ALREADY `#[must_use]`. The lint's own
  suggestion (give the attribute a message) cannot be applied to a
  macro-generated attribute, and the workspace hand-writes no `#[must_use]`
  of its own anywhere (measured: `grep -rn "#\[must_use" crates/` finds only
  the attributes this row adds), so the lint has no true positive here at
  all.

  **(2) `deprecated` on `Atomic::fetch_update` — 2 sites.** The compiler's
  own suggestion is to rename the call to `try_update`. **`try_update` is
  stable since Rust 1.95, and this workspace declares `rust-version =
  "1.89"`** — so taking the compiler's advice would silently RAISE the
  declared MSRV (a policy the repo states in `Cargo.toml`) to silence a
  deprecation warning. Clippy says the same thing in its own note: "you may
  want to conditionally increase the MSRV considered by Clippy using the
  `clippy::msrv` attribute". The call keeps the pre-1.95 spelling and says
  why.

  **Fixed**: the `double_must_use` sites are expected where they are few (3
  in operant-cli, 5 in operant-api, 2 in operant-harness) and once, with
  the reason, in operant-core (18 sites in one crate — the crate the
  concurrent slice works in, so the sweep stays in ONE file instead of
  eighteen, and the reason names the cause once). The two `fetch_update`
  calls carry an `#[expect(deprecated)]` naming the MSRV reason instead of
  taking the rename. The gate now reports **ZERO** (exit 0).

  **MEASURED, not assumed**: the 28 diagnostics were counted on a clean HEAD
  tree with this change stashed, so they were pre-existing and not
  attributable to the TUI work in flight. The `expect` attributes are the
  repo's own style (they fail loudly when the lint stops firing, so a
  future toolchain that fixes the cause says so instead of leaving a stale
  suppression behind).

- [x] **RT-253 (M, A MISPLACED ATTRIBUTE) — iter-1802 published a commit that
  turned the crate's lint gate red.**
  The wheel-routing helper was inserted immediately before
  `handle_mouse_event` — which is exactly where the file's
  `#[expect(clippy::unwrap_used, reason = "…")]` attribute sat. The new
  function was therefore placed BETWEEN the attribute and the item the
  attribute belongs to, and Rust attaches an attribute to the item that
  FOLLOWS it. Two errors followed, both published in the same commit that
  fixed a real defect:

  - the attribute moved onto the helper, which contains no `unwrap` →
    "this lint expectation is unfulfilled" → an error under `-D warnings`;
  - the function that DOES unwrap (`context_menu_state.as_mut().unwrap()`)
    lost its allowance → an `unwrap_used` error.

  **Fixed**: the helper moved above the attribute, so the attribute and its
  item are together again.

  **Pinned** by the crate's own lint gate — the two errors ARE the pin:
  `cargo clippy -p operant-cli --all-targets --no-deps -- -D
  clippy::unwrap_used -D clippy::expect_used -D warnings` is green again.
  The lesson, recorded for the next iteration: when a new item is inserted
  next to an attribute, re-read the attribute's OWNING item — an attribute
  is not a comment, it is a binding to what follows it, and inserting
  between the two silently reparents it.

- [x] **RT-250 (M, THE POST-EXECUTE ENVELOPE DROPPED THE ARGS) — an observer's
  redaction seat could not see what the tool was called with.**
  The observe envelope an interceptor receives is documented as (point, tool,
  args, result, config). In practice the POST-EXECUTE event carried
  `args: Value::Null`, so a plugin deciding whether to REPLACE a tool's
  result — the seat gap G2 built iter-1739, the redaction/enrichment case —
  could see the output but not the input it had to judge. A redactor asked
  "does this result echo the credentials the model passed in?" had nothing
  to compare against.

  **Fixed** in `ToolRegistry::execute`: the call's args ride the
  post-execute envelope like every other point. The same observer already
  received them at pre-execute, so the change exposes no new surface; it
  closes the hole the doc had already promised away. The in-tree fixture's
  observe path (block-on-tool-name, config passthrough) is unaffected.

  **Pinned** by `tools::tests::post_execute_carries_the_args_the_tool_was_called_with`:
  an observer whose Replace verdict is keyed on the args now replaces the
  result. Restoring `Value::Null` fails it with the unreplaced original.
- [x] **RT-254 (M, THE COMPOSER MEASURED A GLYPH IN BYTES) — a plan-mode draft
  wrapped two columns early.**
  The composer reserves room on the right for the send-mode glyph (the plan
  marker, the new-session arrow, the transport icon) and measures the draft's
  wrap width against what is left:

      pub(super) fn send_mode_reserved_width(app: &dyn TuiState) -> usize {
          let (icon, _) = send_mode_indicator(app);
          if icon.is_empty() { 0 } else { icon.len() + 1 }
      }

  `icon.len()` is the UTF-8 **byte** length. The plan marker (📋) is FOUR
  bytes and TWO columns, so the composer charged the draft **five** columns
  for a two-column glyph: at 80 columns the text area is 77 wide and the
  marker leaves 74, but the composer wrapped at **72**. A draft that fits
  wrapped anyway — one row taller than it needed to be, and two columns of
  the composer that no text could ever use. The same shape sat under the
  new-session marker "↗" (three bytes, one column).

  **Fixed**: the reservation is the glyph's DISPLAY width plus one column,
  measured with `unicode-width` — the crate the rest of the TUI already
  measures text with (`render/utils.rs`, `operant_render_core/wrap.rs`), so
  the composer now measures the way its painter does. The marker still
  cannot be reached: the wrap width ends two columns short of the glyph's
  left edge, so the text and the glyph cannot overlap.

  **Pinned** by two tests: `the_plan_marker_costs_two_columns_not_five`
  (the arithmetic — two columns of glyph plus one of room, and NOT the byte
  length) and `a_draft_that_fits_beside_the_plan_marker_does_not_wrap` (a
  73-character draft at 80 columns must stay on ONE row, which is where the
  operator sees it). **Mutation-proven**: restoring `icon.len() + 1` fails
  both by name.

  The class is the one the campaign keeps meeting in a new shape: a length
  measured in the wrong unit — RT-230's byte-sliced title PANICKED, RT-251's
  duplicated catalogue, and here a byte count charged as columns. The
  composer already imports `unicode-width` for its wrapping; the reservation
  was the one place that did not use it.

- [x] **RT-255 (M, THE GATE'S EXPECTATIONS WERE A COIN FLIP ON A FLOATING
  TOOLCHAIN) — 13 unfulfilled expectations and a red gate on stable 1.98.0.**
  `rust-toolchain.toml` pins `channel = "stable"`, so the lint set moves with
  the toolchain. iter-1804 answered the 28 diagnostics one stable produced
  with `#[expect(clippy::double_must_use)]` (11 sites) and
  `#[expect(deprecated)]` (2 sites). An expectation, by definition, FAILS
  when the lint it expects does not fire — so on the other side of the same
  float, where neither lint fires, all 13 became
  `unfulfilled_lint_expectations` warnings, and the gate treats a NEW warning
  as a failure:

      [clippy-gate] seen=13 allowlist=0 new=13 stale=0

  **MEASURED on stable 1.98.0**: `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets
  --all-features` reports 13 unfulfilled expectations and ZERO
  `double_must_use` and ZERO `deprecated` diagnostics; with the
  expectations converted, the same command reports nothing at all and
  `bash scripts/clippy-warning-gate.sh` prints "seen=0 allowlist=0 new=0
  stale=0 — pass" (exit 0).

  **Fixed**: the 13 attributes are `#[allow]` with the SAME reasons. The
  reasons still hold — `async_trait` puts a bare `#[must_use]` on every
  async method it generates and this workspace hand-writes no `#[must_use]`
  of its own, so the lint has no true positive here; and `try_update` is
  stable since 1.95 while the workspace declares `rust-version = "1.89"`,
  so taking the compiler's rename would silently raise the MSRV. What
  changes is the FORM: an `expect` is a promise that the lint fires HERE
  and NOW, which a floating toolchain cannot keep; an `allow` states the
  decision ("this lint has no true positive in this workspace, and the
  deprecation must not raise our MSRV") and is silent in both directions —
  it cannot itself become the next red gate.
- [x] **RT-256 (M, THE OVERVIEW PANEL STOLE THE TODO LIST) — the widget that
  admits itself counted a section it never paints.**
  The TUI floats small info widgets in the transcript's empty margins: the
  todo list, the usage bars, the background tasks, the KV-cache summary, the
  changed files. The **Overview** is the panel that JOINS several of them —
  and while it is on screen it SUPPRESSES the mergeable ones (the layout
  pass calls them "mergeable" and skips them, so the Overview's page IS
  their page).

  That makes the Overview's admission test load-bearing: if it says yes for
  a page with nothing to join, the operator loses the real widget and keeps
  a summary of it. The admission test counted its OWN list of sections:

      let mut sections = 0usize;
      if runtime_has_data(self) { sections += 1; }
      if !self.todos.is_empty() { sections += 1; }
      if background_running { sections += 1; }
      if self.queue_mode.is_some() { sections += 1; }   // ← never painted
      if usage_available { sections += 1; }
      if self.cache_hit_info.is_some() { sections += 1; }
      if self.compaction_info.is_some() { sections += 1; } // ← never painted
      if git_has_data { sections += 1; }
      sections >= 2

  and that list disagreed with the page the Overview paints
  (`render_sections`): it counted the **vestigial plan-mode flag** — a field
  that carried `plan_mode` under a queue-mode name and was never rendered —
  and the **compaction payload**, which the Overview does not paint either;
  and it MISSED **memory**, which the Overview always paints.

  So a session with a todo list and nothing else counted TWO sections, the
  Overview was admitted, and the todo list's own widget was suppressed in
  its favour. The operator read **"3 total · 1 active"** — one line — where
  the list of the three tasks used to be.

  **Fixed**:

  - the count is now `overview_section_count`, derived from the SAME terms
    as the Overview's own height arithmetic (`compact_overview_height`), so
    the admission decision and the page's content cannot drift apart again;
  - the vestigial `queue_mode` field is DELETED (it carried the plan-mode
    flag, had no other consumer, and is the thing that made the count lie);
    the plan-mode state is already visible in the composer (the 📋 marker
    added at iter-1797);
  - the mergeable list is exactly the widgets the Overview PAINTS: the
    **compaction status** and the **swarm session list** keep their own
    widgets (they dock on the other side), because suppressing them behind a
    panel that never shows them would hide their content entirely.

  **Pinned** by three tests, mutation-proven in both halves:
  `a_single_section_keeps_its_own_widget_instead_of_a_one_line_overview`
  (one section → the Overview is NOT eligible and the todo widget IS),
  `the_overview_only_suppresses_the_widgets_it_paints` (the mergeable list
  is exactly the painted set), and the updated
  `overview_requires_multiple_sections` (two REAL sections admit it).
  Restoring the phantom count fails the first and the third by name;
  restoring the suppression list fails the second.

  The shape is the campaign's recurring one: a SECOND catalogue that drifted
  from the first — here a section list beside the renderer's section list.
  The fix is not to align the two but to derive one from the other, so there
  is nothing left to align.
- [x] **RT-257 (M, TWO PROMISES ABOUT A GUARD, BOTH FALSE) — the key-routing
  chain could drift again, and the guard that said it could not was checking
  nothing.**
  The TUI routes keys to overlays twice: the dispatcher's inline chain
  (`if self.<surface>.visible { … }`, the REAL router) and a second chain in
  `dialog_routing.rs` (`dialog_priority()`, the documented priority order,
  currently used only as a debug assertion). A surface that is gated in the
  first and missing from the second is a surface the second chain does not
  describe — the exact failure the repo repaired once before, when
  theme_screen, rewind_flow and memory_file_selector were gated inline and
  absent from the chain.

  **The repair left a promise instead of a guard.** The dispatcher's comment
  says:

      They are now present, and `dialog_covers_every_gated_surface` fails if
      one is ever dropped again.

  **That guard was never written.** What stood in its place was a
  hard-coded list of the three surfaces that repair had recovered:

      #[test]
      fn the_three_recovered_surfaces_are_gated() {
          let gates = chained_fields();
          for field in ["theme_screen", "rewind_selector", "memory_file_selector"] { … }
      }

  — a list of the surfaces that happened to drift ONCE. So the chain drifted
  again: the **inline picker**, the **permission request** and the
  **permissions picker** are gated in the dispatcher and absent from the
  chain (measured: the catalogue's 29 surfaces are all gated in the
  dispatcher, but 26 are in the chain).

  **And the guard that did exist was vacuous.** `every_priority_variant_has_a_gate`
  read the enum's variant names from its own source — but it read the
  **doc-comment** lines and kept only the ones that were alphanumeric:

      let name = name.strip_prefix("///")?.trim().to_string();
      let looks_like_variant = !name.is_empty()
          && name.chars().next()?.is_uppercase()
          && name.chars().all(|c| c.is_alphanumeric());

  Every doc comment in that enum contains a space ("Context menu", "Ask user
  dialog", "Memory file selector. Same omission as ThemeScreen."), so the
  reader kept **NOTHING** and the guard compared an empty list — it passed
  while checking no variant at all. (A guard that cannot fail is worse than
  no guard: it is the promise, in writing, that the chain is covered.)

  **Fixed**:

  - the three drifted surfaces are in the chain — appended, as the earlier
    recovery appended its three, because the chain's ORDER is a documented,
    deferred question (the two chains diverge on 5 of 6 pairs; see
    docs/ROADMAP-TUI-FLEET.md 6.1) and claiming a "correct" slot would be
    false precision;
  - `dialog_covers_every_gated_surface` — the guard the comment names —
    **exists**, and it is derived from the overlay CATALOGUE
    (`App::overlay_flags()`, the ONE list of surfaces the UI has) rather than
    from a hand-kept list of the surfaces that happened to drift once: a
    surface added to the catalogue without a gate in either chain fails, and
    a gate dropped from either chain fails;
  - the variant reader reads the enum's **variant** lines, and the guard
    asserts the reader's count against the number of variant lines the enum
    declares — so a reader that goes quiet again fails loudly instead of
    passing vacuously.

  **Pinned** by `dialog_covers_every_gated_surface` and
  `every_priority_variant_has_a_gate`, mutation-proven in both halves:
  dropping one chain gate fails BOTH by name ("permissions_picker is in the
  overlay catalogue but the priority chain does not gate it"), and restoring
  the prose reader fails the second with "the variant reader returned [] — it
  must read the enum's VARIANT lines, not its prose (a reader that returns
  nothing makes this guard vacuous)".

- [x] **RT-258 (M, THE `[proxy]` TABLE REACHED NO CLIENT AT ALL) — an operator
  behind a proxy had no way through, while the template promised one.**
  `operant-config/src/schema/proxy.rs` carries a complete proxy surface:
  `ProxyConfig` (http/https/all proxy URLs, a `no_proxy` bypass list, a
  scope, a service list), `apply_to_reqwest_builder`, `apply_runtime_proxy_to_builder`,
  a runtime client cache, and the environment export. The CLI applies the
  table at startup (`operant_core::config::apply_startup_proxy`,
  `crates/operant-cli/src/main.rs`), and `operant.example.toml` advertised
  "Outbound HTTP proxy for provider and tool clients. Applied at startup."

  **No client ever read it.** Measured by grep across the workspace:
  `apply_runtime_proxy_to_builder`, `build_runtime_proxy_client` and
  `build_channel_proxy_client` had ZERO callers outside `proxy.rs` itself.
  The only proxy path that reached any HTTP client was the ENVIRONMENT one
  (reqwest follows `HTTP(S)_PROXY`/`ALL_PROXY` by default) — and RT-131
  closed that path for provider traffic in iter-1116, so after that fix the
  provider had NO proxy path at all. RT-131's row named this half as its
  residual: "An operator who needs a proxy requires two follow-ups: plumb
  `[proxy]` into `ClientConfig` and decide whether `scope = "environment"`
  should proxy provider traffic … and only then relax `.no_proxy()`."

  **Fixed**: the provider clients — the OpenAI-compatible client (its request
  client AND its streaming client) and the Anthropic client — apply the
  operator's explicit table on top of the no-proxy builder
  (`client::provider_http_builder`). The two halves of RT-131's contract are
  now both true and neither is traded for the other:

  - the AMBIENT path stays closed: `.no_proxy()` is applied FIRST, so a stale
    `HTTP_PROXY` inherited from another tool can never redirect model traffic
    (RT-131's own guard, `env_proxy_is_ignored_by_the_provider_client`, still
    passes);
  - the EXPLICIT path is open: the table the operator wrote reaches the model
    client. `scope = "environment"` deliberately does NOT reach the provider —
    that IS the ambient path RT-131 closed — so a proxy for the model client
    is written with the default `scope = "zeroclaw"` or with
    `scope = "services"`.

  The service key follows the endpoint (`provider.openai`,
  `provider.openrouter`, otherwise `provider.compatible` for self-hosted
  gateways and LiteLLM), so `scope = "services"` can select one provider or
  the `provider.*` family.

  **Pinned** by `configured_proxy_is_used_by_the_provider_client`: a capture
  listener stands in for the CONFIGURED proxy and must serve the provider
  request (the request targets TEST-NET-1, which cannot answer, so a direct
  attempt is distinguishable from a proxied one; the config's own `no_proxy`
  list keeps every other test's loopback provider out of the proxy while the
  guard is up). Mutation-proven: dropping the apply call fails it BY NAME —
  "the configured proxy must carry the provider request", left 0, right 1.

  **Named residual (not this row):** the TOOL clients still follow the
  process's environment variables rather than the runtime table, so the
  template's old "provider and tool clients" wording was half true. The
  provider half — the model transport, and the one RT-131 named — is closed
  here; the tool half is the next tranche.
- [x] **RT-258 (M, THE CLICK REACHED THROUGH THE PANEL) — with a panel open,
  the mouse acted on the transcript behind it.**
  **ID NOTE (iter-1819)**: this row shares its id with the concurrent slice's
  RT-258 (the `[proxy]` table, iter-1813), which was published first. History
  is append-only, so both rows stay as published; the gate now names the
  collision in its DUPLICATE_IDS list (RG-021) so a reader is never left
  guessing which of the two rows an id means.
  The mouse handler decides what a click means by asking whether a dialog is
  open. It asked by naming ten of the overlay catalogue's 29 surfaces (the
  same hand-written list RT-251 found for the WHEEL), so the other nineteen
  panels let the click fall through to the transcript:

  - the click selected the transcript's text — so **Ctrl+C copied text the
    operator could not see**, under the panel they were looking at;
  - a click on a tool row's position expanded that tool row (RT-146's
    toggle), and a click on a thinking-block header folded or unfolded that
    block — both behind the panel;
  - a right-click opened the transcript's context menu behind the panel.

  The gate's own comment says the opposite of what happens: "Key-input and
  device-auth stay outside this gate so their visible text can still be
  selected and copied with the mouse." The selection machinery resolves a
  click to a TRANSCRIPT row (through the published message-row map), so it
  cannot select a dialog's text — it selects the transcript UNDER the
  dialog. The intent was to keep the dialog's text copyable; the effect was
  to copy the wrong text.

  **Fixed**: a press on the transcript — left button, right button or drag —
  is **absorbed** while any overlay in the catalogue is open, so the
  transcript behind a panel is not reachable. The panels have no mouse
  handling of their own, so the click belongs to the panel (click-to-select
  inside the panels is a FEATURE, and a separate one).

  The WHEEL is deliberately **not** absorbed at the same place: the panels
  that scroll take it (the `/help` overlay, the session hub's preview, the
  three list dialogs) and the rest absorb it in `wheel_scroll` (RT-251) —
  one rule for the wheel, one for the press.

  **Pinned** by `a_click_never_selects_the_transcript_behind_an_open_overlay`
  — a table over EVERY overlay in the catalogue, so a panel cannot fall
  through by being forgotten in a second list — and by the control
  `a_click_still_selects_the_transcript_when_no_overlay_is_open` (without
  the control, "the click does nothing" would pass the table).
  **Mutation-proven**: removing the absorb arm fails the table by name
  ("a click must not select the transcript behind the help_overlay panel").

  **RESIDUAL, named not hidden**: a release that ends a drag still runs the
  transcript's copy branch, so a selection made BEFORE the panel opened can
  be copied by a release inside it. The press and the drag are absorbed, so
  no NEW selection can start behind a panel; closing that last corner means
  splitting the release arm's composer branch from its transcript branch,
  which is a bigger change than this defect needs.

- [x] **RT-259 (M, THE DEFERRED BRIDGE ASKED THE NAME, THE TOOLS ARRAY ASKED
  THE TYPE) — a tool that deferred by declaring itself so was hidden AND
  unreachable.**
  The progressive-disclosure bridge has two halves: `assemble_tools` decides
  what the MODEL sees (it partitions the registry's schemas by the stamped
  `ToolExposure`, i.e. by what the owning TYPE declares), and three bridge
  arms decide what the model can REACH with it (`tool_search`'s catalog,
  `tool_describe`'s guard, `tool_call`'s guard) plus the turn-driven
  `materialise_for_turn`.

  **The two halves read different things.** The bridge arms ran
  `is_deferrable(name)` — an `mcp_` prefix plus a scan of the sourcehound
  composite table — while `assemble_tools` read `s.exposure`. The rules
  agreed only because both production families happen to satisfy both: the
  MCP proxy names its tools `mcp_*` AND types them `Deferred`, and the
  sourcehound composites are in the table AND type themselves `Deferred`.

  **The module's own test had already proved the disagreement.** The exposure
  tests register a type-deferred tool named `zzz_internal_sidecar` — no
  `mcp_` prefix — and assert it lands in the deferred set. Nothing exercised
  the BRIDGE for that fixture, so the defect sat there unnoticed: such a tool
  was withheld from the model's tools array (by type) and then refused by all
  three arms (by name) — hidden AND unreachable, with no recovery path. The
  day a third family deferred by declaring itself so, its tools would have
  been dead on arrival.

  **Fixed**: every arm reads the registry-stamped exposure
  (`s.exposure.is_deferred()`), so the array and the bridge cannot disagree
  about what is deferred. `tool_call` now checks availability FIRST, so an
  absent or disabled tool is reported as absent ("not registered or is
  currently disabled") rather than as "not a deferred tool". `is_deferrable`
  and its composite-table helper are DELETED: with the bridge on the type
  they had no production caller, and a second rule with its own copy of the
  composite table is the drift class this repo keeps repairing.

  **The guard that protected RT-194 was itself reading the name.** The
  sourcehound composite guard asserted each composite's NAME was deferrable
  (`every_composite_is_deferrable`), so it kept passing if the TYPE stopped
  deferring — the ~4,738-tokens-per-request regression would have shipped
  silently. It now asserts the TYPE (`every_composite_is_deferred_by_type`),
  which is the decision the production rule actually reads.

  **Pinned** by `a_type_deferred_tool_is_reachable_through_the_bridge`: a
  type-deferred tool with no `mcp_` prefix must be listed by `tool_search`,
  described by `tool_describe` and executed by `tool_call`. Mutation-proven:
  restoring the name filter in the catalog fails it BY NAME — "the
  type-deferred tool must be in the catalog: []", left 0, right 1. The
  fixtures that modelled MCP tools by name alone are deferred by type now,
  exactly as the registry types them.

  **ID NOTE (iter-1816)**: this row is RT-259. The ledger already carries TWO
  RT-258 rows — the `[proxy]` table row (published in iter-1813) and the
  click-behind-the-panel row (published in iter-1815). The click row took
  RT-258 while my proxy row was already published under it; history is
  append-only, so both rows stay as published and the collision is recorded
  here rather than rewritten.
- [x] **RT-259 (M, THE WHEEL WAS INERT IN THE PANELS THAT SCROLL) — the
  diff viewer had a scroll API and no wheel.**
  **ID NOTE (iter-1819)**: this row shares its id with the concurrent slice's
  RT-259 (the deferred bridge, iter-1816), which was published first. History
  is append-only, so both rows stay as published; the gate now names the
  collision in its DUPLICATE_IDS list (RG-021).
  RT-251 made the wheel belong to the open panel: the panels that scroll
  take it, and the rest absorb it. Two panels with a scroll of their own
  were left on the absorbing side:

  - the **diff viewer** — its detail pane is a long, scrollable text, and
    the panel already had the scroll API its ↑/↓ keys use
    (`scroll_detail_up` / `scroll_detail_down`, three lines a notch). The
    wheel did **nothing** there: the operator scrolled a long diff with the
    arrow keys, because the one control that means "scroll" was inert;
  - the **skills view** — its list is long and its ↑/↓ move a SELECTION
    cursor.

  **Fixed**: the diff viewer's detail pane scrolls with the wheel (three
  lines a notch — the step its own keys use, so the wheel and the keys
  agree), and the skills view's wheel moves the list's selection cursor —
  the way ↑/↓ do, so the cursor never scrolls out of view — and scrolls
  the pane in its detail stage.

  **Pinned** by `the_wheel_scrolls_the_panels_that_can_scroll`, which
  drives both panels' real state (the diff viewer's `detail_scroll` and
  the skills view's `selected`) in both directions.
  **Mutation-proven**: removing the routing fails it by name ("the wheel
  must scroll the diff viewer's detail pane").

  **RESIDUAL, named not hidden**: the panels whose cursor the wheel could
  move but whose scroll API does not exist — the agents menu, the plugins
  hub, the journey view, the history-search and global-search overlays,
  the memory-file selector, the permission picker, the ask-user dialog,
  the theme screen and the rewind selector — still ABSORB the wheel. Each
  has its own selection state and its own key handler, so wiring the wheel
  to them is a per-panel decision rather than one rule; it is left as named
  work rather than smuggled into this change.

- [x] **RT-260 (H, A PLUGIN'S OBSERVER RAN TWICE AFTER ITS FIRST LIVE CHANGE,
  AND A WITHDRAWN OBSERVER KEPT WATCHING) — one plugin, two registrations.**
  `ToolRegistry` holds TWO interceptor lists: the anonymous one iter-1722
  introduced as the general tool-seam waterfall, and the named,
  replace-by-plugin-name one gap G6 added for live re-registration. `execute`
  consults BOTH (it concatenates them into one handler list).

  **The boot path and the watcher wrote to different lists.** Boot registered
  a plugin's observer with `register_tool_interceptor` (anonymous); the
  watcher registered it with `register_plugin_interceptor` (named). So after
  the FIRST watcher-detected change for a plugin, the plugin's `observe`
  export ran TWICE per tool event — and the boot copy still held the
  pre-change module: the wasm pool is resident (iter-1725), so the old module
  stayed alive and kept answering. A policy change therefore did not take
  effect: the stale observer still saw (and could still veto) every call.

  **And the watcher had no "else".** `unregister_plugin_interceptors` and
  `unregister_turn_interceptors` existed — the doc comment even named "the
  watcher's change-undo path" — and had ZERO production callers. So a change
  that dropped the `Observer` capability left the observer watching every tool
  call forever, and a change that dropped the `[config] turn_gate = true`
  opt-in left the turn-seat veto in place forever: a gate the operator turned
  off kept vetoing turns.

  **The count that would have shown it did not exist.** The registry could
  report the NAMED list's size (`plugin_interceptor_count`) and not the
  anonymous one, so "how many interceptors will run for this tool?" had no
  answer — and the double registration was invisible to every surface.

  **Fixed**:
  - the boot path registers into the NAMED list, so one plugin has one
    registration and the watcher's replace semantics apply to it;
  - the watcher withdraws what a change removed: the observer interceptor
    when the capability is gone, the turn interceptor when the turn gate is
    gone;
  - `ToolRegistry::tool_interceptor_count()` counts the anonymous list, so
    the two lists can be counted together.

  **Pinned** by three tests against the REAL fixture module (`fixture.wasm`):
  `a_boot_registration_and_a_watcher_change_leave_one_observer`,
  `a_change_that_drops_the_observer_capability_stops_observing` and
  `a_change_that_drops_turn_gate_no_longer_vetoes_turns`. All three are
  mutation-proved: the boot path back in the anonymous list fails the first
  BY NAME ("one plugin, ONE observer: the boot registration and the watcher
  registration must be the same registration", left 2, right 1); dropping
  the capability-unregister fails the second ("a withdrawn observer must not
  keep watching every tool call", left 1, right 0); dropping the
  turn-gate-unregister fails the third ("a withdrawn turn gate must not keep
  vetoing turns", left 1, right 0).

  **Named residual**: the ANONYMOUS interceptor list has no production user
  after this fix — it stays as iter-1722's general extension point (public
  API, its own tests), and the ledger records that it is currently unwired
  rather than pretending it carries traffic.
- [x] **RT-261 (M, THE CAMPAIGN'S OWN GATE COULD NOT SEE A DUPLICATE ID) — the
  ledger carries eight of them.**
  `scripts/audit-ledger-index.py` is the gate that keeps the audit ledger
  honest: it compares the index table against the checkboxes in both
  directions, because closing a defect flips the checkbox and nothing walks
  back to the table. It does that comparison as a **set difference**:

      open_checkbox = set(re.findall(...))
      all_rows = set()
      ...
      missing_from_table = sorted(open_checkbox - all_rows)

  **A set has no duplicates.** So the one thing that would make the ledger's
  ids ambiguous — two findings answering to the same id — was exactly the one
  thing the gate could not see. And two agents on this shared branch had
  picked the same id **eight times** in this ledger's life:

  - in the index table: RT-218 (the scroll counters / the Ctrl+Q catalogue),
    RT-234 (the empty answer / the /help filter), RT-239 (the /help second
    catalogue / the sessions-list panic), RT-258 (the `[proxy]` table / the
    click behind a panel), RT-259 (the deferred bridge / the wheel in the
    panels);
  - among the detail sections: RT-136, RT-175, RT-218, RT-225, RT-226,
    RT-227, RT-258, RT-259.

  Each collision was recorded only where a reader happened to look — one
  ID NOTE in one row, or in the script's prose — so every tool that read the
  ledger (the index as a lookup table, the gate as a check) saw a perfectly
  reasonable ledger. A lookup table whose ids are ambiguous is not a lookup
  table, and the campaign's own consistency check could not say so.

  **Fixed**: the gate now checks the **id space** as well as the state:

  - every index row's id is unique;
  - every detail section's id is unique;
  - every index row carries the detail section that states its finding (a
    row that states a finding's fate without the finding is half a row — five
    published rows are in that state today, and the script names them);

  and the ids that already collide are named in the script's exception lists
  (`DUPLICATE_IDS`, `INDEX_ROWS_WITHOUT_DETAIL`), each with the reason it is
  there, so the gate fails on the **NEXT** collision instead of on the
  published ones forever. The id pattern was also corrected: `S\d` read
  `S1b` as `S1`, which manufactured a duplicate out of a heading.

  **Pinned** by `scripts/tests/audit_ledger_index_test.sh` (wired into
  `scripts/self-test.sh` beside the gate itself): it plants each defect in a
  COPY of the ledger — never the real one — and asserts that the gate fails
  and NAMES the id, and that the original RG-016 check still fires. The
  published ledger passes.

  The lesson, now three times over in this campaign (RT-212's dead source
  guard, RT-213's red lint gate, RT-257's vacuous reader): **a gate that
  compares sets cannot see multiplicity, and a check that cannot fail is
  worse than no check** — it is the promise, in writing, that the thing is
  covered.

- [x] **RT-262 (M, THE CURATOR ARCHIVED SKILLS THAT WERE IN DAILY USE) — the
  idle clock never moved.**
  The curator owns the lifecycle of agent-created skills: it marks a skill
  STALE after `stale_after_days` and ARCHIVES it after `archive_after_days`,
  both measured from `last_used` in `.curator/usage.json`
  (`curator/mod.rs`: `inactive_days = (now - record.last_used.timestamp()) /
  86400`). The auto-run is live — `agent/prompting.rs` fires the curator on
  the skills lane's cadence and applies the transitions.

  **Nothing recorded a USE.** `UsageTelemetry::bump_use` and `bump_view`
  exist and are documented as "Called when a skill is actively used (e.g.,
  loaded into the prompt path)" and "Called from skill_view or skill
  discovery" — and they had ZERO production callers (grep over `crates/`
  returns their definitions and their own unit tests). The only writer of the
  telemetry file was the skills tool's `record_usage`, whose action map
  covered create / delete / patch only: so `use_count` stayed 0 and
  `last_used` stayed at creation time for EVERY skill.

  **The consequence is data loss, quietly.** A skill the agent invoked every
  day — a background-review skill in active service — was archived 30 days
  after its CREATION, exactly like an abandoned one, and only a count was
  logged. The `never_used` grace floor (`use_count == 0` AND younger than the
  stale window) did not protect it: it is about skills that were never used,
  and it stops protecting a skill once it is older than the stale window.

  **Fixed**:
  - the invocation path records the use. The seam is
    `agent::skill_preprocessing::build_skill_invocation_message_in` — the ONE
    function the TUI's `/skill`, the gateway's skill commands and the agent's
    own lane all come through — so every invocation is counted in one place.
    The write goes through the curator's own `with_exclusive_lock` bridge, so
    it cannot lose a concurrent record, and it is swallowed on failure:
    telemetry never breaks an invocation;
  - `skill_view` records a VIEW (`bump_view`), which moves the same clock
    without claiming a use — a skill the operator still READS is not an
    abandoned one;
  - `SkillUsageTracker` gained `bump_use` / `bump_view` (the tracker had
    `bump_patch` but not the other two), so the production path does not have
    to reach into the telemetry type.

  **Pinned** by `a_used_skill_is_not_archived_by_the_curator` (in
  `crates/operant-core/tests/test_curator.rs`): an agent-created skill whose
  last use was 40 days ago, invoked ONCE through the production path, must
  survive a curator pass with a one-day archive window. Mutation-proven:
  without the recording the curator archives it — "a skill in daily use must
  not be archived", archived 1, expected 0.

  **Named residual**: the curator's auto-run reads
  `<operant_home>/skills/.curator/usage.json` (`platform::operant_skills_dir`),
  while a CONFIGURED `[skills] root_dir` points the skills tool — and now the
  invocation path — at another tree. With a custom root the two read
  different files, so the clock this row fixes is still frozen for that
  operator. The row names it; the fix is a config-resolution change, not a
  patch.

- [x] **RT-263 (M, A SETTING THAT DID NOTHING, OFFERED AS A POLICY) — the
  session-reset policy was a promise no code path kept.**
  `AppConfig::agent.session_reset` (`config.rs`, enum `Never |
  OnSystemPromptChange | OnToolChange | Always`, default `Never`) was:

  - **advertised** in `operant.example.toml` — a live, uncommented line;
  - **offered** by `operant setup`'s wizard with four behavioural promises:
    "Never — Keep context forever (highest cost)", "On system prompt change —
    Reset when system prompt changes", "On tool change — Reset when tool
    configuration changes", "Always — Reset every new session (lowest
    cost)";
  - **shown** in the setup status panel as an ACTIVE setting
    (`print_status("Session reset", …, true)` — the green tick).

  **And READ BY NOTHING.** Measured: a grep over `crates/` returns
  `config.rs` (the declaration and its default) and `cmd_setup.rs` (the
  wizard reading its own value back). No code path resets a conversation when
  the system prompt or the tool set changes, and the gateway's separate
  `SessionResetPolicy` is always `ResetMode::None` — the only non-default
  construction is inside that module's own test module. The key was not in
  `AppConfig::unused_setting_warnings` either, so the PROJECT did not know it
  was unread.

  **The consequence**: an operator who picked "Always" — the option the wizard
  calls "lowest cost" — was told their sessions reset, and they never did, so
  they kept paying the API cost of a context that never shrank.

  **Fixed**: the surface now tells the truth, and the fix is deliberately
  SMALLER than implementing the policy:

  - a SET value is reported by `AppConfig::unused_setting_warnings`
    (accepted but unread — it has no effect), which is the mechanism this
    repo already uses for a parsed-but-unread key (RT-136's pattern);
  - the setup wizard no longer offers the policy — offering four behavioural
    promises for a no-op is the defect;
  - the setup status no longer lists it as active;
  - `operant.example.toml` carries it commented out with the same note.

  The key stays in the schema: `AppConfig` carries `deny_unknown_fields`, so
  deleting a field breaks every existing `operant.toml` that sets it, and an
  operator's config must keep PARSING (the warning tells them it does
  nothing).

  **Pinned** by `a_session_reset_policy_setting_is_reported_as_unread`:
  `[agent] session_reset = "always"` produces exactly one warning naming the
  key, and a DEFAULT config is silent (a clean start must not produce noise,
  and `never` is what the runtime does anyway).

  **Deliberately not done**: implementing the policy. What a reset clears
  (the conversation? the persisted session?) and where it belongs (the
  agent loop? the session switcher? the gateway?) are product decisions, and
  guessing at them would ship a behaviour the wizard did not describe. The
  truth-telling fix is the one that is correct under every answer.
