- [x] **RT-264 (M, THE WHEEL WAS INERT IN TEN PANELS) — the panels whose list
  carries a cursor had nothing.**
  The wheel belongs to the open panel (RT-251). The panels that SCROLL take
  it: the `/help` overlay, the session hub's preview, the three list
  dialogs, and — since RT-259 — the diff viewer's detail pane and the
  skills view.

  The panels whose list carries a **SELECTION CURSOR** had nothing at all.
  The wheel did nothing there, in ten of the TUI's panels:

  - the agents menu,
  - the plugins hub,
  - the journey view,
  - the global search,
  - the history-search overlay,
  - the memory-file selector,
  - the permissions picker,
  - the ask-user dialog,
  - the theme screen,
  - the rewind selector.

  So each of them scrolled with the ARROW KEYS only — the one control that
  means "scroll" was inert, and the operator had to guess which panels those
  were. (The three list dialogs — connect, import-config, command palette —
  already moved their selection with the wheel, so the behaviour existed;
  it just did not exist next door.)

  **Fixed**: the wheel moves the open panel's cursor the way ↑/↓ do — the
  **same methods the key handler calls**, so the wheel and the keys can
  never disagree about where the selection is, and no panel grows a second,
  different notion of "the current row". The rewind selector's wheel is
  eaten while its filter box is open, exactly as its arrows are (the
  operator is typing a filter, not choosing a turn).

  **Pinned** by `the_wheel_moves_the_cursor_of_the_panel_whose_list_is_open`
  — a table over EVERY panel with a cursor, driving each one in both
  directions — and by the control
  `the_wheel_scrolls_the_transcript_and_no_cursor_when_no_panel_is_open`
  (without the control, "the wheel does nothing" would pass the table).
  **Mutation-proven**: removing the routing fails the table by name ("the
  wheel must move the agents_menu panel's cursor").

  **RESIDUAL, named not hidden**: the panels the mouse's own dialog gate
  swallows before the wheel reaches them — the inline picker, the export
  dialog, the settings screen, the stats dialog and the context viz — still
  take no wheel. Their arrows are not list cursors (the settings screen
  moves between SECTIONS; the context viz is a graph), so what the wheel
  should mean in each is a per-panel decision rather than one rule; and
  the inline picker's list-and-options cursor lives in the KEY layer, so
  routing the wheel to it means reaching that handler from the mouse layer.

- [x] **RT-266 (M, THE RELEASE STILL COPIED BEHIND THE PANEL) — the last
  corner of RT-258.**
  The mouse's **release** is where the transcript's copy happens: jcode parity
  (iter-672) is that a finalized drag selection ALWAYS copies on release,
  with no opt-out, and the text is extracted synchronously so a fast drag
  cannot lose the copy to a stale frame.

  RT-258 absorbed the **press** and the **drag** while a panel is open — so
  there is no new selection to end — but the **release** still ran the copy
  branch. So: the operator selected some transcript text, opened a panel, and
  clicked inside it; the release copied the selection they had made BEFORE
  the panel opened, without them asking for it. The clipboard changed on a
  click that belonged to the panel.

  **Fixed**: the release is absorbed with the press and the drag — the panel
  owns the whole gesture, not just its first half.

  **Pinned** by `a_release_inside_an_open_panel_does_not_copy_a_selection_made_
  before_it`, with the control `a_release_with_no_panel_open_still_copies_the_
  selection` — which also pins the copy-on-release feature itself, which had
  **no test at all** before this row: the release path was exercised by
  nothing, so both the bug and the fix were invisible to the suite.
  **Mutation-proven**: removing the release from the absorbed arm fails the
  first by name ("a release inside an open panel must not copy the selection
  made before it") and leaves the control green.

- [x] **RT-265 (M, THE CONFIGURED SKILLS ROOT WAS IGNORED BY SEVEN CALLERS) —
  the operator's tree was never the tree the tooling used.**
  `[skills] root_dir` is the operator's setting for the skills tree. The
  skills TOOLS and the agent's skill manager honour it (the CLI builds
  `SkillManager::new(config.skills.root_dir.clone())`), and the kernel
  tool's own config-aware branch honours it. Seven other callers did not:

  | caller | what it did | consequence with a custom root |
  |---|---|---|
  | `agent/prompting.rs` (the curator's auto-run) | `platform::operant_skills_dir()` | the curator archived the lifecycle of a tree the operator does not use — and the use clock RT-262 records stayed invisible to it |
  | `agent/skill_bundle.rs` (the bundle loader) | `platform::operant_skills_dir()` — under a comment that claimed "config-aware" | every skill in a bundle came back "missing" and the bundle injected nothing |
  | `cmd_skills.rs` (`skill marketplace install`) | `platform::operant_skills_dir()` | the skill was installed where the agent never looks: the install "succeeded" and the skill did not exist for the model |
  | `cmd_skills.rs` (`skill marketplace updates`) | `platform::operant_skills_dir()` | the update check read the wrong tree ("No installed skills to check") |
  | `cmd_status.rs` | `platform::operant_skills_dir()` (skills dir, curator state, archive count) | the panel reported a tree nobody configured |
  | `cmd_dump.rs` | `platform::operant_skills_dir()` (twice) | the setup dump named a tree nobody configured |

  The default is the platform path, so an operator who never set
  `root_dir` saw no difference — which is why the drift survived: it is
  invisible until the setting is used, and then EVERY skill-facing feature
  except the tools themselves points somewhere else.

  **Fixed**: one rule — the skills tree is the operator's configured root.
  `crate::skills::configured_skills_dir()` resolves it from the runtime
  config (falling back to the platform default when the setting is empty,
  which is what the kernel tool's branch has always done), and the core
  callers use it; the CLI callers use the config they already hold. The
  bundle loader's comment is now true.

  **Pinned** by `the_bundle_loader_reads_the_configured_skills_root`: with
  `[skills] root_dir` pointing at a temp tree that holds the bundle's skill,
  the bundle resolves, loads it and injects its body. Mutation-proven:
  putting the platform default back fails it BY NAME ("the bundle must
  resolve").

- [x] **RT-267 (H, THE CURATOR'S "NEVER ARCHIVE A SKILL A CRON JOB CALLS" RULE
  PROTECTED NOTHING) — three defects on one rule, and the rule is the one
  that decides what gets deleted.**
  The curator owns the lifecycle of agent-created skills: it moves a skill
  out of the way when it looks idle. One class of skill must never be moved:
  the skill a CRON JOB calls — deleting it breaks a schedule, not a
  conversation. The rule existed in the manual review path and was inert in
  three ways:

  1. **It read a database no cron job writes to.** The curator opened
     `<skills>/.curator/cron.db` (`cmd_curator.rs`), while every cron job —
     `operant cron`, the agent runtime, the gateway scheduler — writes
     `<database dir>/operant_cron.db` (`cmd_cron.rs`). The protection set was
     therefore ALWAYS EMPTY: the guard ran, and protected nothing.
  2. **The automatic path had no guard at all.** `run_review` (the manual
     `operant curator run`) skipped cron-referenced skills;
     `apply_automatic_transitions` — the path the agent's curator daemon
     actually runs, and the one that archives on its own cadence — had no
     cron check whatsoever. The same rule, two sibling layers, opposite
     outcomes.
  3. **A failed read read as "nothing is protected".** `run_review` logged
     the error and carried on with an EMPTY set. A transient sqlite error
     (a locked db, an I/O hiccup) therefore turned into the permanent
     archival of a skill a cron job still calls.

  **And the archive was not durable.** `apply_automatic_transitions` dropped
  the errors of the three writes that make an archive real — the tracker's
  `set_state`, the state file, the tracker's save — so `SKILL.md` could end
  up in `.archive` while `usage.json` still said Active: the next pass then
  tries to archive a skill that is gone, and the "active skills" surface
  lists a file that no longer exists. The first-run seed dropped its state
  write too, so a failed seed re-deferred the curator by a full interval on
  every restart.

  **Fixed**:
  - the core owns the cron database path — `cronjobs::db_path(&database_path)`
    → `<database dir>/operant_cron.db` — and the CLI's `operant cron` and
    the curator both go through it. ONE rule, ONE file: a reader that opens
    a different file sees an empty database and reports "nothing references
    this skill";
  - both curator paths read the protection set through ONE helper
    (`cron_protected_skills`) that FAILS CLOSED: an unreadable set is an
    error, not an empty set, so the pass aborts instead of archiving blind;
  - `apply_automatic_transitions` applies the same cron guard (and counts
    the skips as `skipped_cron`), and the agent's daemon opens the live cron
    db — if it cannot be opened, the pass is SKIPPED, not run blind;
  - the tracker's and the state's writes are propagated, so an archive is
    durable or the pass says why it is not; the first-run seed's failure is
    logged with the consequence ("deferred again after a restart").

  **Pinned** by two tests:
  - `the_automatic_curator_never_archives_a_cron_referenced_skill` — an
    agent-created skill a cron job calls survives the automatic pass, and
    the skip is COUNTED. Mutation-proven: the guard removed → archived 1,
    expected 0;
  - `an_unreadable_cron_reference_set_aborts_the_review` — a cron db whose
    reference query fails makes `run_review` return an error instead of
    archiving. Mutation-proven: the empty-set fallback → the review no
    longer aborts.

- [x] **RT-269 (M, THE PERSISTED CURATOR SUMMARY WAS ALWAYS THE PREVIOUS RUN'S)
  — two status panels, one run apart.**
  `run_review` built the run's summary, then **saved** `state.json`, and only
  THEN set `state.last_run_summary` — the field the summary belongs to. So
  the file on disk carried the PREVIOUS run's summary, and none at all after
  the very first run.

  The two readers disagreed: `operant curator status` read the engine's live
  state (`engine.get_state()` — the value in memory, which is the current
  run's), while `operant status` read `<skills>/.curator/state.json` straight
  off disk — the stale copy. So the operator's status line described a run
  that had already been superseded, and after the first run it described
  nothing at all.

  **Fixed**: the summary is set before the state is written, so the persisted
  copy IS the current run's. (The sibling path already had the order right:
  `apply_automatic_transitions` sets the fields, snapshots, then saves.)

  **Pinned** by `the_persisted_summary_is_the_current_runs`: two runs with
  different outcomes (the first scans nothing, the second archives a skill),
  then the file on disk must carry the SECOND run's summary. Mutation-proven:
  the old order (save, then set) fails it BY NAME — the persisted summary is
  the first run's.

- [x] **RT-268 (M, THE UNIFIED PICKER'S WHEEL DID NOTHING) — a hundred
  models, and only the arrow keys.**
  The **inline picker** (the model / account / effort chooser) owns the
  keyboard while it is open: its keys are the picker's own semantics, not
  the transcript's. It also sat in the mouse's hand-written **dialog gate**
  — the same list RT-251 and RT-258 found — and that gate swallows the
  wheel. So the picker's cursor could only be moved with ↑/↓, and a model
  list of a hundred entries was an arrow-key marathon.

  **Fixed**: the picker left the dialog gate, and the wheel now goes through
  the **same handler the keys use** —

      self.handle_inline_interactive_key(
          if up { KeyCode::Up } else { KeyCode::Down },
          KeyModifiers::empty(),
      );

  — so the picker's cursor moves exactly as ↑/↓ move it: the list cursor in
  its first column, the selected entry's option in the others. One source
  of truth: the key handler decides, and the wheel is a vertical key.

  Leaving the gate costs the picker nothing: it has no click handling of
  its own, and the press is absorbed by the **catalogue** gate RT-258 added
  (which covers every panel in `overlay_flags()`), so the picker still
  cannot select the transcript behind itself.

  **Pinned** by `the_wheel_moves_the_inline_pickers_cursor` —
  **mutation-proven**: removing the routing fails it by name ("the wheel
  must move the inline picker's cursor") — and by the RT-258 click table,
  which gained the inline picker so the gate's removal cannot leave the
  picker selecting the transcript behind it.

  **RESIDUAL, named not hidden**: the panels the dialog gate still swallows
  take no wheel: the export dialog (a horizontal format choice — Tab and
  ←/→), the stats dialog (tabs — Tab and ←/→), the context viz (a graph,
  with no cursor at all) and the settings screen (whose ↑/↓ move a cursor
  over the FILTERED entries — a count that only the settings module's own
  key layer can compute, together with the scroll offset that keeps the
  cursor in view). Each is a per-panel decision, not one rule; the settings
  screen's is worth doing, and it belongs to the settings module's key
  layer rather than to the mouse's.
- [x] **RT-270 (M, `${OPERANT_SESSION_ID}` REACHED THE MODEL AS A LITERAL) —
  the setting promised a substitution nothing performed.**
  `[skills] template_vars` is documented as substituting
  `${OPERANT_SKILL_DIR}` / `${OPERANT_SESSION_ID}` in SKILL.md before
  injection (hermes `template_vars` parity, default true), and the
  substitution function itself is correct: given a session id it replaces
  the token, and without one it leaves the token alone.

  **The production call passed no session id.** The only production call —
  `agent::skill_preprocessing::build_skill_invocation_message_in`, the ONE
  function the TUI's `/skill`, the gateway's `/skill` and the gateway's
  `/skills` all come through — hardcoded `None` for the session id, so the
  literal `${OPERANT_SESSION_ID}` was injected into the model's context and
  the skill's own instructions told the model to use a placeholder that does
  not exist. `${OPERANT_SKILL_DIR}` was substituted (the skill dir was
  passed ✓) — only the session id was not, which is why the gap sat in the
  ONE place all three surfaces share.

  **Fixed**: the invocation builder takes the session id it is invoked in,
  and the surfaces that know it pass it: the TUI's current session, the
  gateway's runtime command (the agent's session id inside the
  session-scoped closure). The gateway's SYNC command arm carries no session
  id — its context holds the platform and channel, and the gateway's session
  key also folds in the chat thread — so there the token stays literal: the
  substitution function's documented fallback, named in the config's doc
  rather than left as a silent difference between surfaces.

  **Pinned** by `the_session_id_token_is_substituted_before_injection`: a
  skill whose body names `${OPERANT_SESSION_ID}` must come back with the
  session id in place and the literal token GONE. Mutation-proven: passing
  `None` again fails it BY NAME (the literal token reaches the model).
- [x] **RT-271 (M, THE ARGUMENT WAS DROPPED) — `/model gpt-5` opened the
  whole catalogue.**
  `/model` and `/effort` open the unified inline picker. Both ignored their
  `args`:

      "model" => { … self.open_model_picker_inline(); true }
      "effort" => { … self.open_effort_picker_inline(); true }

  So the operator typed `/model gpt-5`, the picker opened with EVERY row, and
  they had to find the model they had just named — the one thing an argument
  is for. The picker has a filter, and the endpoint fetch's drain RE-APPLIES
  it (`channel_drains.rs` — a filter set at open time survives the 1-2
  second fetch), so the fix is the argument BEING the filter:

      let mut picker = InlineInteractiveState { filter: filter.to_string(), … };
      Self::apply_inline_interactive_filter(&mut picker);
      self.inline_interactive = Some(picker);

  **Pinned** by `a_commands_argument_narrows_the_picker_it_opens`, which
  drives both commands and asserts both halves — the filter text the
  argument becomes and the narrowed list it produces (`/effort high` shows
  exactly one row).
  **Mutation-proven**: passing `""` instead of `args` at either call site
  fails it by name.

- [x] **RT-273 (M, THE FOOTER ADVERTISED A KEY THAT DID NOTHING) — the diff
  viewer's `d toggle scope`.**
  The diff viewer's footer read:

      tab switch pane  ·  ↑↓ navigate  ·  space collapse  ·  d toggle scope

  **Nothing dispatched 'd'.** The panel's key handler has arms for Esc/q,
  Tab/Left/Right, ↑/↓, PageUp/PageDown and Space — and the panel has no
  scope concept at all (its state is: the files, the selected file, the
  active pane, the detail scroll, the render cache, the collapsed set). So
  the operator pressed the key the panel's own footer named, and got
  silence.

  It was worse than a missing feature: the footer is how a panel tells the
  operator what it can do, so a claim in it is a PROMISE. And the footer was
  also silent about the keys that DO work — PageUp/PageDown scroll the
  detail pane, and so does the wheel (since iter-1828) — so it advertised a
  dead key and hid two live ones.

  **Fixed**: the footer names only keys the panel dispatches, and it names
  the page keys and the wheel, which it had left out:

      tab switch pane  ·  ↑↓ navigate  ·  pgup/pgdn/wheel scroll  ·  space collapse

  The text is now a `FOOTER_HINT` constant with the claim's reason beside
  it, so the next reader sees WHY the scope toggle is not named.

  **Pinned** by `the_diff_viewers_footer_only_names_keys_it_dispatches`:
  a table of (the label the footer shows, the key it means, the handler's
  arm that implements it) — every claim is checked against the handler —
  plus the absence of the scope claim (the needle is built by
  concatenation, so the test's own source cannot satisfy it).
  **Mutation-proven**: putting the `d toggle scope` claim back fails it by
  name.
- [x] **RT-272 (M, SEVENTEEN PROVIDER-PROFILE KNOBS WERE ACCEPTED IN SILENCE
  AND THEIR OWN DOCS PROMISED THE OPPOSITE) — the config described a wire
  the runtime does not have.**
  A provider model profile (`[providers.models.<name>]`) carries seventeen
  keys that NOTHING reads: `api_path`, `extra_headers`, `wire_api`,
  `requires_openai_auth`, `azure_openai_resource`, `azure_openai_deployment`,
  `azure_openai_api_version`, `temperature`, `merge_system_into_user`,
  `provider_extra`, `pricing`, `native_tools`, `think`,
  `chat_template_kwargs`, `ollama_num_ctx`, `ollama_num_predict`,
  `ollama_temperature_override`. The client reads only `base_url`, `api_key`,
  `api_keys`, `model`, `timeout_secs`, `max_tokens` and `name`.

  Each of the seventeen carries a doc comment PROMISING a behaviour — extra
  headers "sent with every request", credentials "pulled from
  `OPENAI_API_KEY` or `~/.codex/auth.json`", pricing "merged into the
  cost-tracking lookup", native tools "consulted only by the Groq factory",
  thinking "forwarded as `enable_thinking` in the request body". None of
  those happens. An operator who sets `extra_headers` for a corporate proxy
  gets no header; one who sets `ollama_num_ctx` gets the framework default.

  **And the doctor made it worse**: `operant doctor` hard-ERRORed on a
  provider profile's out-of-range `temperature` — a knob that cannot change
  any request, because nothing reads it. The operator was told their config
  was broken over a setting that does nothing.

  The keys stay in the schema: deleting a field would fail every existing
  `operant.toml` (the config carries `deny_unknown_fields`), and the
  operator's file is not ours to rewrite silently.

  **Fixed**:
  - every one of the seventeen now says so in its own doc comment
    ("ACCEPTED BUT NOT APPLIED ... it has NO effect") — the promise is
    replaced by the truth;
  - `ModelProviderConfig::unread_wire_knobs()` lists them, next to the
    fields it names, so a new key cannot be added to the struct without
    deciding whether it is read;
  - `AppConfig::unused_setting_warnings` REPORTS a set value: one line per
    profile, naming the exact keys the operator must delete ("accepted but
    unread — the runtime applies none of it");
  - the doctor's temperature check is a WARNING that says the value is not
    applied, not an ERROR the operator cannot act on.

  **Pinned** by `a_provider_profile_wire_knob_is_reported_as_unread`: a
  profile that sets `wire_api`, `temperature` and `extra_headers` (and a
  `base_url` the runtime DOES read) produces exactly ONE warning, naming
  the three unread keys and not the base URL; a default config stays
  silent. Mutation-proven: the warning removed → no warning at all.

  removed the schema, config, doctor, CHANGELOG and ledger changes my

  iter-1841; nothing was rewritten, and c6c00d8c remains the original.

  (every `pub fn` / `pub struct` with no reference outside its own file,

  `operant-config` would fail any `operant.toml` that names its table; the
  same rule that kept the seventeen unread provider-profile KEYS in the
  schema (RT-274) keeps these TYPES in the crate.
- [x] **RT-276 (M, A KANBAN RUN WAS NEVER CLOSED) — the task said done, the run
  said running, and the board's own detector called it a zombie.**
  A worker claims a task: `Dispatcher::claim_task` inserts a `task_runs` row
  with status `running`, sets `tasks.status = 'running'` and points
  `tasks.current_run_id` at the run. The work then finishes and the task is
  completed through the LIVE path — `KanbanDb::complete_task` (the
  `operant kanban complete` command and the kanban tool) — which ran:

      UPDATE tasks SET status = 'done', completed_at = ?1, result = ?2 WHERE id = ?3

  No `current_run_id = NULL`, and no `task_runs` update at all. So the run row
  stayed `running` forever and the task kept pointing at it. The subsystem's
  OWN diagnostics (`kanban/diagnostics.rs`) classify exactly that state as a
  **zombie run** and tell the operator to run SQL by hand:

      UPDATE task_runs SET status='orphaned' WHERE id={}

  The only code that closed a run properly — `Dispatcher::complete_run` /
  `fail_run`, which set the run's status, `ended_at` and outcome and cleared

  it (`status = 'completed'`, `ended_at`, the outcome) and clears

  instead of `None`. The board's own detector is clean afterwards.

- [x] **RT-277 (M, THE SUITE'S OWN GATE FLAKED) — another test's delegation
  landed in the frame.**
  `tui::app::tests::highlight_covers_only_the_text_a_copy_carries` has been
  named as a flake since iter-1762 — "1 failure in ~4 full-suite runs", never
  reproduced in isolation. This time it reproduced: three failures in four
  full-suite runs, and the improved panic said exactly what was wrong.

  The app's transcript carries the **process-wide delegation registry's** rows
  as well as its own tool rows (`App::swarm_gallery_members` →
  `async_delegation::list_records()`). The registry is process-wide and its
  seeds live until a drain, so a delegation created by another test — the
  registry tests make two, labelled "first job" and "second job" — landed in
  this test's frame between its two renders. The frame's tool row was another
  test's `○ dlg-1794022236-8 spawned 0s  second job` row, and the `TOOLROW`
  needle was simply gone. The whole transcript moved under the test.

  The file's own discipline already says it:

  > take one at the top of any test that seeds or **reads** the delegation
  > registry

  The transcript READS it, so the transcript's readers take it. **Fixed**: all
  ten transcript-content tests hold `registry_lock()`.

  **Pinned** by `every_transcript_content_test_holds_the_delegation_registry_lock`
  — a table of the ten tests, each checked to hold the lock —
  **mutation-proven**: dropping the lock from one of them fails it by name
  ("the transcript-content test `copy_slices_exact_columns_on_wrapped_rows`
  must hold the delegation registry lock").

  And the panic now says what a reader needs: the needle that is missing and
  the frame's non-empty lines, instead of "called `Option::unwrap()` on a
  `None` value" — which named neither the needle nor the frame, so the one
  fact needed to tell a layout race from a lost message was missing. The
  frame above is what turned a fifteen-iteration mystery into a one-line
  diagnosis.

  **Lesson, now recorded four times in this campaign** (RT-212's dead source
  guard, RT-213's red lint gate, RT-257's vacuous reader, and this): a check
  that cannot fail is worse than no check — and a check that fails without
  saying WHY is a check that costs more than it saves.

- [x] **RT-279 (M, A REFRESHED OAUTH TOKEN THAT COULD NOT BE WRITTEN BACK WAS
  REPORTED AS "REFRESHED SUCCESSFULLY") — the on-disk credential stayed stale
  and nobody said so.**
  The credential pool refreshes an OAuth token and then writes it back to
  `~/.operant/auth.json`. The write's error was dropped with `let _ =` at
  both call sites, and the line above it logged "OAuth token refreshed
  successfully" either way:

      let _ = refresher.persist_to_auth_store(&self.provider, cred, &response);

  `persist_to_auth_store` writes the store atomically (temp file + rename)
  and CAN fail — a read-only home, a full disk, an unparsable store. When it
  did, the in-memory credential was good (the refresh had succeeded) but
  the ON-DISK credential stayed the pre-refresh one. After a restart the
  provider rejects that expired token, and the operator sees an auth error
  with no hint that the write failed — the log said everything was fine.

  **Fixed**: the write's error is reported at both call sites (the provider
  and the credential are named, and the message says the on-disk credential
  stays stale), and the "successfully" line above it now claims only what
  happened — the token was refreshed.

  **Pinned** by `the_credential_pool_does_not_swallow_the_auth_store_write_error`
  — a source-grep contract in the repo's own shape (cf.
  `the_cli_surface_is_phase_one_config_only` in config.rs): the pool must not
  discard the persist error. The needle is built by concatenation so the
  test's own source cannot satisfy it. Mutation-proven: the `let _ =` back
  fails it by name.
- [ ] **RT-280 (M, THE GATEWAY'S "RESUME AFTER A RESTART" AND "RESET AFTER
  /STOP" ARE IMPLEMENTED AND NEVER SWITCHED ON) — a documented behaviour
  that cannot happen, and the decision it needs is a product's.**
  `PersistentSessionStore` carries two persisted flags with live read
  branches in `get_or_create_session` — the production path every session
  access takes:

  - `suspended` — "When true, next access auto-resets (from /stop)";
  - `resume_pending` — "Session was interrupted by restart, resume on next
    access" (the branch returns the SAME session id).

  Both are read on every access, and **neither is written by any production
  path**: the only writers are `suspend_session` (`:1153`),
  `mark_resume_pending` (`:1176`) and `suspend_recently_active` (`:1886`),
  and a whole-repo grep finds only their declarations and their tests. The
  live `/stop` arm signals the interrupt flag and then writes an in-memory
  breadcrumb into the gateway's in-memory `SessionStore` — no I/O at all.

  So the two documented behaviours cannot fire: after a gateway restart no
  session is ever resume-pending (the session id is not preserved), and the
  `/stop` auto-reset never happens. The columns are persisted, read back on
  every load, and `prune_old_entries` skips suspended entries — a branch
  that can never be taken.

  **Why this is open and not fixed**: wiring it is a product decision, not
  a patch. "Resume the interrupted session after a restart" needs an answer
  to *how recently active* a session must be to be resumed (the sweep takes
  a `max_age_seconds`), and "auto-reset after /stop" changes what a chat
  keeps. Both are observable behaviours an operator would notice. The
  supporting note from the audit is recorded here too: the state writers
  drop the SQLite error (`let _ = self.save_entry(&entry);` at `:1156`,
  `:1181`, `:1206`, `:1781`) while sibling writers in the SAME struct
  propagate it (`:1226`, `:1455`) — so wiring the feature as-is would
  import a silent failure (the map says "suspended" while the database says
  otherwise). **The honest step taken here**: the two fields' doc comments
  now say they are not set by any production path, so the code no longer
  promises a behaviour it does not have.

  **LABEL NOTE**: the concurrent slice committed its own `iter-1851`
  ("the suite's own gate flaked — another test's delegation landed in the
  frame", 14eba567) while this row was in flight; both commits carry the
  label `iter-1851` and history was NOT rewritten. Mine is `bf2d7bdd`; the
  collision is recorded here rather than papered over.

  The `/help` overlay lists the commands, the Skills section, the whole

      Esc to close · ↑↓/pgup/pgdn/wheel scroll · type to filter · /help <cmd>

  Space does nothing" is a bug report about the HELP, not about the key.

  row's above it (`RewindError::SaveFailed`), and the tail-commit logs the

  plainly that it is missing a row.

- [x] **RT-282 (M, THE SETTINGS SCREEN'S WHEEL DID NOTHING) — and it could
  not simply move the cursor.**
  The settings screen's list carries a cursor, and the wheel did nothing in
  it. The mouse's hand-written **dialog gate** — the same list RT-251 and
  RT-258 found — swallowed the wheel before it could reach the panel, so a
  long settings list could only be walked with the arrow keys.

  And the wheel could not simply move the cursor the way the other panels
  do: the visible count here is the **FILTERED** entry count (the search
  query hides rows), and the cursor must stay in view. Both facts live in
  the settings module's own key layer — a module the mouse layer cannot
  reach.

  **Fixed**: the settings screen left the dialog gate (it loses nothing: its
  press is absorbed by the **catalogue** gate RT-258 added, which covers
  every panel in `overlay_flags()`), and the wheel calls the settings
  module's OWN rule:

      pub(crate) fn select_next_visible(screen: &mut SettingsScreen) { … }
      pub(crate) fn select_prev_visible(screen: &mut SettingsScreen) { … }

  — extracted from the ↑/↓ arms themselves, so the arrow keys and the wheel
  run **one** rule. A second copy of "move the settings cursor" in the mouse
  layer would be a second rule, and two rules drift.

  **Pinned** by `the_wheel_moves_the_settings_screens_cursor` — both
  directions — **mutation-proven**: removing the routing fails it by name
  ("the wheel must move the settings screen's cursor").

  This closes the wheel residual RT-264 named: of the five panels the dialog
  gate still swallowed, the inline picker (RT-268) and the settings screen
  (this row) have a cursor and now take the wheel; the export dialog, the
  stats dialog and the context viz have no vertical cursor at all — their
  choices are horizontal (a format, tabs) or a graph — so the wheel stays
  absorbed there, and that is the right answer rather than a leftover.

- [ ] **RT-285 (M-H, THREE DORMANT SURFACES THAT LOOK LIVE) — each needs a
  product decision, and one of them can already be seen not working.**
  A third read-only sweep of `crates/operant-core` (the agent, session,
  gateway, org, context, cost, provider-catalog and cron-scheduler
  subsystems) found three surfaces that are implemented, documented and
  never switched on. None is a wrong behaviour today; each reads as a live
  feature to anyone reading the code, and each is named here rather than
  wired or deleted on a guess.

  | surface | what it claims | what actually happens |
  |---|---|---|
  | `session::autocompact::Autocompactor` (766 lines, config, stats, marker format) | "It runs **after** a session's scheduled execution has already finished"; "the scheduler drives it" | nothing constructs it outside its own integration test; the cron scheduler — the named driver — has no compaction call at all (`grep -rn "compact" crates/operant-core/src/cronjobs` finds no matches), and no config key exposes it. Cron seat sessions grow unbounded. |
  | `SessionStore::discard` | "Delete a session's transcript from memory **and disk**. Destructive, and named as such. This is the only operation here that loses data." | it only drops the resident copy (`self.warm().remove(key)`); the rows survive in the database, so `clear_history()` does NOT durably wipe a session — switching away and back rehydrates the "wiped" history. The only production caller (`agent/events.rs`) believes otherwise ("without this the very next acquire would rehydrate the history"), and the negative-control test in `cron_session_isolation.rs` proves nothing (it uses the memory-only `add_message` and re-selects the same id, which `set_session_id` skips). |
  | `TurnRetryState`'s restart signals (`restart_with_compressed`, `restart_with_rotated_credential`, `restart_with_rebuilt_messages` + `has_restart_signal` / `clear_restart_signals`) | "Restart signals (set by error handlers, read by outer loop)"; the "rebuild messages" restart is described as a content-filter-stall recovery | every hit is inside the declaring file (the rest are its own tests); `agent/run.rs` — the consumer — never reads them and implements the compress/rotate recovery inline via its own flags. The rebuild-messages restart does not exist anywhere, and `ContentPolicyBlocked` is never handled. The fields are `pub` in a public module, so removing them is a semver-visible change. |

  **Why these are open**: each one needs a decision this campaign must not
  make silently — mount the autocompactor (where does the post-run hook go:
  the cron scheduler or the agent's turn end? marker or summarising
  default? which config?), make `/reset` destroy the persisted transcript or
  only the in-memory view, and build or delete the rebuild-messages restart.
  The autocompactor and the `discard` question are observable to an
  operator (a cron session that grows forever; a "wiped" history that comes
  back), which is exactly why they are decisions rather than bugs to patch.
- [x] **RT-286 (M, THE NON-STREAMING CONTEXT-OVERFLOW RETRY NEVER FAILED
  TYPED) — the arm's own comment said it did, and the gateway's only
  self-heal could not fire.**
  `[agent] stream = false` is a documented, supported knob. On that path the
  context-overflow compression arm ended in a bare `.await?`:

      self.call_with_loop_timeout(self.client.chat(retry_request)).await?

  so a second overflow after a compression that did not shrink the history
  escaped as the RAW provider error — even though the arm's own comment
  ("the SECOND overflow fails typed") and the compression callee's doc
  ("the caller ... fails typed instead") both promise the typed failure. The
  streaming arm does exactly that; the rule also exists in the non-streaming
  ROTATION arm. The port landed in the wrong arm.

  It matters because the gateway's recovery keys ONLY on the typed error
  (`crates/operant-cli/src/gateway_runner.rs`: "compact the stored history and
  retry the turn once"). On the non-streaming path the raw error never
  reached it, and the operator got the provider's message instead of "Run
  /compact, then send the message again."

  **Fixed**: the non-streaming compression arm applies the same two-strike
  rule as its streaming sibling — the retry's error is classified, and a
  second overflow that the compression did not reduce fails with the typed
  context-exhausted error (the token count and the window it compared
  against).

  **Pinned** by `the_non_streaming_compression_arm_fails_typed` — a
  source-grep contract over the ARM (the repo's own shape): the
  non-streaming compression arm must contain the typed return. The needle is
  the CODE shape, built by concatenation, so neither the test's own source
  nor a comment that merely names the error can satisfy it. Mutation-proven:
  the bare `.await?` back fails it by name.

- [x] **RT-288 (H, EVERY PER-SEAT BUDGET OVERRIDE WAS A SILENT NO-OP) — the
  command wrote one sqlite file and the enforcement read another.**
  `operant budget set <seat> --cap N` printed "Budget override set for
  '<seat>'". The row went into the **app** database
  (`~/.operant/database.db`). Both enforcement paths — the gateway's turn
  gate (`seat_budget_db().get(employee_id)`) and the cron scheduler's budget
  gate (`with_budgets(...)`) — read the **org sibling**

  org family's rows (seat policies, context injection, seat budgets) live
  in the sibling of the app database, and a store opened at the app
  database path is a store the enforcement never sees. The budget command
  was the odd one out.

  **Fixed**: the core owns the path — `SeatBudgetDb::init_org_sibling(app_db_path)`
  (the same rule `org::context_injection` follows) — and BOTH the command
  and the gateway mount use it. Rows an earlier build wrote into the app
  database are copied across **once** (recorded in the sibling), so an
  operator's existing override is not orphaned by the fix.

  **Pinned** by two tests: `the_org_sibling_store_sees_the_rows_the_app_db_store_wrote`
  (the core: a row written to the app database is visible to the store the
  enforcement opens, the sibling is the file it opens, and the migration
  runs ONCE — a row written to the app database afterwards must not come
  back) and `the_budget_command_writes_to_the_store_the_enforcement_reads`
  (the CLI: the command's row is visible to the enforcement's store AND
  the command does not create the app database at all — without that
  assertion the one-time migration masked the wrong path). Both
  mutation-proven: the app database back → each fails by name.

- [x] **RT-290 (M, `verify_task`'s `phases` PARAMETER WAS ACCEPTED AND
  IGNORED) — the model asked for a subset and got the whole recipe.**
  The tool's schema says "For \"run\": subset of phases to run, e.g.
  [\"build\", \"test\"]", and the parameter was in the args struct. The
  body never read it: `handle_run` detected the recipe and ran every phase
  it had — bootstrap, build and test — whatever the model asked for. A model
  that asked for just the tests also paid for the build, and a model that
  asked for a phase that does not exist got the full recipe with no error.

  recipe whose build and test phases each leave a marker: only the
  requested phase may leave its marker) and
  `verify_task_rejects_an_unknown_phase_name` (an unknown name is an error
  that names the problem). Mutation-proven: the filter removed → both fail
  by name.
- [x] **RT-291 (M-H, `delegate_task`'s `toolsets` PARAMETER WAS ACCEPTED AND
  SILENTLY IGNORED) — the model was told it could scope the child and
  could not.**
  The tool's model-facing schema carries `toolsets` twice — top level
  ("Optional toolsets to enable for the sub-agent") and per task ("Optional
  toolsets to enable for this task"). The body never read either: the
  child's toolset came from the parent's policy alone
  (`compute_child_toolsets` derives it from the parent's list, the parent's
  disabled list and the role). The struct's `#[expect(dead_code)]` — "fields
  deserialized from tool-call JSON; optional fields kept for schema parity"
  — is what silenced the compiler for the unread field.

  So a model that asked "delegate this with only the terminal toolset" got
  a child with the parent's full set, and nothing said so.

  **Fixed**: the request is honoured, **narrow-only** — the child's set is
  intersected with the requested one, so a request can only lower what the
  parent allows and can never add a toolset the parent does not have (the
  parent's policy is the ceiling). An empty request means no toolsets. The
  narrowing is applied before the orchestrator's own delegation grant, so
  an orchestrator keeps the ability to delegate. The parameter now reaches
  all three arms — the foreground single call, the background dispatch and
  the swarm (a task's own request wins over the top-level one).

  **Pinned** by `the_requested_toolsets_narrow_the_child_set`: a request of
  `["terminal"]` leaves exactly that toolset; an empty request leaves
  none; and a request naming a toolset the parent lacks does NOT add it.
  Mutation-proven: the narrowing removed → it fails by name.
- [x] **RT-292 (L-M, THE VERIFICATION EVIDENCE LEDGER'S WRITE ERROR WAS

  record none.**
  `verify_task`'s module doc promises it "records every phase in the
  `verification_events` evidence ledger". The write's error was dropped
  with `let _ =`:

      let _ = self.database.record_verification_event(...);

  so a failed write left the ledger missing a phase while the tool returned
  success — and `operant verify evidence` (the surface that reads the
  ledger) showed a history that quietly disagrees with what the tool
  reported.

  **Fixed**: the error is reported (the recipe, the phase and the error are
  named in the warning), so a missing evidence row is visible instead of

  **Pinned** by `the_verification_evidence_write_error_is_not_dropped` — a
  source-grep contract in the repo's own shape (the needle is built by

  Mutation-proven: the dropped form back → it fails by name.
- [ ] **RT-293 (M, TWO SURFACES THAT CLAIM A DELIVERY OR A MEMORY ENGINE

  Two more "looks live" surfaces from the fourth sweep of the core:

  | surface | what it claims | what actually happens |

Useful for alerting when background tasks complete." | it writes a tracing log and returns `{"delivered": true}`. Nothing is delivered: there is no notify/dbus/desktop sink anywhere in the workspace, and the schema's `priority` parameter is never read. The false claim is pinned by a test (`assert_eq!(parsed["delivered"], true)`). |

  deleted (memory-wire owns MEMORY.md/USER.md) or wired for real?

  The honest half that CAN be done without a decision is recorded in the

- [x] **RT-294 (M, A FAILED INSIGHTS QUERY READ AS "NO ACTIVITY") — the
  model could not tell a broken database from a quiet week.**
  `session_insights` asks the engine for a report over a window. When the
  session query FAILED, the engine logged a warning and returned the plain
  empty report — so the tool answered `{"empty": true}` and the model read
  "no activity in that window". A database fault was indistinguishable from
  a quiet week, and the only trace was a log line.

  **Fixed**: the report carries the failure (`error`), the failed path fills
  it in, and the tool's output includes it — so a failed query says so.

  **Pinned** by `a_failed_insights_query_is_not_reported_as_an_empty_report`:
  the sessions table is dropped so the query really fails, and the report
  AND the tool's output must carry the error. Mutation-proven: the plain
  empty report back → it fails by name.
- [x] **RT-295 (M, A BROKEN RECALL ENGINE READ AS "ZERO HITS") — the caller
  could not tell a failed store from an empty session.**
  The adaptive retrieval's round gathered its candidates with
  `engine.recall(...).await.unwrap_or_default()`. A store error therefore
  became an EMPTY hit list — and the round came back `Ok` with no evidence
  and no leads, exactly like a session with nothing to recall. The model
  was told "no hits", the operator saw nothing, and the real failure (a
  database error) was never reported.

  **Fixed**: the recall's error PROPAGATES — `next_round` already returns a
  `Result`, so the failure now surfaces to the caller (the LCM tool) instead
  of being flattened into "nothing found".

  **Pinned** by `a_failed_recall_is_not_reported_as_zero_hits`: the FTS
  table the recall reads is dropped, so the recall really fails, and the
  round must come back as an ERROR — not as a round with no hits.
  Mutation-proven: the `unwrap_or_default()` back → the round comes back
  `Ok` with `evidence_found: []` and the test fails by name.
- [x] **RT-296 (M-H, THE FTS INDEX WAS NEVER BACKFILLED) — every message
  that predated it was permanently invisible to `session_search`.**
  `messages_fts` is an **external-content** FTS5 table: it starts EMPTY,
  and only the triggers populate it — and they fire for NEW inserts only.
  The creation path created the table, created the triggers, and returned:

      if exists { return Ok(()); }

  so the one moment a backfill could have happened was the moment it was
  missed. There is no `rebuild` anywhere in the crate.

  The consequence: on any database that held messages before the FTS table
  existed, those messages can never be found again. The search path the
  `session_search` tool uses (`search_sessions_filtered`) joins
  `messages_fts` with **no LIKE fallback** — the LIKE path exists but only
  fires on an error, and an empty-but-healthy index returns `Ok(vec![])`.
  So an install's whole pre-FTS history was silently unsearchable.

  **Fixed**: when the index is first created, it is rebuilt once
  (`INSERT INTO messages_fts(messages_fts) VALUES('rebuild')`), inside the
  same migration pass — so a failure aborts the init rather than leaving a
  half-indexed database. The triggers keep it in sync afterwards.

  **Pinned** by `fts_index_backfills_messages_that_predate_it`: a message is
  written, the index and its triggers are dropped (simulating a pre-FTS
  database), the database is re-opened — and the search must find the
  message that predates the index. Mutation-proven: the rebuild removed →
  the search finds nothing.
- [x] **RT-297 (M, THE CHECKPOINT STORE'S EXCLUDE FILE WAS WRITTEN WITH THE
  ERROR DROPPED) — the store could snapshot itself, exactly as the code
  warns.**
  The shadow store's exclude file is the ONLY thing that stops the store
  from snapshotting itself — the code says so in the comment right above
  it, and explains why the file is rewritten every time ("a store created
  before the list grew kept the old one forever, and the self-snapshot loop
  below is exactly what that let happen"). Both writes were dropped:

      let _ = std::fs::create_dir_all(store.join("info"));
      let _ = std::fs::write(&exclude, ...);

  so a failed write left `ensure_store` returning `Ok`, and `take_checkpoint`
  went on to `git add -A` — into precisely that self-snapshot loop. The
  working-tree size bounds do not stop it: they measure the tree, not the
  store's own packed objects. The code records the incident it caused (11
  commits whose reachable blobs total 2.6 GiB).

  **Fixed**: both errors PROPAGATE. The caller already turns an `Err` from
  `ensure_store` into "checkpoint refused" (and a warning), so the write
  failure now stops the checkpoint instead of hiding inside it.

  **Pinned** by `ensure_store_fails_when_the_exclude_file_cannot_be_written`:
  a store that already looks like a git store (so the failure under test is
  the exclude WRITE, not `git init`) with `info` as a file — the exclude
  file cannot be written, and the store must be refused.
  Mutation-proven: the swallowed shape back → `ensure_store` returns `Ok(())`
  and the test fails by name.

  **Alongside**: the existing test
  `an_existing_store_gets_its_exclude_file_repaired` used to run against the
  LIVE store on the operator's box, which made it depend on that box's home
  being writable — and a read-only home is exactly the case the repair now
  refuses loudly. It uses a temp store with a stale exclude file instead,
  which is the property the test is actually about.

- [x] **RT-298 (M, THE `cron` TOOL REJECTED SCHEMA-COMPLIANT CALLS) — the
  model could not create a cron job without a string the schema says it may
  omit, and the tool reported the wrong next run for the form its own doc
  advertises.**
  Two defects in the same arm:

  1. `scheduleDisplay` is `Option<String>` in the args struct — so
     schemars does NOT list it as required — but the body demanded it:
     `ok_or_else(... "Missing 'schedule_display' for job creation")`. No
     prompt or doc told the model the field exists, so a model that
     followed the schema got an error. The sibling CLI path
     (`cmd_cron.rs`) never asks the operator for a display string: it
     derives one from the schedule.
  2. the tool computed `next_run_at` with a PRIVATE copy of the schedule
     rule, and that copy parsed only what the `cron` crate accepts — so
     the 5-field form the module's own doc advertises ("`0 9 * * *` fires
     at 09:00 UTC") produced `None`, and the tool answered
     `"next_run_at": null` for a job the DATABASE had already scheduled
     correctly (the database uses the shared rule).

  **Fixed**: the display is DERIVED from the schedule when the caller did
  not supply one (exactly what the CLI does), and the next run comes from
  the SHARED rule (`cronjobs::schedule::next_run_from_schedule`) — the one
  the database and the scheduler use. The private copy is deleted.

  **Pinned** by `cron_create_accepts_a_five_field_schedule_and_reports_the_next_run`:
  a create call with `schedule = "0 9 * * *"` and NO `scheduleDisplay` must
  succeed, must report a non-null `next_run_at`, and must store the derived
  display. Mutation-proven: the display demanded again → the call is
  rejected and the test fails by name.

      /transcript, /cancel, /clear, /cls, /clear-view,

- [x] **RT-300 (M, THE SESSION HUB'S SUBAGENT DETAIL PROMISED A WAY BACK THAT
  DID NOT EXIST) — one ← clears it, and Esc closes the whole hub.**
  The hub's RIGHT pane carries the subagent's detail (its goal, model and
  dispatch time), and the last line of that pane said:

      ←← / Esc returns to the list

  Neither half was true. The hub's **Left** arm clears the detail on ONE
  press (a second press would fall through to the close-tap, which arms and
  then closes the hub), and the hub's **Esc** arm closes the WHOLE hub:

      KeyCode::Left => {
          if self.session_hub.focused_subagent.is_some() {
              self.session_hub.focused_subagent = None;
          } else {
              self.session_hub.left_tap_close();
          }
      }
      …
      KeyCode::Esc => self.session_hub.close(),

  So the key the panel named — Esc — did the one thing the operator was NOT
  asking for: it closed the session browser they were using, and the
  subagent detail they had opened went with it. The claim also contradicted
  the hub's OWN header, painted on the same screen: "s cycles filters · Esc
  closes".

  **Fixed**: the line names what the keys do — "← clears this detail · Esc
  closes the hub" — so the hub keeps ONE Esc rule (Esc closes) and the
  detail view says which key clears it. The behaviour is unchanged: the
  detail is a PANE-level view (it replaces the message preview; the session
  list was never covered), so Esc closing the modal is the hub's rule and
  the line was the thing that lied.

  **Pinned** by `the_session_hubs_subagent_detail_names_only_the_keys_that_leave_it`:
  the test paints the REAL hub into a TestBackend, reads back the frame the
  OPERATOR reads, and then drives the REAL handler for every key the line
  names — Left must clear the detail, Esc must close the hub. It is
  behavioural on purpose: a source-level check could not have caught this
  class, because the arm the line named (Left) EXISTS — it just does
  something else — and the Esc it named lives in a different arm entirely.
  **Mutation-proven**: putting the old claim back fails the test with the
  painted frame in the message ("←← / Esc returns to the list").

  **The sweep this came from**: the three panels whose hints were not yet
  audited — the session hub, the plugins hub and the journey view — were
  compared, claim by claim, against the arms that dispatch them. The plugins
  hub's "↑/↓ navigate · Enter/t toggle · Esc close" and the journey view's
  "↑/↓ navigate · Tab switch · Esc close" are honoured by their handlers
  (both take Up/Down, the hub also Enter/'t'/Space, the view also Tab, and
  both close on Esc), and the session hub's other claims are honest too
  ("Esc to clear" on the search row — Esc clears the query while the search
  is active; "s cycle"; "No transcript cached — press r to load"; "Enter
  switches to this session"). This row is the one false claim of the sweep.
- [x] **RT-301 (M, FIVE PLACES CUT FREE TEXT WITH A BYTE SLICE) — a panic
  waiting for one multi-byte character.**
  A byte slice panics when the cut lands inside a multi-byte character.
  The repo already paid for this once: the CLI's `cmd_checkpoints.rs` says
  so in a comment — "a byte slice panics when the cut lands inside a
  multi-byte character (the same defect that killed `operant sessions list`

  | site | what is cut | the panic |
  |---|---|---|
  | `agent/insights.rs` | a model id (`&m.model[..28]`) | the insights report formatter panics |
  | `agent/learning_graph.rs` | a memory file's first heading (`&first_line[..80]`) | the learning graph panics while building a card |
  | `gateway/webhook_subscriptions.rs` | a webhook response body (`&text[..500]`) | the subscription probe panics on any unicode body |
  | `tools/cli_discovery.rs` | a discovered CLI's description (`&description[..197]`) | the discovery panics |

- [x] **RT-303 (M, THE KEYBINDING CATALOGUE'S COMPLETION CONTEXT NAMED TWO
  ACTIONS THE POPUP DOES NOT PERFORM) — Tab accepts; Shift+Tab cycles the
  effort.**
  The keybinding registry is the source of truth for *what the bindings are*:
  `/keys` and `/hotkeys` print its rows, and every accepted key event is
  matched against it to count usage. It is deliberately NOT the dispatcher —
  `app/key_handling.rs` runs the if-chain — so the two tables drift, and
  the catalogue is the one the operator READS.

  The Completion context ("In completion menu" — the slash typeahead popup
  and the `@` file-ref popup) had six rows. Two of them were false:

  | catalogue said | what the key actually does |
  |---|---|
  | Tab → "Next completion" | Tab ACCEPTS the highlighted completion (`accept_suggestion()`), and the popup's list shrinks by one |
  | Shift+Tab → "Previous completion" | Shift+Tab does nothing to the completion — it cycles the reasoning effort (`cycle_effort()`), which the GLOBAL context's row already names |

  Two details make the Shift+Tab row doubly dead: the completion index does
  not move (pinned at iter-455 by
  `test_shift_tab_cycles_permission_mode_not_completions`), and crossterm
  delivers Shift+Tab as `KeyCode::BackTab` — so a row spelled `Tab` +
  `KeyModifiers::SHIFT` could not have matched the event even if its action
  were right. The Global context's own row spells it `BackTab` + `SHIFT` ✓.

  MEASURED through the real handler with the popup genuinely open (typed
  "/", so the app computes its own 111 suggestions):

      AFTER SLASH      text="/" suggestions=111 idx=Some(0)
      AFTER DOWN       idx=Some(1)
      AFTER DOWN2      idx=Some(2)
      AFTER UP         idx=Some(1)
      AFTER TAB        text="/thinking-display"   <- accepted, not stepped
      AFTER ENTER      text="/todos"              <- accepted
      AFTER SHIFT+TAB  idx unchanged, suggestions unchanged

  **Fixed**: the Tab row now says "Accept completion" (the action it names
  is `KeyAction::CompletionAccept`, the same action the Enter row names and
  the same one the PROMPT context's Tab row already named), and the
  Shift+Tab row is removed. The effort cycle keeps its Global row ✓, so
  nothing is lost from the catalogue.

  **Pinned** by `the_completion_contexts_catalogue_rows_match_the_typeahead_popup`:
  a table-driven (context, chord) -> action check. Every Completion row is
  driven through the REAL handler with the popup open, and the observed
  effect must match the row's action — Down moves the highlight forward, Up
  moves it back, Tab and Enter accept (the composer's text changes and the
  popup shrinks), Esc dismisses. The pin also requires that NO completion
  row names Shift+Tab in either spelling (`Tab`+SHIFT or `BackTab`).
  Behavioural on purpose: a source grep cannot tell "Tab accepts" from "Tab
  steps", because both are one arm. **Mutation-proven**: the old rows back
  fail it by name ("the Completion context's Tab+KeyModifiers(0x0) row names
  the wrong action").

  **The method this came from**: the catalogue was audited as a (context,
  chord) matrix, the way the skill asks — 155 rows over 12 contexts, with
  the chords taken from the registry itself rather than retyped. The Global
  context (29 rows) is already pinned by
  `global_bindings_should_be_dispatched_in_key_handling` (a source grep
  over the dispatch), the vim contexts by
  `every_string_dispatched_vim_binding_is_reachable`, and the scroll ladder
  by `scroll_ladder_catalogue_matches_dispatch`. The PROMPT context (34
  rows) and the Completion context (6) were NOT pinned against the dispatch
  — the Completion context is this row, and the PROMPT context's rows were
  checked row by row against the arms (its Tab row is right ✓, its
  Shift+Tab absence is right ✓ because the Global row names the effort
  cycle). The DIALOG context's four rows (Esc / Enter / Tab / Shift+Tab)
  are the next context to pin: the command palette — the app's main dialog —
  has no Tab arm at all, so "Next field" is true for the ask-user dialog
  and false for the palette; that split is named here rather than fixed in
  this row.
- [x] **RT-304 (M, THE `tool_backend` TOOL ADVERTISED A SWITCH IT NEVER
  PERFORMED) — and four search engines that no longer exist.**
  The tool's model-facing description said it "optionally switches the
  active backend", and its schema exposed a `backend` parameter. The body
  never read it: `execute` parses the args, reads `tool_name`, and prints
  a static table. There is no writer anywhere in the crate
  (`set_backend` / `switch_backend` / `active_backend` — no hits), and the
  struct's `#[expect(dead_code)]` ("optional fields kept for schema
  parity") is what silenced the compiler for the unread field.

  Worse, the table still advertised **tavily, exa, searxng and ddg** as
  web_search backends — all four were deleted from the tree by plan 11C1
  (`build_search_candidates` returns exactly one provider: sourcehound).
  So a model could read the schema, ask to "switch web_search to tavily",
  and be told the switch happened (it was ignored) against a list of
  engines that do not exist.

  **Fixed**: the tool is honest — the `backend` parameter is gone from the
  schema, the description says it reports (READ-ONLY) and does not switch,
  and the web_search backends are the one engine that is actually there.

  **Pinned** by `tool_backend_is_query_only_and_lists_no_deleted_provider`:
  the schema has no `backend` property, the description does not promise a
  switch, and web_search's available backends are exactly
  `["sourcehound"]`. The existing "known tool" test was updated to the same
  truth (it asserted the five deleted engines).
  Mutation-proven: the four engines back → both tests fail by name.

  **Still a product decision (not a defect)**: if the product wants a REAL
  backend switch, that is a new feature — it needs a live selection seam
  (a per-session override read by each tool), which does not exist today.

- [x] **RT-306 (M, `web_fetch` READ THE WHOLE RESPONSE BODY INTO MEMORY) —
  the RAM-exhaustion path `http_request` had already closed.**
  `http_request` reads its body through a 2 MiB chunked cap with a
  truncation marker — the fix R48-7 was filed for ("`text()` read the
  whole response into memory with no cap, so one large or hostile
  endpoint streamed the process out of RAM"). Its sibling `web_fetch`,
  registered right beside it, did not: it called `response.text().await`
  and kept the whole body — one large (or hostile) endpoint away from
  taking the agent's process down.

  It also drifted on the method: `http_request` uppercases it, `web_fetch`
  matched the raw string, so `{"method":"post"}` was rejected as
  "Unsupported HTTP method: post" while the sibling accepted it.

  **Fixed**: `web_fetch` uses the SHARED bounded reader
  (`http_tool::read_bounded_body`, now `pub(crate)`) and normalises the
  method case exactly like its sibling.

  **Pinned** by `web_fetch_reads_its_body_through_the_bounded_reader` — a
  source-grep contract in the repo's own shape whose needles are the CODE
  SHAPE ("match response.text().await"), because the file's own comment
  quotes the old call and a bare needle matched it. Mutation-proven: the
  unbounded read back → the contract fails by name.

  credential reached the model and the transcript.**
  The tool's own doc says it "dump[s] the effective configuration as JSON

  `api_key`, `token`, `secret`, `password` or exactly `auth`. The config's
  field is `email_smtp_pass` — which matches NONE of them — so the SMTP

  **Fixed**: the mask rule also covers `pass` (`email_smtp_pass` is the
  only `pass`-like field in the config, so nothing else is over-masked).

  **Pinned** by `redact_masks_email_smtp_pass`: the password is masked,
  a token is masked, and a host is not.
  Mutation-proven: the `pass` rule removed → the password comes back

- [x] **RT-308 (M, THE TUI'S GOLDEN CORPUS WAS RED AT THE TIP — EVERY SCENARIO
  IT PINNED WAS ALSO RED) — eleven drifted baselines and one dead assertion,
  all from one un-proven rendering change.**
  `crates/operant-cli/tests/tui_scenarios` is the TUI's regression gate: each
  scenario drives the real app through a scripted key sequence and compares the
  captured frame byte-for-byte with a committed baseline. `_run.py verify`
  reported:

      status-row            status_message contains Session status (actual: null)
      status-row.80x24      status_message contains Session status (actual: null)
      ask-user-dialog                 Rendered screen differs from baseline
      failed-turn-no-duplicate-prompt  Rendered screen differs from baseline
      model-picker / model-picker.80x24  Rendered screen differs from baseline
      permission-dialog              Rendered screen differs from baseline
      permission-request             Rendered screen differs from baseline
      skills-view / skills-view.80x24 Rendered screen differs from baseline
      thinking-block-reasoning-attr  Rendered screen differs from baseline
      tool-error-then-success        Rendered screen differs from baseline
      transcript-tool-error-line     Rendered screen differs from baseline

  The cause was a single earlier rendering change in this repo — the notice
  TTL — which made transient notifications (copied to clipboard, Agent init
  failed, steer queued, shell results, /status) expire after three seconds
  instead of persisting forever, released their reserved notification row, and
  pushed eleven baselines and one assertion out of date in one step. The
  change itself is correct: an immortal "copied to clipboard" line is a
  rendering bug, and the corpus's own NOTES for the affected scenarios
  documented the span the new behaviour removes. What was missing was
  proof: the goldens are the record of the rendering contract, and a
  behaviour change that is not re-proven leaves the gate red and useless.

  **The scenario fix.** `status-row` asserted a one-shot event that the new
  TTL had made transient. It now arms the status row with a MODE message
  instead: `<alt+y>` enters copy mode, whose hint is set through
  `set_status_message_persistent` and therefore has no TTL, so the row IS in
  the captured frame. `/status` is still the first half of the key sequence,
  so the system-annotation transcript style it pushes is still pinned, and
  the assertion now reads `status_message contains Copy mode` — a message the
  frame cannot lose.

  **The goldens.** All nine drifted scenarios (eleven runs, counting the
  80x24 variants) were re-proven — plus `skills-view`, which was already green
  and was re-proven as a control, thirteen runs in all — with `_run.py
  prove`, which renders each scenario four times: twice for determinism, once
  writing the golden through the tool's own writer, and a fourth gating the
  committed file with no accept flag. Result:

      deterministic + goldened : 13   (10 scenarios, 13 runs with the 80x24 variants)
      unstable (3rd run drift) : 0
      nondeterministic         : 0
      broken (non-zero exit)   : 0

  and the full corpus now re-verifies with zero drift.

  **Why this is RT-worthy and not chore.** A red gate is not a small cosmetic
  problem: it is the difference between a regression suite and a suggestion
  box. Eleven baselines disagreeing with the renderer means the corpus cannot
  catch a new rendering regression, because it is already failing. And the
  assertion failure is the sharper half of the same defect: a scenario whose
  assertion cannot hold is not a regression test, it is a false claim that one
  exists. Restoring the gate re-arms every other scenario in the corpus.

- [x] **RT-309 (M, /settings OFFERED TWO ROWS WHOSE VALUES NOTHING READ) — a
  dead toggle, a dead number, and two live settings hidden behind the dead
  one.**
  The settings screen is the catalogue of what the operator can change, so a
  row it offers is a promise the app has to keep. Two of its rows broke that
  promise, and the mechanical sweep that found them is the one the skill
  prescribes for settings surfaces — "confirm the value is actually read by
  the code that applies it":

      config key                        read outside the settings screen?
      file_autocomplete_limit           yes — app/prompt.rs (the suggestion limit)
      file_autocomplete_show_hidden     yes — app/prompt.rs (the fuzzy walk)
      file_injection_enabled            NO — nothing reads it
      file_injection_max_size           NO — nothing reads it

  The two dead rows were:

      File injection (@)          Auto-inject @file references into message context.
      File injection max size     Max file size to auto-inject (KB, 0=no limit).

  and what the TUI actually does with an @-file reference is insert its
  PATH: the suggestion's text is the path, the agent reads the file with its
  own tools, and no code path injects a file's CONTENT anywhere (the only
  `read_to_string` calls in the TUI are the /file command, the history
  search, the banner, the external editor, the config and the auth store).
  So the operator could toggle the switch, edit the number, watch both
  persist into settings.json — the save path worked perfectly, which is why
  the defect was invisible for so long — and change nothing at all.

  **The second half is the sharper one.** `all_entries` pushed the two LIVE
  @-autocomplete rows — "File autocomplete limit" and "Show hidden files" —
  only when the dead toggle was on:

      // Only show these if file injection is enabled
      if screen.file_injection_enabled { entries.push(...) }

  so turning "File injection (@)" off hid the settings of a feature that
  kept working exactly as before (the limit and the hidden-files flag are
  read by `app/prompt.rs` on every suggestion refresh). An operator who
  tidied up the settings screen lost the ability to configure the @-mention
  behaviour they actually use.

  **Fixed**: the two dead rows are gone, together with the plumbing that
  existed only to serve them — the `apply_and_save` arms, the keyboard edit
  arm, the screen's own fields, and the two `InnerConfig` fields (so
  settings.json stops carrying keys for a feature that does not exist; an
  old file's keys are ignored by serde, which does not deny unknown
  fields). The two live rows are now unconditional.

  **Pinned** by two tests:
  `the_settings_screen_offers_no_row_nothing_reads` walks the screen's own
  row list — the dead keys must not be offered, the live ones must be — and
  `the_file_autocomplete_rows_apply` walks the operator's real path: edit
  the limit, save, and the value must land in the settings the app reads.
  The guard `every_settings_entry_has_an_applier` loses its second screen
  (there is no conditional branch left to check) and keeps its first.

  **The corpus never saw the rows either.** The settings screen shows its
  first thirteen rows and the @-rows sat at sixteen and below, under the fold,
  so the committed golden does not contain them at all — the corpus's
  settings-screen scenario could not have caught this defect, and this fix
  leaves that golden unchanged. The gap is named here rather than papered
  over: a settings surface whose interesting rows are below the fold is a
  scenario that needs a scrolling variant of its own.

  **Why the guard missed it, and what it still cannot catch.** The guard
  checks that every OFFERED row has an applier — that the operator's edit is
  not dropped on save — and both dead rows had one, so they passed it. A
  save-path guard cannot see a value that is saved and then never read; that
  is the other half of the defect class, and it is why the row list itself
  is now pinned.

- [x] **RT-310 (M, /settings OFFERED TWO DISPLAY FLAGS THE HEADER IGNORED) —
  a false claim, not a dead toggle, because the thing each row claims to
  control is on screen.**
  iter-1896 closed the first half of this family: two rows whose values
  NOTHING read, anywhere. This is the worse half — two rows whose values
  nothing read even though the surface they describe is the one painting
  right now:

      Row                       Claim                     What the header does
      Show current directory    hide the cwd row          paints it, always
      Show git branch           hide the branch suffix    paints it, always

  `build_header_lines_with_auth` (`crates/operant-cli/src/tui/operant_ui/
  ui_header.rs`) had exactly one condition on the row:

      if let Some(dir) = app.working_dir() { ... if let Some(branch) =
          app.git_branch() { ... } }

  `working_dir()` is `self.current_dir` (set once at startup from the process
  cwd) and `git_branch()` runs `git rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD` once at
  startup. Neither is asked what the operator chose — and the settings
  screen DOES offer both rows, persists them, round-trips them and displays
  their values, so the operator has every reason to believe they work.

  **Fixed**: the header reads the flags. Each is a tri-state
  (`Option<bool>`):

      show_cwd: None          -> shown  (a settings.json written before the
                                         field existed, or a fresh install)
      show_cwd: Some(false)   -> hidden
      show_cwd: Some(true)    -> shown

  `None` means shown because that is the rendering every earlier version
  had: a settings file predating the field must not silently lose the
  directory row because a new version started reading it. The screen's own
  literal defaults move to `true` so the row's displayed value and the
  rendering agree, `apply_settings_from_snapshot` reads through
  `unwrap_or(true)`, and both writers (the Enter applier and the keyboard
  toggle) persist `Some(on)`.

  **Live, not restart-gated.** `handle_settings_key` already ends with
  `*settings = screen.settings_snapshot.clone()`, so the App's live
  settings carry the screen's writes on the same frame; the only thing
  missing was a reader. No mirror in `key_handling.rs` and no dependence on
  `/reload` (which is the only other path that refreshes `self.settings`).

  **Pinned** by two behavioural tests:
  `the_headers_directory_row_obeys_the_settings_display_flags` drives the
  REAL render path — `build_header_sections`, the one the frame loop calls —
  with the two inputs set directly (the detection paths are not what this
  pins), asserting: absent shows both, `Some(false)` on the directory hides
  the row AND the branch (the branch is painted as part of the same row),
  each flag alone, and both back on. Mutation-proven by removing each gate
  in turn — both fail the pin by name.
  `toggling_show_current_directory_in_settings_reaches_the_app_live`
  drives the operator's real path through `handle_key_event` — open
  /settings, land on the row, press Enter — and asserts the App's live flag
  flips and the snapshot records it. It runs in a sandboxed HERMES_HOME:
  `SettingsScreen::new()` loads the ambient settings.json, and an earlier
  version of this test that did not sandbox flipped the flag the wrong way
  on a machine whose home directory held a settings file from a previous
  run.

  **The corpus's golden changes with this fix**, and that is the point:
  `settings-screen` now shows `true` for both rows instead of `false`,
  because the row finally describes the rendering.

- [x] **RT-312 (H, THE `send_message` CHUNKER PANICKED ON A MULTI-BYTE
  CHARACTER) — the panic took the turn with it.**
  The chunker searches for a split boundary by slicing backwards from a
  char boundary:

      &s[byte_off - 2..byte_off] == "\n\n"
      &s[byte_off - 1..byte_off] == "\n"
      &s[byte_off - 1..byte_off] == " "

  `byte_off` comes from `char_indices` (so it IS a char boundary), but
  `byte_off - 1` and `byte_off - 2` are not — when the preceding character
  is multi-byte ('é' is 2 bytes, '🚀' is 4), the slice PANICS with "start
  byte index N is not a char boundary". The trigger is ordinary: a
  message over the platform limit (Telegram >4096, Discord >2000, Slack
  >40000) whose split region contains a multi-byte character — the
  boundary walk reaches the character and the tool call panics.

  **Fixed**: the separators are ASCII, so the BYTES are compared instead of
  slicing (`bytes[byte_off - 1] == b'\n'`): no copy, no panic, and the
  boundary search is exact.

  **Pinned** by `chunk_message_does_not_panic_when_a_multibyte_char_precedes_a_boundary`:
  a message that starts with "é" and then 5000 ASCII characters (so the
  split region offers no newline or space and the boundary walk reaches
  the multi-byte character) must chunk without panicking, and every chunk
  must fit the limit. Mutation-proven: the byte slice back → the test
  panics with "start byte index 1 is not a char boundary; it is inside 'é'"
  — the defect itself.

- [x] **RT-313 (H, THE ADVISORY VIEW'S TOOL-RESULT CUTS BYTE-SLICED FREE TEXT — the panic took the recap/advisor loop with it) — the sixth site of the RT-301 class, in the one path the guard could not see.**
  The advisory view's head+tail preview of a tool result cut free text with a BYTE slice:

      out.push_str(&text[..half]);
      out.push_str(&text[text.len() - half..]);

  `text` is arbitrary tool output (file reads, git logs, web pages carry emoji, CJK and accented text), so byte 2000 — and byte `len - 2000` — is not a char boundary whenever a multi-byte character straddles it: the slice panics with "byte index 2000 is not a char boundary; it is inside '日'". RT-301 (iter-1883) fixed FIVE sites of exactly this class and pinned them with a source-grep contract over five files; `moa.rs` was not among them, which is why it survived to iter-1900. The panic lands inside a `tokio::spawn`ed task whose `JoinHandle` is discarded, so the gateway's idle-recap loop (attached unconditionally through `recap_idle_seconds`, default 240) and the advisor path die SILENTLY — no crash report, no note, just "recap never arrives".

  **Fixed**: the head cut uses the crate's own char-safe helper (`crate::agent::safe_truncate_str`) and the tail cut walks FORWARD to the next boundary (`text.len()` is always one, so the walk terminates). **The RT-301 guard gained its sixth case** (`moa.rs` / `&text[..half]`), so the class cannot return to this file.

  **Pinned** by `advisory_view_survives_a_multibyte_char_at_the_truncation_boundary` ("日".repeat(4000) = 12,000 bytes, both cuts mid-character — the pre-existing ASCII-only test passes on the defective code, this one cannot) — mutation-proven (the byte slice back → the test panics with "end byte index 2000 is not a char boundary; it is inside '日'" — the defect itself).

- [x] **RT-314 (H, A SLACK APP-LEVEL TOKEN BYPASSED THE ENTIRE REDACTION PIPELINE) — the pre-screen's own superset invariant was false for one token shape.**
  The pre-screen `needs_redaction` (`redaction.rs`) is a cheap needle-set short-circuit; its doc states the invariant:

      /// The needle set is a *superset* of every trigger the regexes can fire on
      /// … so a real secret is never skipped

  The 60-entry needle set carried `xox` (Slack bot/user tokens) but not `xapp` (Slack app-level tokens), while `patterns()`'s token-prefix regex has carried `xapp-\d+-[A-Za-z0-9-]{10,}` all along. `redact_sensitive_text` early-returns on a needle miss, so the token was emitted VERBATIM — to the model, the logs and the transcript, the exact class the module exists to prevent. The only second-chance pre-screen branch is the Telegram `<8-10 digits>:<35 chars>` shape, which an app-level token does not carry.

  **Fixed**: one needle (`"xapp"`) — the array's documented superset is whole again.

  **Pinned** two ways: `a_slack_app_level_token_is_redacted` (the behavior — the literal is built by concatenation so the repo's own scrubber cannot weaken it) and `every_token_prefix_has_a_prescreen_needle`, a structural contract that parses this file's own two arrays and asserts every token prefix in the regex has a needle that is a prefix of it — so the class cannot return for ANY future prefix. Both mutation-proven (the needle to a non-covering value → both fail by name).

- [x] **RT-315 (H, THE TOOL SCHEMAS ADVERTISED camelCase AND THE BODIES READ snake_case — a schema-following model could not use half the parameterized tools) — fixed once, at the ONE dispatch seam.**
  Tool argument structs are generated with `#[serde(rename_all = "camelCase")]`, so the schema the model reads advertises `sessionId` / `filePath` / `messageThreadId` / `entityId` — while the tool bodies read the snake_case field names with `args.get("session_id")` and friends. A model that followed the schema hit "Missing required parameter" on SIX tools, and three of them were worse than an error: `session_search`'s scroll mode was UNREACHABLE (it needs `around_message_id`, which only the snake spelling the schema never sends can supply — and its own schema test was vacuous, reading the wrong JSON key), `skills_tool`'s `filePath` silently returned the whole SKILL.md instead of the referenced file, and `checkpoint`'s `workingDir` fell back to the process CWD with `commitHash` to "", so `restore` ran `git checkout` against the WRONG tree. `home_assistant`'s `entityId` made `call_service` POST with NO entity_id, and `send_message`'s `messageThreadId` always dropped the Telegram forum-topic id.

  **Fixed at the ONE dispatch seam** — `normalize_arg_keys` (`tools.rs`) adds a camelCase key's snake_case twin in `execute_with_timeout`, so every tool reads the spelling its schema advertises: an explicit snake key always wins, and a no-uppercase args object is byte-identical, so the majority of tools (which never advertise camelCase) are untouched. `discord` was the INVERSE of the class — a hand-written snake_case schema with `rename_all` on the struct, so `from_value` silently dropped every advertised key and every parameterized action failed its required-param check — and its rename is gone, so the struct accepts its own wire contract.

  so `smtp.example.com:465` (the STANDARD implicit-TLS form, and exactly the host port that SMTP's own RFC advertises) is passed through as-is, gets a plaintext TCP connection, and the greeting read fails — producing a bare `"SMTP connect failed: …"` with no mention of the shape.
